en: The Śrī Śiva Mahāpurāṇa;
now begins the Vidyeśvara Saṃhitā of the Śrī Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Homage to the glorious gurus.
Salutation to Śrī Sarasvatī.
Now begins the first Saṃhitā, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, in the Śiva Purāṇa.

I meditate in my mind upon that Lord Śaṅkara, the Lord of Ambikā, who is auspicious from beginning to end, whose nature is unborn and equal, the noble one, ageless and immortal, the God of the Self; he who has five faces and whose nature is the powerful play of the five. (Śiva Purāṇa 1, Mangala, verses ab and cd) Chapter 1.
Vyāsa said: In the field of dharma, the great field, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Kālindī,
at Prayāga, the supreme and most meritorious place on the path to the world of Brahmā.
Sages of purified souls, devoted to the vow of truth,
possessed of great luster and great fortune, performed a great sacrificial session (*mahāsatra*).
Hearing of that sacrificial session there, the great sage who was a disciple of Vyāsa [arrived].

The Sūta, the best of Paurāṇikas, arrived to see the lord of sages. Seeing the Sūta approaching, the sages were then filled with joy; with very serene minds, they performed worship for him according to the prescribed rites.
Then those great-souled ones, well-pleased, having offered praise according to the prescribed rite with palms joined in reverence, spoke words connected with the Vinaya:
"O omniscient Romaharṣaṇa, it is indeed through the weight of our good fortune that you [have come]."
From Vyāsa you have received the entirety of the Purāṇic lore in its full detail;
therefore, you are indeed a vessel for these wondrous stories,
just as the ocean is the repository of jewels of great value.
Whatever has been, whatever is yet to be, and whatever other entity exists—
there is nothing in the three worlds unknown to you.
By the power of my prayer, you have come here for the purpose of seeing him.
Doing us some favor, you ought not to depart in vain.
We have already heard all that truth concerning what is auspicious and inauspicious;
yet we do not attain satiety, for our desire to hear it arises again and again.
"Now, O Sūta of noble mind, there is but one thing that remains to be heard;
tell us that secret as well, if you would grant us your favor.
For when the terrible Kali age has arrived, men will be devoid of merit."
All were devoted to wicked conduct and turned their backs on truthful speech;
they delighted in slandering others, coveted the property of others,
had their minds attached to the wives of others, and were intent upon harming others.
Fools with the view that the body is the self, atheists with the intellect of beasts,
hating their mother and father, regarding women as deities, slaves to passion;
Brahmins seized by the planet of greed, living by the sale of the Vedas.
Having mastered the sciences for the sake of acquiring wealth, they were deluded by pride; having abandoned the duties of their own caste, they were generally deceivers of others;
they were devoid of the twilight prayers performed at the three junctions of the day and were bereft of the awakening to Brahman.
Lacking compassion, considering themselves wise, and violating their own conduct and vows;
devoted to the toil of agriculture, cruel by nature, and impure in intention;
and likewise all the Kṣatriyas, habitually abandoning their own duty (svadharma).
They associate with the wicked, delight in sin, and are devoted to infidelity;
they are not brave, take pleasure in strife, and are intent on flight;
these Śūdras follow the conduct of base thieves, their minds enslaved by desire.
Deprived of the knowledge of weapons and missiles, neglecting cows and Brahmins,

and lacking both protectors and forests as refuges, they were like deer constantly pursued by female hunters; bereft of the true dharma of protecting their subjects, they were solely intent upon sensual enjoyment.
The wicked Vaiśyas will joyfully engage in the slaughter of living beings for the destruction of the people; devoid of purificatory rites, they will be habituated to abandoning their own duties,
following evil paths, intent on amassing wealth, and practicing dishonest dealings with the scales.
They are devoid of devotion toward their gurus, gods, and the twice-born, and possess wicked intellects;
generally, they fail to feed the twice-born, being miserly and tight-fisted;
and with impure intentions, they take delight in the company of women and paramours.
Those whose minds are agitated by greed and delusion, who have abandoned the excellent merits of public works and other virtuous deeds;
likewise, those śūdras who are intent on the conduct of brāhmaṇas—
fools of radiant appearance who are habituated to abandoning their own dharma.
They were further performers of austerities who robbed the splendor of the twice-born;
they brought about the early death of children and were devoted to the recitation of mantras;
they were worshippers of the Śīligrama-Śilā and others, and were intent upon the performance of fire-offerings (homa).
They will harbor hostile thoughts, be crooked, and revile the twice-born;

though wealthy, they will perform evil deeds, and though learned, they will be contentious. They will preach the worship [of deities] while proclaiming themselves as teachers of dharma, yet they will be destroyers of dharma.

Hypocrites who assume the appearance of the virtuous, great givers possessed by immense pride, considering themselves masters while regarding Brahmins and others as their servants— these fools are devoid of their own duty, creators of social confusion, and cruel-minded.

Constantly possessed of great pride, they were destroyers of the fourfold social order; considering themselves to be of noble birth, they excluded others from the four castes. These fools brought about the downfall of all classes, yet they performed virtuous deeds.
And women for the most part have fallen away, showing disrespect toward their husbands;
they commit acts of treachery against their fathers-in-law, are fearless, and eat impure food.
They are devoted to deceit and hypocrisy, are of evil conduct, and are overwhelmed by the god of love.
Constantly devoted to union with paramours, they likewise turn their backs on their own masters;
their sons are devoid of devotion toward mother and father, being evil-minded.
They are perpetually reciters of ignorance, their bodies consumed by disease.
"O Sūta, how can there be a destination for these people who have lost their understanding and are habituated to abandoning their own dharma, both in this world and in the next?
Indeed, our minds are constantly filled with such anxiety. (Śiva Purāṇa 1.1.35–36ab)
Indeed, there is no higher dharma than that which resembles helping others;
for by means of an easy method, the destruction of their great sins may occur immediately.
Therefore, out of compassion, please tell me now how one may come to know all the established doctrines.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of those sages of purified souls,
Sūta, having mentally remembered Śaṅkara, spoke to those sages.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Sages' Questions," in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Two.
Sūta said:
"Well asked, O virtuous ones! You who act for the welfare of the three worlds.
Having called to mind my Guru, I shall speak out of affection for you; listen to it with reverence.
This is the supreme Śiva Purāṇa, the very essence of the entire Vedānta."
It removes the flood of all sins, bestows the supreme goal in the hereafter,
and destroys the impurities of the Kali age; for in it,
O Brahmins, the supreme glory of Śiva always unfolds, granting the fruits of the four aims of life.
O best of the twice-born, by the mere study of this Purāṇa,
which is the most excellent of all Śaiva works, they shall attain a very good state;
meanwhile, sin— headed by the killing of a Brahmin— continues to expand.

Indeed, as long as the Śiva Purāṇa does not rise in the world, alas, so long will the great portents of the Kali age roam about without fear. Indeed, as long as the Śiva Purāṇa does not rise in the world, alas! ŚivP 1.2.5cd–6ab. ŚivP 1.2.6cd.
All the scriptures indeed dispute with one another as long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not risen in the world; until then,
the true nature of Śiva remains difficult to comprehend even for the great.

As long as the Śiva Purāṇa does not indeed arise in the world, alas, so long will the cruel servants of Yama roam about without fear. As long as the Śiva Purāṇa does not indeed arise in the world, alas! ŚivP 1.2.8cd–9ab. ŚivP 1.2.9cd.
All the Purāṇas indeed roar upon the surface of the earth only so long, alas,
as the Śiva Purāṇa has not risen in this world. All the sacred fords (tīrthas) likewise dispute upon the surface of the earth only so long.
Indeed, as long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not arisen in this world, O wonder,
all other mantras contend with one another upon the surface of the earth.
Indeed, as long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not arisen upon the surface of the earth...
All sacred fields on the surface of the earth will remain in dispute as long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not risen upon the earth; likewise,
all sacred seats (pīṭhas) on the surface of the earth will remain in dispute for that same duration.

For as long as the Śiva Purāṇa does not rise upon the surface of the earth, all other gifts shall continue to be disputed upon the earth. For as long as the Śiva Purāṇa does not rise upon the surface of the earth... [ŚivaP 1.2.14cd–15ab]. For as long as the Śiva Purāṇa does not rise upon the surface of the earth... [ŚivaP 1.2.15cd].
All those gods dispute upon the surface of the earth for as long as the Śiva Purāṇa has not arisen on the surface of the earth;
all philosophical systems likewise dispute upon the surface of the earth for that same duration.
"O twice-born ones, O best of sages, as long as this *Śivapurāṇa* has not indeed arisen upon the surface of the earth,
I am unable to describe in its entirety the fruit resulting from the recitation and hearing of this *Śaiva Purāṇa*."
Nevertheless, O sinless ones, I shall speak something of its majesty;
listen with focused minds to what was told to me long ago by Vyāsa.
For even a single verse or half a verse of this Śiva Purāṇa [is of great merit].

He who recites this with devotion is liberated from sin in an instant. Indeed, he who, being free from sloth, recites this Śiva Purāṇa every day according to his ability with devotion, is called one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Indeed, whoever always honors this Śiva Purāṇa with devotion obtains,
day by day, the fruit of the horse sacrifice without a doubt. Whoever [honors] this Śiva Purāṇa out of a desire for an ordinary station...

Even one who hears it from another shall be liberated from sin. Whoever pays homage to this *Śivapurāṇa* from even a short distance obtains the fruit of worshipping all the gods; of this there is no doubt.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of him who, having himself written this book of the Śiva Purāṇa, gives it to the devotees of Śiva;
[the merit] of one who has studied the treatises and the Vedas, and who has explained them.
Whatever fruit is difficult to attain in the world, that fruit shall accrue to him who,
having fasted on the fourteenth day,
expounds this Śiva Purāṇa in an assembly of devotees of Śiva; he is most excellent.
For every syllable, however, one shall obtain the fruit of the *gāyatrī-puraścaryā*;
having enjoyed all desires in this world, one shall attain liberation at the end.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day and remained awake during the night, [one attains this].
I shall declare the merit of one who either recites or even listens to this:
[the merit gained] many times at all the holy pilgrimage sites such as Kurukṣetra,
and [the merit of giving] wealth equal to one's own self during a solar eclipse that is visible everywhere.
Having given [this] to Brahmins headed by Vyāsa, one enjoys its great fruit;
that same fruit shall accrue to him who sings this Śiva Purāṇa day and night— this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
The gods, led by Indra, should await his command.
Indeed, for one who constantly reads or hears this Śiva Purāṇa,
whatever virtuous deed they perform shall become multiplied ten millionfold.
He who, being composed in meditation, recites the Śrī Rudrasaṃhitā there—
even if he is a slayer of a Brahmin— becomes a purified soul in just three days.
He who [recites] that Rudrasaṃhitā in the presence of an image of Bhairava...

If one recites it three times daily while observing silence, one shall obtain all desires. Whoever recites that Rudrasaṃhitā while performing circumambulation at a banyan tree or a bilva tree, the sin of killing a Brahmin is averted.
Beyond that, the Kailāsa-saṃhitā is remembered as even more supreme;
it is the very embodiment of Brahman and the illuminator of the meaning of the Praṇava.
Only Śaṅkara knows the majesty of the Kailāsa-saṃhitā.
O twice-born ones, Vyāsa knows half of that, and I know half of that;
I shall speak a small portion of it there, for it is not possible to tell it in its entirety.
By knowing which, people may attain purity of heart at that very moment.
O twice-born ones, that *Raudrī Saṃhitā* does not destroy whatever sin exists;
though I search for it constantly throughout the world, I do not see it,
even though it was joyfully produced by Śiva from the churning of the ocean of Upaniṣads.

By drinking that nectar offered to the Youth (Kumāra), one indeed becomes immortal. One who is intent on performing expiation for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin is liberated from them by reciting that Saṃhitā for just one month.

That *Saṃhitā* shall destroy, by its mere recitation, the sin arising from improper acceptance of gifts, unfit food, or wicked speech. Whoever recites that *Saṃhitā* in a temple of Śiva or in a grove of *bilva* trees— 43–44ab.
He obtains that fruit which is beyond even the range of speech.
He who, reciting this *Saṃhitā* with devotion, feeds the twice-born at a *śrāddha*,
all his ancestors go to the supreme abode of Śambhu.
He who, fasting on the fourteenth day, recites that Saṃhitā at the foot of a Bilva tree is worshipped by Śiva himself along with the gods. Furthermore,
any other Saṃhitā recited there bestows the fruit of all desires.
Both are distinguished and should be known as being filled with both *līlā* (divine play) and *vijñāna* (higher knowledge).
This *Śaiva Purāṇa*, equal to the Vedas, has been proclaimed;
it was created by Śiva himself as the first [Purāṇa], equal to the Brahman.
Likewise, the Vidyeśa, the Raudra, the Vaināyaka, and the Aumika;
the Mātra, the eleven Rudras, Kailāsa, and the Śatarudraka;
as well as the Koṭirudrasahasrādya and the Koṭirudra.
Due to their divisions, they are known as the Vāyavīya, the Dharmasaṃjñaka, and the Purāṇa;
these twelve Saṃhitās are considered to be most meritorious.
O Brahmins, listen with respect as I declare their total number in its entirety.
The Vidyeśa consists of ten thousand verses, as does the Rudra and the Vaināyaka;
likewise, the Auma and that known as the Mātṛpurāṇa each contain eight thousand verses, O twice-born ones. The Rudraikādaśaka, however, contains thirteen thousand verses.
The *Kailāsa* consists of six thousand verses, the *Śatarudra* half of that;
the *Koṭirudra* is three times eleven thousand,
and that which is called the *Sahasrakoṭirudra* is declared to have one million verses by way of its textual count.
The Vāyavīya consists of four hundred [verses], the Gharma of one thousand, and the Ravi of ten thousand;
thus, according to the various divisions of the Śaiva numbering, it totals one hundred thousand.
However, that was condensed by Vyāsa into twenty-four thousand verses.

The fourth among them is indeed the Śaiva Purāṇa, consisting of seven Saṃhitās. This Purāṇa was formerly intended for Śiva; at the time of the original creation, it measured one hundred crores [of verses], but it has since been largely forgotten.
In former times, during the Dvāpara and subsequent ages, the Purāṇa was divided eighteenfold;
then, when it was condensed by Dvaipāyana and others into four hundred thousand verses,
the Śiva Purāṇa was proclaimed as consisting of twenty-four thousand verses.
It consists of seven compendia (saṃhitās) totaling seventy thousand verses, equal in authority to the Vedas.
Among them, the first is known as the Vidyeśvara; the second should be known as the Raudrī;
the third is named the Śatarudra; and the fourth is the Koṭirudra.

The fifth is indeed named Mauma, the sixth is known as Kailāsa, and the seventh is called Vāyavīya; thus, seven Saṃhitās are recognized. This divine Purāṇa, consisting of these seven Saṃhitās, is designated as Śiva.
It abounds like Brahman, bestowing the highest state upon all;
indeed, he who reads this complete *Śivapurāṇa*, consisting of seven compendia, with devotion,
is said to be liberated while living.
Hundreds of Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Itihāsas,
and Āgamas do not equal even a small fraction of this Śiva Purāṇa.
That stainless Śaiva Purāṇa, proclaimed by Śiva himself, was not compiled by Vyāsa, who was devoted to the Śaiva tradition.

In brief, it is proclaimed here that the primary Dharma is free from deceit, consisting of the knowledge of Vedānta, which bestows welfare upon all living beings, destroys the threefold suffering, grants incomparable auspiciousness to the virtuous,
is understood by the wise within their hearts without envy, and is well-established as being endowed with the three aims of life.
This *Śiva Purāṇa* is indeed the ornament of the Purāṇas, a true Purāṇa that sings of the supreme reality shining forth in the Vedāntas and the Vedas.
Whoever reads or listens to it with supreme devotion shall indeed become dear to Śambhu and attain the highest goal.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Vidyēśvara Saṃhitā* in the glorious *Śiva Mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 3. Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Sūta, the supreme sages spoke to him.
"Recite the wonderful Purāṇa, which is the very essence of the entire Vedānta.
Having heard these words of the sages, Sūta was greatly delighted;
recollecting Śaṅkara, he spoke to the best of the sages.
Sūta said:
"Let all you sages listen, having called to mind the faultless Śiva—
the Śaiva Purāṇa, which is devoted to the Purāṇas and born from the essence of the Vedas."
Wherein the triad of devotion, knowledge, and dispassion is sung with love,
and the Reality that is to be known through the Vedānta is specifically described.
Sūta said:
"Let all the sages listen to this Purāṇa, which is born from the essence of the Vedas.
Long ago, after great time had passed and kalpas had repeatedly elapsed,
when this present kalpa arrived and the work of creation had begun..."
As the sages of the six lineages were speaking to one another,
"This is supreme" and "This is not," a very great dispute arose.
They went to the imperishable Creator, Brahmā, in order to question him.
With words imbued with humility, they all spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"For you are the sustainer of the entire world, the cause of all causes.
What person could be more ancient than all principles, higher than the highest?"
Brahmā said:
From whom words turn back, unable to reach Him along with the mind;
from whom all this proceeds, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra.
Together with all the co-existent sense organs, he is first brought forth.
This god is Mahādeva, the omniscient Lord of the universe.
He is perceived through supreme devotion; never otherwise.
Rudra, Hari, Hara, and likewise other lords of the gods, constantly desire to behold him with supreme devotion. What need is there for much speaking here? Through devotion to Śiva, one is liberated.
Devotion to the deity arises from grace, and grace is born of devotion;
just as here a seed comes from a sprout, or a sprout from a seed.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, go to the earth for the sake of the Lord’s grace.
"Perform for a thousand years this long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*).
By the grace of Śiva alone, the Lord of Sacrifice,
the essence of the knowledge declared in the Vedas— the means and the goal— shall be known."
The sages said:
"Now, what is the supreme goal to be attained, and what is that supreme means to it?
What kind of practitioner is required therein? Tell us this according to the truth."
Brahmā said:
The goal to be accomplished is the attainment of the state of Śiva; the means for that is service to Him.
The practitioner is one who, through His grace, is free from desire for transient fruits and the like.
Having performed the actions prescribed by the Vedas and offered them [to Him],
one attains the state of the Supreme Lord through the sequence beginning with *sālokya* and so forth;
thus, for all, the supreme fruit follows according to their respective degrees of devotion.
The means for accomplishing that [liberation] has been taught in many ways directly by the Lord;
having condensed them, I shall now proclaim to you the essence of those means.
[This consists of] listening to Him with the ear, as well as chanting His names with speech.
Mental reflection upon Him is declared to be the great means of accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*).
"Maheśvara is to be heard, celebrated, and reflected upon"—
this is our scriptural authority (*śrutipramāṇa*) for attaining the Supreme through this very means.
Go forth to accomplish your goal, being solely intent upon the means for achieving every purpose.
For in this world, people proceed after seeing with their own eyes what is perceptible;
indeed, they act everywhere based on what is imperceptible, having understood it through the ear.

Therefore, at the outset, the wise one should first hear [the teaching] from the mouth of the guru; thereafter, the intelligent person should accomplish the other stages: recitation and reflection. When this practice, culminating in reflection, has been properly accomplished in due order— ||| ŚivP_1,3.25ab || ŚivP_1,3.25cd || ŚivP_1,3.26ab |||

Through that, one becomes a Śivayogin; gradually, by means of the sequence beginning with *sālokya*, all diseases of the limbs subsequently dissolve, and all-bliss is absorbed. Indeed, through practice, this [state] is initially a hardship, but it is auspicious from beginning to end.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Sādhyasādhana-khaṇḍa of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa. The Sages said:
"O Brahman, what is the nature of reflection (*manana*), and what is the nature of hearing (*śravaṇa*)?
Or how is its glorification (*kīrtana*) performed? Please explain these things as they truly are.
Brahmā said:

That thorough purification of [the Lord’s] worship, recitation, qualities, form, pastimes, and names—performed with a mind that delights in logical reasoning—is constant contemplation (*manana*). Attainable through the vision of the Lord, it is the most preeminent among all excellent means of realization. Whether through song, Vedic verses, or common speech, it concerns the majesty, qualities, form, pastimes, and names of Śambhu.

That which is a clear and flavorful praise of Him through speech is *kīrtana*; that is considered the middling form of wealth in this context. When, by whatever means, a mass of sounds centered on Śiva is directed with great intensity toward the faculty of hearing—just like the playful attentiveness of a woman toward her lover—that, indeed, O wise ones, is the world-renowned *śravaṇa* here.
Through association with the virtuous, there first arises hearing [of the Lord], and then the glorification of Paśupati; thereafter, that [glorification] becomes firm.
Then comes reflection, which is the most excellent of all; for indeed, everything is possible when the glance of Śaṅkara falls upon one.
Sūta said:

O lords of sages, I shall relate to you an ancient account concerning the greatness of this means of accomplishment; listen with close attention. Formerly, my guru Vyāsa, the son of the sage Parāśara, [spoke thus].
Agitated, he performed austerities on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī. Then,
traveling by chance in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun,
the venerable Sanatkumāra beheld my preceptor there.
Having ascended into meditation and become awakened, he beheld that son of the Unborn (Aja). Prostrating himself, the sage, filled with great curiosity and agitation, spoke.
Having offered him the arghya water, he provided a seat worthy of a god.
The Lord, being pleased, spoke with a deep voice to him who was bowed before him.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O sage, you have meditated upon the true reality; it has come within the range of your direct perception."
"O Śiva, why do you perform austerities here alone and without a companion?
Thus addressed by Kumāra, the sage spoke of his own intention:
"Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are held in high regard within the path of the Vedas."
Thus, out of compassion for you, I have established [this teaching] in many ways throughout the world. Yet,
even though I am such as I am and am a teacher in every respect,
this most wonderful knowledge that is the means to liberation does not arise [in me].
"I perform penance for the sake of liberation, yet I do not know the cause for that.
Thus requested by the sage Vyāsa, the venerable Kumāra,
being capable, spoke, O best of Brahmins, the definitive cause of liberation.
"Hearing, chanting, and meditating upon Śambhu are the most excellent;
these three are declared as the means of attainment and are sanctioned by the Vedas.
Previously, however, I was deluded, being preoccupied with other means."
While I was performing austerities on the immovable Mount Mandara,
the blessed Lord Nandikeśvara arrived there by the command of Śiva.
That compassionate Lord, the witness of all, is the sovereign of the Gaṇas.

He spoke to me with affection regarding the supreme means for liberation: "Hearing of Śambhu, chanting his praises, and reflecting upon him according to the Vedas—this triad was taught by Śiva to me as the means for liberation. (Śiva Purāṇa 1.4.19–20ab)
"O Brahmin, perform the hearing [of this] and so forth," he said again and again.
Having spoken thus to Vyāsa, the son of Vidhi (Brahmā), accompanied by his followers,
then departed in his own celestial chariot to that most magnificent abode.
Thus has the supreme ancient account been told in brief.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, you have described the triad beginning with hearing as the means to liberation."
If one is incapable of the triad beginning with hearing [the scriptures], what must a person do to be liberated?
By what cause or by what action can liberation be attained without effort?
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Sādhyasādhanakhaṇḍa of the first Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 5. Sūta said:
One who is incapable of the triad beginning with hearing [the scriptures] should worship the Liṅga and the image (bera) of Śaṅkara. ŚivP 1.5.1ab.
Having established [the Liṅga] and worshipped it constantly, one shall cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
One should indeed carry wealth according to one's ability without deception,
and one should offer it for the sake of the Liṅga and the image (bera), and worship them continuously.
The pavilion, the gateway, the sacred ford, the monastery, the holy field, as well as the festival;
with devotion, [he offers] clothing, fragrance, garlands, incense, and lamps;
and various kinds of food as an offering, accompanied by cakes and side dishes.
One should maintain the parasol, the banner, the fan, and the chowrie,
along with all their accessories, for both the *liṅga* and the *bera* (image), just as one would perform royal services.
Likewise, one should perform circumambulation, prostration, and recitation according to one's capacity.
One should perform the daily rites with true devotion, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the dismissal (visarga).
Having thus worshipped the Lord Śiva in either his phallic form (liṅga) or his anthropomorphic image (bera),
one attains perfection through the grace of Śiva, even if one has abandoned such practices as listening to the scriptures (śravaṇa) and so forth.
"By the mere worship of the *liṅga* and the *bera*, the great men of old were liberated.
Manu and the others said:
"Indeed, in every case, the hosts of deities are worshipped in the form of the *bera* alone."
"And how is Śiva worshipped everywhere in the Liṅgas?
Sūta said:
"O lords of sages, this meritorious question is truly most wonderful!"
In this matter, the speaker is Mahādeva; there is no other person anywhere.
I shall proclaim what was spoken by Śiva, as heard in due order from the mouth of my guru.
Because he is of the nature of Brahman, Śiva alone is celebrated as being partless (*niṣkala*).
Because he possesses form, he is likewise possessed of parts; therefore, he is both with parts and without parts.
Because he is without parts, his *liṅga* is appropriately formless; because he possesses parts, his *bera* (image) is appropriately endowed with form.
Because he possesses both the forms of the manifest and the unmanifest, the Supreme is designated by the word "Brahman.
He is eternally worshipped by people both in the *liṅga* and in the *bera* (image).
Since others are not Brahman, they never possess the state of being partless (*niṣkala*).

Therefore, those lords of the gods are not worshipped in the partless *liṅga*; nor are the other hosts of deities worshipped there, because they lack the nature of Brahman and possess the nature of individual souls (*jīva*). However, [the deities] are worshipped in mere anthropomorphic forms (*bera*), for they consist only of the "manifested" (*sakala*) aspect and are [thus] silent [in their lower state].
The state of being the individual soul belongs to others than Śaṅkara, while the state of being Brahman belongs to Śaṅkara;
this is established by the essence of the Vedāntas through the illumination of the meaning of the Praṇava.
Thus indeed was Nandikeśvara questioned in the past on Mount Mandara.
By the wise sage Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā.
Sanatkumāra said:
[This concerns] all those who are subject to deities other than Śiva, in every respect.
An image (*bera*) is seen frequently for the purpose of worship, as is the *liṅga*;
yet, in the worship of Śiva alone, both the *liṅga* and the image are observed.
Therefore, O auspicious one, tell me that truth which provides perfect understanding.
Nandikeśvara said: O sinless one, I shall tell you this unsurpassed question, a secret concerning the characteristics of Brahman, as it was spoken by Śiva to you who are endowed with devotion.
Because Śiva is of the nature of Brahman and is partless (*niṣkala*), his *liṅga* is partless;
this is the consensus in all the Vedas regarding its worship. Furthermore, because he possesses parts (*sakala*), his *liṅga* is likewise both with parts and partless (*sakalaniṣkala*).
Furthermore, in worship, the *sakala* (with-form) image is approved by the world;
because others [the *niṣkala*] are living beings and because the *sakala* possesses form in every respect,
the mere image alone is accepted for worship according to the determination of the Vedas.
Indeed, upon the manifestation of the gods, the entire form of Śiva—
both his *liṅga* and his *bera* (image)— is truly seen in the vision. Sanatkumāra said:
"O illustrious one, you have explained the practice of the *liṅga* and the *bera*,
distinguishing between that of Śiva and others according to the ultimate truth.
Therefore, that alone is the supreme [reality] arising from the *liṅga*, the *bera*, and so forth."
"O Lord of Yogins, I wish to hear the characteristics of the manifestation of the Liṅga.
Nandikeśvara said:
"Listen, my child; out of affection for you, I shall speak according to the ultimate truth."
Long ago, in a great age that had arrived, renowned throughout the world,
the two high-souled ones, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, fought with one another.
To dispel their pride, the Supreme Lord stood between them.

He revealed his own form as a pillar that was partless (*niṣkala*). Then, because it was marked by his own *liṅga*, Śiva manifested his own *liṅga* from that pillar out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
From that time forward, among the worlds, the partless (niṣkala) emblem of the Lord was established as belonging to Śiva alone, and likewise his embodied (sakala) form; however,
for the gods other than Śiva, only an embodied form was established.
The respective *bera* (image) of each deity is auspicious and bestows its particular enjoyment;
the *liṅga-bera* nature of Śiva is auspicious and bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 6. Nandikeśvara said:
Once upon a time, O lord of yogis, Viṣṇu was seated upon a serpent-throne.

Surrounded by his own attendants, he slept with supreme splendor. Then Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, arrived there by chance and asked the lotus-eyed one about that most beautiful bed.
"Who are you that lie there like a man, even upon seeing me, acting so haughtily?
Arise, my child! Behold me, your protector, who has come here.
For he who, upon seeing his venerable guru arrived, should behave with such arrogance—"
"For that treacherous fool, an expiation is ordained.
Having heard these words, he became enraged, yet he behaved outwardly as if calm:
"Well-being to you! Welcome, my child; stay here and sit upon this seat."
"Why does your face, with its uneven eyes, shine like that of a tiger?
Brahmā said:
"O child Viṣṇu, the Great Pride has come upon you through the force of Time."
"And you are the grandfather of the world and its protector,
my dear child," Viṣṇu said. "For you, my child, imagine this entire world to be situated within me, like a thief."
"Born from the lotus of Manu's navel, you speak in vain.
Nandikeśvara said:
"While those two deluded ones were thus conversing there at that time, Ajā—"
"I alone am the bridegroom, not you; I am the lord, I am the lord!
Desiring thus to slay one another, they both made preparations for battle.
Those two immortal heroes, whose vehicles were the swan and the king of birds, fought together.
Then the Vairañcyas and the Vaiṣṇavas fought with one another; meanwhile,
all the classes of gods, traveling in their celestial chariots,
arrived, desiring to witness that most wonderful battle.
Showering rains of flowers while gazing freely at him in the sky,
he who has Suparṇa as his vehicle became enraged there and discharged many unbearable arrows and various kinds of weapons at the chest of Brahmā.
Then the enraged Brahmā discharged upon Viṣṇu’s chest unbearable arrows resembling fire,
as well as many weapons at that time. That spectacle of their combat was clearly a marvel to behold.
Having observed this, the hosts of deities, deeply distressed, offered their praise.
Then Viṣṇu, highly incensed and sighing, emaciated by his own misfortune,
the wise one, aimed the Māheśvara weapon at Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, becoming violently enraged and indeed causing the entire universe to tremble,
aimed the terrible Pāśupata weapon at Viṣṇu’s chest.
Then that [weapon] rose into the sky, resembling ten thousand suns.
With a thousand mouths, exceedingly fierce, and terrifying with its violent winds—
these two weapons there were formidable even to Brahmā and Viṣṇu. Thus did the battle between Brahmā and Viṣṇu unfold.
Then all the hosts of gods, despondent and deeply distressed,
spoke to one another, O dear one, like Brahmins during a royal upheaval:
"Creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace— "
"To that Brahman who possesses the trident, from whom [all this] proceeds;
for without his grace, it is impossible for others even to consume a blade of grass here by chance.
Having thus granted fearlessness to the gods, they searched for the abode of Śiva.
They went to the peak of Kailāsa where the Moon-crested Lord resides. Having thus seen that supreme abode of the Lord, the gods were filled with joy;
they prostrated before Him whose form is the Praṇava and entered that palace.
There, in the midst of that assembly hall within the pavilion, upon a jeweled seat,
they beheld the bull among gods shining together with Umā; his left foot was placed over the other, while her lotus-hand rested upon it.
He was attended on all sides by his own hosts, endowed with every auspicious mark;
he was being fanned by women born of various castes who possessed intense devotion,
while the Vedas were constantly praising him as the Lord bestowing grace.

Having thus seen the Lord, O child, the immortals and the great hosts of attendants, their eyes filled with the water of joy, prostrated themselves like a staff from afar. Beholding them, the Lord summoned those gods to his presence along with his attendants.

Then the God, the crest-jewel of the gods, gladdening the deities, spoke words that were profound in meaning and sweet with auspiciousness. Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Vidyeśvara Saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 7. The Lord said:
"O calves, may it be well with you; does all proceed according to my command?"
Is the world, which is the lineage of the deities, not already engaged in its respective duties?
O Asuras, the battle between Brahmā and Viṣṇu was already known to me;
it has been recounted by you merely out of excessive anxiety and redundancy.
Thus, with these sweet words spoken with a smile, he,
the husband of Ambā, satisfied both her and that host of gods.
Then, the Lord of Hari and Dhātṛ set out to go to the field of battle.
In that very assembly, he commanded a hundred lords of the Gaṇas. Then, for the departure of the Supreme Lord, various kinds of musical instruments were played;
and the lords of the Gaṇas, equipped with armor and adorned with diverse mounts and ornaments, [prepared themselves].

The Lord Īśvara, the husband of Ambikā, ascended the auspicious chariot, which was shaped like the syllable Om (praṇava), beginning and ending with it, and adorned with five circles. Indra and all the other gods followed him along with their sons and attendants.
Honored by multitudes of dancing, showers of flowers, variegated banners, fans, chowries, and various musical ensembles,
Paśupati, together with the supreme Goddess and his army, went to their battlefield.
Having observed their battle, he remained hidden, stationed upon a cloud.
The sound of the musical instruments ceased, and the clamor of the hosts of gods was stilled.
Then the two heroes, Brahmā and Acyuta, desiring to slay one another,
[armed themselves] with the Māheśvara weapon and likewise the Pāśupata weapon.
Then the three worlds of Brahmā and Viṣṇu were scorched by the flames of the missiles.
Seeing that premature and terrible dissolution, Īśvara himself,
who is partless (niṣkala), assumed a terrifying form like a great pillar of fire in the midst of it.
Those two blazing missiles, capable of destroying the world,
fell down in an instant, for the great fire had indeed manifested;
seeing that wonderful, marvelous, and auspicious pacification of the weapons, they were amazed.
"What is this of such wondrous form? they said to one another.
"What is this pillar, appearing like fire, that has arisen beyond the reach of the senses?
Indeed, its upper and lower limits are visible only to us two."

Thus resolved, the two heroes, who prided themselves on their valor, met together; intent upon that [task] and desiring to test it, they then set out with haste. "If we are joined together there, a single purpose cannot be achieved."
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu, in the form of a boar, went to its beginning;
likewise, I, Brahmā, in embodied form, went to see its end.
Having pierced through the abode of Pātāla, Hari traveled a very great distance.
Nor could the form of that pillar, which possessed the brilliance of fire, be discerned.
Exhausted, that boar-emanation reached the front of the battlefield as before.
Then, O dear one, your father Brahmā was traveling through the sky.

He beheld a wondrous *ketakī* flower that had slightly fallen away— exceedingly fragrant, unfading, and yet as if it had fallen many years ago. And having observed the conduct of those two, the Blessed Lord Parameśvara [reflected].
Out of jest, he shook his head, causing it to move;
therefore, to show favor to that fallen, excellent *ketaka* flower, [Śiva said]:
"O Lord of Flowers, why do you fall? By whom were you held? (ŚivP 1.7.21–22ab).
"I have long fallen from the middle of the pillar of that primordial, immeasurable one; therefore, I do not perceive him. For this reason, abandon your hope for seeing him.
To serve him here, I have come in the form of a swan."
"Friend, from now on you must do what I desire today:
you must speak this together with me in the presence of Viṣṇu. 'The pillar was seen by the Creator; I am the witness there, O Acyuta.'"
Having spoken thus, he bowed again there to the *ketaka* flower.
"Even that which is untrue may be commendable in times of distress," such is the traditional teaching.
Observing Acyuta there, his efforts exhausted and his joy vanished, he danced with delight.
Then that Creator, whose speech was like that of a eunuch, spoke to Acyuta regarding the supreme truth:
"O Hari, this very top of the pillar is being observed; indeed, this ketaka flower is the witness right there.
Thereupon, in his presence, the ketaka spoke falsely in agreement with the words of its creator, saying, "So it is."
Hari, reflecting as it were that this was indeed true, himself offered salutations to that Brahmā;
he then worshipped that Brahmā with the sixteen types of ritual offerings. To strike down that deceitful Brahmā, the Lord manifested there in person from within the fire-liṅga.
Rising up again upon beholding his master, with trembling hands he grasped his feet.
"O You whose form is without beginning or end, let no further reflection born of desire arise here through the deluded intellect.
Be gracious, O Mine of Compassion; forgive this impurity of ours, which was brought about by You Yourself in sport."
Īśvara said:
"O child Hara, I am pleased with you because, even though you desire lordship, you have spoken words of truth.
Therefore, among people, there shall be equality between you and me; you have also requested honor."
"From now on, you shall have a separate self, as well as the establishment, festivals, and worship of your own sacred field (*kṣetra*).
Thus, in former times, the Lord, being highly pleased by Satya’s truthfulness,
granted him a state of extreme equality with Himself while the assembly of gods looked on.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Eight. Nandikeśvara said:
Then Mahādeva, desiring to destroy the pride of Brahmā, created from the middle of his eyebrows a certain wondrous being named Bhairava. At that time,
he indeed prostrated before the Lord Śiva there in the courtyard.
"O Lord, command me quickly: what task shall I perform here?
This child is Brahmā himself, the primordial deity of the worlds;
surely you should worship your own sword with supreme, sharp speed."
Seizing that fifth hair, which was arrogant and characterized by false speech, with one hand, he—
shaking his sword very clearly in his hands— prepared to strike off his heads.
Your father [Śiva], having cast off his ornaments, garments, garlands, upper cloths, and mass of pure hair...
Trembling like a creeper at the onset of a strong wind, he fell indeed at the lotus-feet of Bhairava.
At that moment, O dear one, Acyuta, desiring to see Brahmā and being compassionate toward the sprout-like feet of our Lord,
drenched them with tears and spoke with joined palms in soft, childlike words, as a son would to his own father.
Acyuta said:
"Since you previously bestowed upon him this five-faced head, the emblem of the Lord, through your own effort, therefore forgive him now; he is worthy of grace, so show favor toward this Vidhi."

Thus entreated by Acyuta, the Lord, being pleased in the assembly of the hosts of gods, then withdrew Bhairava from the Brahma-staff (*brahmadaṇḍa*). Then the God spoke to the deceitful Vidhi, whose neck was severed:
"O Brahmā, desiring honor for yourself, you have deceitfully assumed lordship.
Therefore, no hospitality, nor any festival for your station and such, shall be granted to you in this world.
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of great majesty, be gracious today! O Giver of Boons, I consider the release of my head to be a blessing.
Salutations to you, the Blessed One, the kinsman, the source of the universe;
to the endurer of all faults, to Śambhu, whose bow is made of rock."
The Lord said: "Without the fear of a king, this entire world will surely perish.
Therefore, O child, slay those deserving of punishment and bear the burden of the world."
"I grant you a boon; accept this supreme and rare gift.
In the rites of the Vedas, the domestic rituals, and the sacrifices, you shall be the preceptor.
Without you, a sacrifice—even if complete in its parts and accompanied by sacrificial fees—is fruitless."
Then the God spoke to the deceitful gambler Ketaka:
"O Ketaka, you are wicked! You rogue, go far away from here!
Let there be no love for me even for your flower; let there be no worship of it from now on."
When this was said by the Lord, all the divine classes then warded off the *ketaka* from his side and moved it elsewhere. The *ketaka* said:
Salutations to you, O Lord! By your command, let my birth, which has been fruitless, be made fruitful;
O Father, may my transgression be forgiven.
Your mere remembrance destroys the sin committed through both knowledge and ignorance.
"When someone like you is seen by me, how could there be any fault of falsehood?
Thus praised by Ketaka in the assembly hall, the Blessed One said:
'It is not fitting for me to wear you; I am the Lord whose word is truth.'"
"I shall bear you; thus your birth will be fruitful.
Indeed, under the pretext of being a canopy, you shall be over me.
Having thus blessed the Ketaka flower, the Blessed One [Śiva] [dismissed] Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
He shone in the midst of the assembly, being praised by all the gods.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 9.
Nandikeśvara said:
In the meantime, Vidhi and Mādhava, having bowed to the Lord,
stood silently with their palms joined in reverence, positioned to his right and left.

Having seated the God together with his family upon an excellent throne there, they two worshipped the worshipful one with meritorious human offerings. Human and natural objects should be known as being of either long or short duration.
With necklaces, anklets, armlets, crowns, and jeweled earrings;
with sacred threads, upper garments, garlands, silken cloths, flower wreaths, and finger-rings;
and with flowers, betel, camphor, sandalwood, and the application of agallochum.
With incense, lamps, white umbrellas, fans, banners, and chowries,
and with other divine offerings whose majesty transcends speech and mind—
offerings worthy of a husband and unattainable by bound souls— they both worshipped their Lord.
Whatever object was most excellent and suitable for his consort, the Lord,
desiring to bring them all to completion,
joyfully bestowed each of those things upon the members of the assembly there in due order.
A great clamor arose there from those who were seizing that object. Long ago, at that very place, Śaṅkara was worshipped by Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
being pleased, the increaser of devotion spoke with a smile to the two of them as they bowed before him.
The Lord said:
"I am pleased today with you both, my children, because of your worship on this great day.
Therefore, this day shall become most exceedingly meritorious."
This lunar day, known as Śivarātri, is dear to me.
If a man performs worship of my liṅga and image at this time,
he shall perform the task of the universe, such as its maintenance and creation.
On Śivarātri, fasting for a full day and night with senses subdued,
one who is free from deceit should worship according to the prescribed rule and according to one's ability.
Whatever fruit is obtained from my worship performed continuously for one year, [that same fruit is gained by this].

One obtains that fruit immediately by worshipping me on Śivarātri. This is a time for the increase of my dharma, like the waxing moon for the ocean; it is a festival beginning with consecration, wherein my auspicious path resides.
Furthermore, that time when I formerly manifested myself in the form of a pillar was during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, under the asterism Ārdrā,
O children. Whoever beholds me, the consort of Umā, in Mārgaśīrṣa under the asterism Ārdrā—
Even one who worships my linga made of mud is dearer to me than Guha;
on that auspicious day, the mere sight of it yields sufficient fruit,
while worshiping it brings even greater fruit beyond the reach of words.
"Since I have expanded upon this surface of the battlefield in the form of a *liṅga*,
just like a *liṅga* itself, therefore this shall become a *liṅga-sthāna*.
This pillar, beginningless and endless, shall exist as minute as an atom."
For he is indeed for the sake of the worlds’ vision and for their worship;
this Liṅga brings about enjoyment and is the sole means for both worldly experience and liberation.
Through seeing, touching, and meditating upon it, living beings are released from birth.
"This linga that has arisen,
resembling a mountain of fire, shall indeed attain renown as Aruṇācala.
And here, a most magnificent sacred bathing place (tīrtha) shall come into being in many forms."

In this place, liberation is attained by living beings both through residing here and through death. Furthermore, all auspicious events such as festivals and the like, as well as the dwellings of people, exist everywhere here. Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, or chanted here becomes ten million times more meritorious.
This field is even greater than all my other fields;
by merely remembering it here, embodied beings attain liberation.
Therefore, this field is most excellent and exceedingly magnificent.
Having worshipped me here— the Lord who possesses the *liṅga*— within this *liṅga*, which is complete with all auspiciousness, brings about all liberation, and is pure,
one attains *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, and *sārṣṭi*.
"Union (sāyujya)—these five are considered the fruits of ritual action and the rest.
All of you shall quickly attain every desire in its entirety.
Nandikeśvara said:
Having thus favored Vidhi and Mādhava, who were now disciplined,
the Blessed One raised up with the stream of nectar from his own power their respective armies that had previously been struck down in battle.
To dispel their poverty and enmity, he said to them:
"I possess two forms, the *sakala* (with parts) and the *niṣkala* (without parts).
This belongs to no one else; therefore, everyone other than me is not the Supreme Lord (*anīśvara*)."
In front, in the form of a pillar, and behind, in the form of two children—
Brahmanhood is declared to be partless (niṣkala), while lordship (īśatva) is likewise possessed of parts (sakala).
This twofold nature is established as belonging to me alone, and to no one other than me.
Therefore, sovereignty belongs neither to others nor to you two anywhere.
Out of ignorance, this most extraordinary assumption of lordship has been acted upon by you;
it is for the sake of refuting that very thing that I have arisen here on the field of battle.
Abandon your pride and set your minds upon me, the Lord.
By my grace, every purpose in the worlds shall be revealed.
In this regard, the word of the Guru is the manifesting authority, again and again.
Out of affection for you, I shall declare this secret reality of Brahman:
I alone am the Supreme Brahman; my own nature is both the manifest and the unmanifest. Because of my state as Brahman, I am the Lord (Īśvara), and my function consists of grace and the like.
Because of my vastness and because of my nourishing power, I am Brahmā; O Brahmā and Keśava, I am [also] you both.
Because of my equanimity and because of my pervasiveness, likewise, O children, I am the Self (Ātman).
All others are non-Selves (anātman); they are merely individual souls (jīva), of this there is no doubt.

The lotus, which is the first limb of creation consisting of grace and so forth, is my eternal world-activity arising solely from my lordship, and not that of anyone other than me. At the beginning, for the purpose of establishing the consciousness of Brahma-hood, the partless *liṅga* arose.

Therefore, in order to manifest clearly to you both that my lordship was previously unknown, I have become the "Sakala" (the embodied one) at that very moment; thus, my lordship should be understood as being "sakalatva" (embodied state). Śiva Purāṇa 1.9.40–41ab.
"This is my stainless pillar, which makes known my status as Brahmā;
because it possesses the characteristics of a *liṅga*, this shall be my *liṅga*.
Therefore, my two sons, you must worship this constantly here."

This [liṅga] is eternally of my own nature and the cause of my presence; it is always to be worshipped as great, because of the non-difference between the liṅga and its possessor (the deity). Wherever such a liṅga of mine is installed by anyone, [there I am present].
Established therein, O dear ones, I am established even though I am without foundation. It is declared that the fruit of installing a single *liṅga* is equality with me;
indeed, when a second *liṅga* is installed, the fruit is identity with me.
"The Liṅga should be established as the primary [object of worship], while the image (bera) is secondary.
Without a Liṅga, that sacred field (kṣetra), even if it contains an image, is deficient in every respect.
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 10.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu said:
"O Lord, tell us the characteristics of the fivefold duties beginning with creation."
Śiva said:
Out of compassion, I shall explain to you both the secret of my functions:
creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace.

My fivefold world-activity is eternally established in the unborn and infallible [Śiva]. Emanation is the exertion of worldly existence; its maintenance is considered to be stability. Withdrawal is its crushing, and concealment is its departure from that state.
Liberation from that [bondage] is grace; thus, my fivefold duty is as follows:
another bears this duty silently, like the image on a city gate.
The fourfold duty beginning with creation is the expansion of worldly existence.
The fifth is indeed the cause of liberation, eternally and firmly established within me.
This very [cause] is perceived among the five elements by my devotees:
creation in earth, maintenance in water, and likewise dissolution in fire.
Concealment occurs in the wind, and likewise, grace occurs here in the ether;
everything is created by the earth, everything grows by the waters,
everything is dried up by fire, and it is carried away by the wind.
For in this way, all that is to be known is sustained by the sky; indeed, the wise understand it thus.
To comprehend these fivefold acts, I possess five faces:
four faces in the four directions, and the fifth face in their midst.

"O sons, these two tasks— creation and preservation, which are dearer to me than anything else— have been obtained by you through your ascetic penance from me, who am pleased. Likewise, there are two other supreme tasks for Rudra and Maheśa."
Indeed, that which is called grace cannot be obtained by anyone at all.
All that former karma of yours has been forgotten due to the passage of time;
yet, O Rudra, such karma was never forgotten by Maheśa.
"In appearance, dress, action, vehicle, and likewise in seat,
as well as in weapons and so forth, we have granted him equality with me. Yet,
O dear ones, because of the absence of meditation upon me, such delusion has come upon you both."

If there were knowledge of the self, such pride would not exist, as in the case of Maheśvara regarding his form. Therefore, for the sake of attaining knowledge of the self, recite from now on this mantra of mine named Oṃkāra, which shatters pride.
I taught him my own mantra, the syllable Oṃ, which is of great auspiciousness.
The syllable Oṃ was born from my mouth as the first awakening of me;
it is the designator (vācaka), and I am that which is designated (vācya), for this mantra is identical with my own self.
The constant recollection of that [Oṃ] shall be the recollection of me.
The letter *A* comes from the northern face, the letter *U* from the western face,
the letter *M* from the southern face, and likewise the Bindu from the eastern face.
Thus, this *nāda* unfolds in five ways from the central opening;
then, becoming unified once more, it becomes the single syllable "Om.
All that consists of name and form—the two classes of beings and the Vedas—is [contained therein].
Pervaded by this mantra, it is the awakener of both Śiva and Śakti.
From this [mantra], the five-syllabled [mantra] was born, which awakens all things;
it follows the sequence beginning with the letter *ā* and likewise the sequence beginning with the letter *na*.

From this five-syllabled [mantra], the Mātṛkās were born in fivefold divisions. From that head with four faces, the entire Veda was indeed produced three times; from that, millions of mantras were born.
Through its respective mantra, that specific attainment is achieved; from this, all attainments arise.
By means of this root-mantra (mantrakanda), both worldly enjoyment and liberation are accomplished.
All the auspicious kings of mantras directly bestow enjoyment.
Nandikeśvara said:
Then, having again placed a curtain between them there, the Guru imparted the supreme mantra.
Having slowly placed his lotus-hand upon their heads as they stood facing north, he did so together with Ambikā.
Having recited the mantra three times according to the rules of the *yantras* and *tantras*,
those two disciples offered themselves as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). With hands joined in reverence, they indeed approached that very God, the Teacher of the World, and spoke to him.
Brahmā and Acyuta said: "Salutations to you whose form is partless; salutations to you whose splendor is partless.
Salutations to the Lord of all; salutations to you, the soul of all."
Salutations to the one expressed by the *praṇava*, salutations to the one whose symbol is the *praṇava*;
salutations to the creator of the world and its origins, and salutations to the one who possesses five faces.
Salutation to you who are the embodiment of the five Brahmans and who perform the five cosmic acts;
salutation to you, the Self, the Brahman, possessed of infinite qualities and powers;
salutation to Śambhu, the Guru, who takes both manifest and unmanifest forms.
Having thus praised the Guru with verses, Brahmā and Viṣṇu bowed down. The Lord said:
"O dear children, the entire truth has been told and demonstrated to you."
Chant the Praṇava mantra as instructed by the Goddess, which is identical with my own self;

then knowledge shall become well-firm, and all fortune shall be eternal. Furthermore, when that same mantra is chanted under the constellation Ārdrā on the fourteenth lunar day, it becomes inexhaustible.

By the movement of the sun, when it is in Mahārdrā, [the merit] becomes ten millionfold. The final portion of Mṛgaśīrṣa as well as the initial portion of Punarvasu should always be known as equal to Ārdrā for worship, fire-oblations, and libations.

The viewing [of the deity] should take place at dawn, during the morning, and during the *saṃgava* period. Likewise, the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) should be accepted when it extends through the midnight hour; it is highly praised when it extends through the evening (*pradoṣa*) and is joined with the following day.

The *liṅga* and the *bera* (image) are equal for those who worship; however, for those seeking liberation, the supreme *liṅga* is to be worshipped even more than the *bera*. The *liṅga* is worshipped with the *oṃkāra* mantra, while the *bera* is worshipped with the five-syllabled (*pañcākṣara*) mantra.

"Indeed, having installed [the image] oneself with ritual substances, or even having it installed by others, one should worship it with the various offerings; thus my state shall become easily attainable.
Having thus instructed his two disciples, Śiva vanished on that very spot.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Eleven.
The Sages said:
How is the *liṅga* to be installed, and what are its characteristics?
How indeed should it be worshipped, in which place and at what time, and by whom?
Sūta said:
I shall speak for your sake; understand this with focused attention.
At an auspicious and favorable time, and likewise at a holy pilgrimage site or on a riverbank, one should install a *liṅga* as desired, where there may be perpetual worship.
Furthermore, by means of an earthen or a metallic [liṅga] according to one's preference—
one endowed with the characteristics of a *kalpa*— one shall obtain the fruit of worship.
A [liṅga] endowed with all characteristics bestows the fruit of worship immediately.
In the mobile [world] it is subtle, while in the immobile it is indeed gross;
one should install that which was fashioned by Śiva, complete with its characteristics and its pedestal.
The mandala may be square or likewise triangular.

Like the central shaft of a bedstead, a subtle linga-pīṭha yields great fruit. First, a linga made from clay, stone, and so forth, or fashioned from metals and other materials—whichever material the linga is made of, by that same material the pīṭha should be made; indeed, this is especially recommended for a stationary (sthāvara) installation.
In the case of a mobile linga, there should be only one pedestal, except for those made of stone (bāṇakṛta).
For those who fashion the lingas, the best measurement is twelve finger-breadths;
if it is smaller, the fruit will be meager, but if it is larger, it is not at all defective.
The *cara* [shrine] should likewise be one finger less than the *kartṛ* [the maker’s span].
First, the temple (*vimāna*) must be constructed by craftsmen, adorned with the assembly of deities.
Therein, within a beautiful and firm inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), it should be decorated like a mirror.
And at the gates of the directions, he [adorned them] with the nine principal gems:
blue sapphire, ruby, lapis lazuli, dark emerald, pearl, coral, hessonite, and diamond; these constitute the nine gems.
In the center, one should deposit the great substance, the *liṅga*, together with the Vedic [mantras].
Having worshipped the *liṅga* in the five locations in due order with the [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta,
and having offered oblations in many ways with clarified butter into the fire, [one should worship] me, who am partless (*niṣkala*).
Having honored his guru and preceptor with wealth and desired objects, as well as his kinsmen;
he should bestow sovereignty upon those who seek it, whether they be insentient or sentient.
Having diligently satisfied every living being, both stationary and moving, [he should proceed].
In a pit filled with gold and filled with the nine jewels,
having uttered the Brahman-mantras beginning with "Sadyojāta" and meditated upon the supreme, auspicious Deity,
he should recite the great mantra, the syllable Om, resonating with the sound of *nāda*.

Having installed the *liṅga* there, one should join the *liṅga* with its pedestal (*pīṭha*). Having set down the *liṅga* together with its pedestal, one should bind it with a permanent coating (*nityalepa*).
In this same manner, the most auspicious image (*bera*) should be installed in that very place.
One should likewise fashion an image with five syllables for the purpose of a festival outside;
or one may receive an image that has been worshipped by virtuous gurus.
In this way, worship performed toward both the *liṅga* and the *bera* bestows the state of Śiva.
Furthermore, it is said to be of two kinds: the stationary (sthāvara) and likewise the moving (jaṅgama).
They say that the stationary is the *liṅga*, as well as trees, shrubs, and so forth;
they say that the moving is the *liṅga*, as well as worms, insects, and so forth.
The wise know that the worship of Śiva consists of service toward the immobile and the gratification of the mobile,
performed with devotion to their respective joys.
The entire seat (pīṭha) is composed of Ambā, and the Śiva-liṅga is composed of consciousness (cinmaya).
Just as Śaṅkara remains holding Queen Umā upon his lap,
so too does he remain constantly holding this Liṅga upon its pedestal.
Having thus installed the Great Liṅga, one should worship it with ritual offerings.
Just as one performs daily worship and constructs a banner or other such items,
so too should one consecrate a *liṅga* that directly bestows the state of Śiva;
or else, one may worship a mobile *liṅga* with the sixteen types of ritual offerings (*upacāra*).
And one should worship according to the rule, in due order, that which bestows the state of Śiva:
the invocation (āvāhana), the seat (āsana), the water for honor (arghya), and likewise the water for the feet (pādya);
then the sipping of water (ācamana) as part of those limbs, and the bath preceded by anointing with oil (abhyaṅga).
Garment, perfume, as well as flowers, incense, a lamp, and an offering;
the waving of lights, betel, prostration, and the dismissal;
or else, having performed the offering of water (arghya) and so forth, [one should offer] the food offering (naivedya) according to the rule.
Then, one should always perform the consecration, the offering of food, prostration, and libation according to one's ability; these, performed in due order, bestow the state of Śiva.
Alternatively, [one may do so] at a human-made linga, or at one made by sages, or at a divine one, or at a self-manifested one.
When a previously unestablished *liṅga* has been installed,
whatever fruit one enjoys by offering articles of worship with due ceremony,
through circumambulations and prostrations, it bestows the state of Śiva in due course.
Even the mere sight of a *liṅga* invariably bestows auspiciousness (*śiva*).
It may be made of clay, flour, cow dung, flowers, or *karavīra* blossoms and fruits;
or it may be made of jaggery, fresh butter, ashes, or food offerings, according to one's preference.
Having fashioned a liṅga with effort, one should worship it at the end according to that [prescribed] method.
Some maintain that worship may likewise be performed even on the thumb and other parts of the body.
In all matters concerning the liṅga, there is never any prohibition whatsoever.
For Śiva indeed bestows fruit everywhere in accordance with the effort expended. Alternatively, the gift of a *liṅga*, or even the value of a *liṅga*,
when given with faith to a devotee of Śiva, grants the state of Śiva.
Alternatively, one should constantly recite the *praṇava* ten thousand times;

or at the two junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*), it should be known that reciting it a thousand times bestows the state of Śiva. At the time of recitation, one should practice the form ending in the letter *m*, which purifies the mind.

Mental recitation is prescribed during meditative absorption (*samādhi*), while whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) is for all other times. They know this [mantra] to consist of the *samāna* and the *praṇava*, joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*. Then, one should constantly recite the five-syllabled mantra ten thousand times with devotion.
Or, at the two twilights, one thousand [recitations] should be known as bestowing the state of Śiva.
For Brahmins, it is especially distinguished when joined with the *praṇava* (OM) at the beginning.
Furthermore, for the attainment of results, the mantra should be received from a guru who is endowed with initiation (*dīkṣā*).
The ritual bath with the water-pot (*kuṃbhasnāna*), initiation into the mantras, and the ritual placement of the *mātṛkā*—
a Brāhmaṇa whose soul is purified by truth and who possesses knowledge is distinguished as the preceptor (*guru*).
For the twice-born, [the mantra] begins with "namaḥ," while for others, it ends with "namaḥ."
And some desire that for women,
as well as for Brahmin women, this [mantra] preceded by "namas" should be recited according to the rule;
having performed five crores of recitations, one becomes equal to Sadāśiva.

One shall attain the station of Brahmā and the other gods through one, two, three, or four crores [of recitations]. Alternatively, one may recite each syllable individually for one hundred thousand times; indeed, it should be known that reciting a hundred thousand syllables bestows the state of Śiva.

Indeed, by reciting [the mantra] one thousand times for each of a thousand [days] over the course of a thousand days, one attains the desired success; this is achieved through the daily feeding of Brāhmaṇas. One should indeed recite the Gāyatrī one thousand and eight times every morning.
A Brahmin, however, should daily recite the Vedic mantras and hymns that bestow the state of Śiva in due order,
remaining established in his observances;
he should recite at least one mantra of ten syllables, or more than a hundred.
One hundred thousand, one thousand, and one hundred [recitations] would be required;

indeed, the complete recitation of the Vedas (vedapārāyaṇa) should be known as that which bestows the state of Śiva. One should mutter other numerous mantras until a hundred thousand syllables have been reached.
One should likewise recite monosyllabic mantras for ten million syllables;
thereafter, one should recite them a thousand times with devotion.
One should act in this manner according to one's capacity, and through this sequence, one shall attain the state of Śiva.
One should constantly recite, until the end of one's life, this single mantra that is pleasing to the heart—
"Om"— a thousand times, for the fulfillment of all desires by the command of Śiva.
Likewise, one should perform tasks such as tending flower gardens or sweeping [the temple grounds].
Having performed [this] for the sake of Śiva and for the purpose of Śiva’s work, one shall attain the state of Śiva.
Likewise, one should always dwell with devotion in a sacred field of Śiva (śivakṣetra),
which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon all beings, whether insentient or sentient.
Therefore, a wise person should reside in a sacred field of Śiva until death.
They know that in a human sacred field, the area within a hundred cubits of the Liṅga is meritorious;
likewise, in a sacred field of the Ṛṣis, it extends for a thousand *aratnis*.
Likewise, it should be known that at a *daivaliṅga*, the sacred area extends for a thousand *aratnis*;
in a holy field (*puṇyakṣetra*) on the earth itself, it is a thousand *dhanus*.
Furthermore, ponds, wells, and other reservoirs situated within a holy field [confer merit].
It should be known as the Śivagaṅgā, according to the word of Śiva.
Having bathed there, likewise having given gifts, and having recited prayers, one shall indeed go to Śiva.
Having taken refuge in the sacred field of Śiva (Śivakṣetra), one may dwell there until death.
Whether it be on the tenth day, on the anniversary of death, or during the month, or even at the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
or at the annual anniversary (*ābdika*), or by offering a funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) in a sacred field of Śiva—
being liberated from all sins, one shall immediately attain the state of Śiva.

Alternatively, one may stay for seven nights, or five nights, or three nights, or even a single night; in due order, one shall attain the state of Śiva. In this world, a person attains [their goal] through conduct consistent with their own caste and through their own observances.
By means of the extraction of the phonemes (*varṇoddhāra*) and through devotion, a person obtains the excellence of its fruit;
everything performed with desire yields immediate fruit,
while everything performed without desire directly bestows the state of Śiva.
In the three periods of the day—morning, midday, and evening—the great day is divided sequentially.

Morning is to be known as the time for performing rites (*vidhikara*), likewise midday is for rites of desire (*kāmika*), and evening is to be known as the time for pacifying rites (*śāntika*); it is exactly the same during the night as well.
Midnight is indeed declared to be the time consisting of two middle watches of the night;
worship of Śiva performed specifically at that time grants the fulfillment of one's desires.
Knowing this, a man who acts accordingly shall partake of the fruit as it has been described.

In the Kali age, however, the attainment of results through ritual action occurs especially by means of whatever [action] has been prescribed, according to the distinction of one's qualification. If one is of good conduct and fearful of sin, one shall obtain that fruit.
The sages said:
Now, tell us in brief of the holy fields (kṣetras),
by resorting to which all women and men may attain the supreme state.
"O Sūta, best among the foremost of yogis, [tell us] likewise of the sacred sites of Śiva and their traditional accounts.
Sūta said:
"Listen with faith to all the sacred sites and their traditional accounts."
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Twelve.
Sūta said:
Listen, O wise sages, to the sacred field of Śiva which bestows liberation.
Therefore, for the very purpose of protecting the world, I shall proclaim its traditional scriptures.
It extends for fifty crores [of yojanas], including its mountains, forests, and groves.
Indeed, by the command of Śiva, the earth remains supporting the world.
In various places,
the Lord, the Master, out of compassion, has fashioned sacred fields (*kṣetra*) for the sake of the liberation of those dwelling therein.
Because they are accepted by the Ṛṣis and because they are accepted by the gods,
other [sites] have indeed become self-manifested solely for the purpose of protecting the world.
At a holy ford (tīrtha) or a sacred field (kṣetra), bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, and so forth, should always be performed.
Otherwise, a man may incur disease, poverty, or dumbness; however,
if a man dies here in this land of Bhārata,
he shall regain human birth by virtue of having dwelt in the abode of the Self-Existent (Svayaṃbhū).
O Brahmins, the commission of sin becomes firmly established in such a field;
for one should not commit even the slightest sin while residing in a sacred field (puṇyakṣetra).
By whatever means possible, a person should dwell in a sacred field.
On the shores of the ocean, there are many sacred fields (*kṣetra*) along hundreds of rivers.
Likewise, the holy river Sarasvatī is said to have sixty mouths.
A wise man should dwell on those respective banks; in due course, he shall attain the state of Brahman.
The Gaṅgā, born from the Himavat mountain, is a meritorious river with a hundred mouths;
and on its banks are numerous sacred fields such as Kāśī and others.
Indeed, that bank is highly praised when Jupiter is in Capricorn.
Śoṇabhadra has ten faces; it is meritorious and bestows desired fruits.
By bathing and fasting there, one attains the state of Vaināyaka.
The great river Narmadā is also meritorious and possesses twenty-four mouths.
By bathing and dwelling there, one shall indeed attain the state of Viṣṇu.
The Tamasā has twelve mouths, and the Revā river has ten mouths;
the Godāvarī is greatly meritorious and destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin or a cow.

The Kṛṣṇaveṇī, a meritorious river that brings about the destruction of all sins, is said to have twenty-one mouths and bestows the world of Rudra. It is further said to have eighteen mouths and grants access to the world of Viṣṇu.
The Tuṅgabhadrā has ten mouths and bestows the world of Brahmā;
likewise, the meritorious Suvarṇamukharī is said to have nine mouths.
It is there indeed that those who have fallen from the world of Brahmā are born as noble offspring.
The Sarasvatī, the Paṃpā, the Kanyā, and the auspicious Śvetanadī—
by dwelling on the banks of these rivers, one shall attain the world of Indra.
The great river known as the Kāverī, born from the Sahya mountain, is exceedingly meritorious.
She is said to have twenty-seven mouths and bestows all that is desired.
Her banks grant heaven and bestow the stations of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
the Śaiva [shrines] there likewise grant the world of Śiva and bestow the fruits of one's desires.
One should bathe at Naimiṣa and Badara when Jupiter and the Sun are in Aries;
one should know that this bestows the world of Brahmā, as does worship and other rites performed there.
Likewise, one should bathe in the Sindhu river when the Sun is in Leo or Cancer.
They know that drinking the water of Kedāra and bathing there bestows knowledge.
One should bathe in the Godāvarī during the month of Siṃha when Jupiter is in Leo;
it was declared by Śiva in the past that this grants the world of Śiva.
One should bathe in the Yamunā and the Śoṇa when Jupiter has entered Virgo;
they know this to bestow great enjoyment in the world of Dharma and the world of Dantila.
Likewise, one should bathe in the Kāverī when Jupiter has entered Libra.
They know that, by the greatness of Viṣṇu’s word, it bestows all desired objects.
When the month of Vṛścika has arrived, and likewise when the sun is in Scorpio (Vṛścika) and Jupiter is in Scorpio,
one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu by bathing in the river Narmadā.
"Bathing in the Suvarṇamukharī when Jupiter is in Capricorn bestows the world of Śiva," according to the words of the Brāhmaṇas; likewise,
one should bathe in the Jāhnavī when the moon is in Capricorn and Jupiter is in Capricorn.
"Just as it was the word of Brahmā that 'it bestows the world of Śiva,' so too,
after enjoying the stations of Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
one shall attain knowledge at the end [of that experience] by bathing in the Gaṅgā during the month of Māgha when the sun has entered Aquarius."

They know that a *śrāddha*, the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), or even an offering of water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*) performed here effects the deliverance of ten million ancestors from both paternal lineages.
They praise [this rite] at the Kṛṣṇaveṇī when Jupiter and the Sun are in the sign of Pisces.
Bathing at each respective sacred ford during that month bestows the station of Indra.
Or, having resorted to either the Gaṅgā or the Sahyajā (Kāverī), the wise man should dwell there;
the destruction of whatever sin was committed during that time will certainly occur.
There are indeed numerous sacred fields that bestow the world of Rudra.
The Tāmraparṇī and the Vegavatī grant the fruit of the world of Brahmā;
on their banks, there are indeed sacred fields that bestow heaven.
Within that [region], there are many fields that bestow great merit;
by dwelling here and there, a wise person obtains such fruit through constant right conduct,
virtuous livelihood, and constant contemplation.
A wise person should indeed dwell [there] with compassion; otherwise, one will not obtain that fruit.
Merit performed in a sacred field (puṇyakṣetra) attains manifold prosperity.
Even a very small sin committed in a sacred field becomes great.
