If it is for the sake of livelihood at that time, it will go to destruction through merit. O twice-born ones, they say that merit—whether physical, vocal, or likewise mental—bestows sovereignty; such [merit] shall destroy [the corresponding] evil.

But mental [sin], which is like adamantine cement and persists for kalpa after kalpa, perishes only through meditation; it does not meet its destruction in any other way. Verbal [sin] is destroyed by the net of recitation (*japa*), and bodily [sin] by the emaciation of the body.
Through giving, that which is produced by wealth perishes; it does not perish otherwise even in ten million kalpas.
In some cases, merit perishes through sin, while [sin] perishes preceded by growth.
Of both merit and sin, there is a portion consisting of seed, a portion consisting of growth, and a portion consisting of enjoyment.
For the seed-portion is destroyed by knowledge, while the growth occurs according to the manner described;
however, the enjoyment-portion is destroyed only by experience, and not otherwise even by ten million merits.
When the sprouting of the seed has perished, the remainder is fit for enjoyment.
Through the worship of the gods, through giving to Brahmins,
and through the excellence of asceticism over time, that suffering may become bearable for men.
Therefore, one who desires happiness should dwell without having committed any sin at all.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Vidyeśvara Saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Thirteen.
The Sages said:
"Quickly proclaim the conduct of the virtuous by which a wise man may conquer the worlds;
likewise, tell us of those things consisting of dharma and adharma that bestow heaven or hell.
Sūta said:

One who is endowed with good conduct and is learned is called a *brāhmaṇa* by name; indeed, a *vipra* is one endowed with both Vedic knowledge and right conduct, while a *dvija* is one who possesses only one of these. A *kṣatriya*, however, is one of little conduct and little Vedic learning, serving as a king’s attendant.

A Vaiśya who possesses some degree of proper conduct but engages in agriculture and trade is called a *śūdra-brāhmaṇa* by his very nature as a cultivator. One who is envious and malicious toward others is called a *caṇḍāla-dvija*.
The king is considered the protector of the earth, while others are regarded as kṣatriyas;
one who deals in the purchase of grain and other goods is a vaiśya, while another is called a merchant (vaṇij).
One who serves the brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas is called a śūdra.
The plowman is to be known as a *vṛṣala*, and others are indeed *dasyus*.
At dawn, everyone facing the east should first contemplate the gods,
then their duties and purposes, their hardships, and their income and expenditure.
Longevity, hatred, death, sin, and likewise fortune;
illness, nourishment, and power—these are the fruits of rising in the morning and so forth. The final watch of the night is known as *uṣā*, and half a watch is called *saṃdhi*.
At that time, having risen, the twice-born man should void his excrement and urine;
having gone far from the house, he should likewise proceed outside. Facing north, or facing another direction if there is an obstruction, he should enter [the place for evacuation].
Not facing water, fire, Brahmins, or other deities,
one should cover the *liṅga* with the left hand and the mouth with the other hand;
having discharged the waste and stood up, one must not look at that excrement.
One should perform purification with water drawn out from the source when outside the water;
or otherwise, without descending into the *deva*, *pitṛ*, or *ārṣa* tirthas,
one should cleanse the anus seven, five, or three times with earth.
For the penis, a piece the size of a *karkoṭa* fruit is required; for the anus, one *prasṛti* is prescribed.
Then, having risen, one should perform the cleansing of the feet and hands and take eight mouthfuls of water (*gaṇḍūṣa*) with whatever leaf or wooden stick is available, outside of the water.
Having abandoned other tasks, one should perform the cleaning of the teeth with the index finger;
then, having paid homage to the water-deities with the mantra, one should perform the bath. If unable [to submerge the whole body], one may bathe up to the neck or even up to the waist.
Having entered the water up to the knees, one should perform the ritual bath with mantras;
there, the wise man should offer libations to the gods and others with the water of the sacred site.
Then, taking a washed cloth, he should wear it with the five-fold fold (pañcakaccha).
And an upper garment (uttarīya) should be worn during all ritual acts.
However, when bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) such as a river, one should not wash the bathing cloth;
but in the case of bathing in a step-well, a well, a house, or similar places, the wise man should wash it after the bath.
O twice-born ones, having purified a cloth made of stone, wood, or other materials, whether in water or on land,
one should wring it out for the satisfaction of the ancestors;
likewise, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark with ashes while reciting the mantra spoken by Jābāla.
Otherwise, if one falls into the water from there, one goes to hell.
For the pacification of sin, one should sprinkle water on the head with the mantra *āpo hi ṣṭhā*.
It is taught that the sprinkling of the joints on the feet is performed with the mantra *yasya*.
Sprinkling [the water] on the feet, the head, and the heart; then on the head, the heart, and the feet;
and finally on the heart, the feet, and the head—the wise know this to be the *mantra-snāna*.
It should be performed when there is slight physical discomfort, ill health, or even fear for the king and the kingdom.
And when the time for going has passed, one should perform the mantra-bath:
in the morning with the Sūryānuvāka, and in the evening with the Agnyanuvāka.
Having likewise drunk water in the middle [of the day], one should again perform the ritual sprinkling.
At the conclusion of the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra, one should first cast water upwards;
O twice-born ones, one should indeed offer a single *arghya* oblation to the Sun in the middle with the mantra.
Then, when evening has arrived, facing the western direction upon the ground—

Having lifted [the vessel], one should offer [the water] in the morning; likewise at midday, one should view the hanging sun through the openings between the fingers. Having performed circumambulation of oneself, one should perform the pure sipping of water (ācamana).

If the evening twilight rite is performed even a moment before [the proper time], it becomes fruitless. When the time has passed, that which was not the proper time is declared to be the proper time according to the sequence. And when the day has passed, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred times daily in the prescribed order.
After one year has passed, one should practice the Gāyatrī for a hundred thousand times;
but when a month has passed since the daily [practice], one must indeed undergo initiation again.
[The presiding deities are] Īśa, Gaurī, Guha, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, and Yama.
In this manner, one should indeed gratify such deities for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Then, having performed the offering to Brahman,
the wise man should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in a commendable monastery or temple of mantras to the right of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
In that temple or even in his own home, in a fixed place,
having paid homage to all the gods with a steady mind and a steady posture,
he should first practice the *praṇava* and thereafter practice the *gāyatrī*.

Having realized the subject matter of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman, one should practice the recitation of the Praṇava. We worship Rudra— the creator of the three worlds, the sustainer, the infallible one, as well as the destroyer— who is self-luminous.
One should always impel the functions of the organs of knowledge and action, as well as the mental states and the intellect,
toward virtue and knowledge which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By contemplating this meaning with the intellect in this manner, one certainly attains Brahman.
Or he may recite it alone daily for the fulfillment of his Brahminhood;
the best of Brahmins should practice it a thousand times every morning. For others, he should recite according to their capacity, and at midday he should recite it one hundred times.
In the evening, one should know there are twenty-two [deities], together with the eight tufts (śikhās).
Beginning from the *mūlādhāra*, they are situated up to the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*):
namely, Vidyeśa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, Jīvātman, and Parameśvara.
With the thought that it is Brahman, one should recite the mantra "So 'ham" while contemplating their unity;
one should contemplate those very [elements] within the body, starting from the aperture of Brahma (the crown of the head), and externally as well,
beginning from the principle of Mahat up to the thousand-fold body.

Skipping one by one from each [syllable], gradually and slowly, one should unite the individual soul (jīva) with the Supreme; this is declared to be the true nature of recitation (japa-tattva). The body consists of two hundred and ten [syllables], provided with eight tufts of hair (śikhās).
Thus, the wise know that the recitation of mantras follows a specific sequence beginning with *japa*:
one should know that a thousand repetitions bestow the state of Brahmā, while a hundred are known to bestow the state of Indra;
any other [fewer] repetitions serve for self-protection, and one is born into the wombs of Brahmins.
Having performed his worship of the Sun, he should always conduct himself in this manner.

One who is endowed with twelve hundred thousand [repetitions] is declared to be a "complete Brāhmaṇa. However, one who lacks a hundred thousand repetitions of the Gāyatrī should be employed in Vedic duties.
One should observe this discipline until the age of seventy, after which one should practice renunciation (*pravrājana*).
A renunciant should mutter the *praṇava* twelve thousand times every morning;
thus, as each day passes, he should always mutter it in this sequence.
When a month or more has gradually elapsed, one must indeed perform half a lakh of recitations;
if more time than that passes, one should perform the *praiṣa* rite once again.
By doing so, the fault is pacified; otherwise, one shall go to the Raurava hell.
Therefore, one who desires [worldly] objects should exert effort toward dharma and artha, but not otherwise.
A Brāhmaṇa should desire liberation and should constantly practice the knowledge of Brahman.
From dharma comes artha; from artha comes enjoyment; and from enjoyment arises dispassion.
Through the enjoyment of wealth acquired through righteousness, dispassion arises;
through the enjoyment of wealth acquired in the opposite manner, passion alone is produced.
And righteousness is said to be twofold, consisting of both material objects and the body.
Material wealth consists of sacrifice and the like, while bodily purification consists of bathing at sacred fords and so forth.
Through wealth one obtains wealth; through austerity, one attains a divine form.
One who is free from desire attains purity, and through purity, knowledge—of this there is no doubt.
In the Kṛta age and those preceding it, austerity is praiseworthy; in the Kali age, the dharma of material offerings prevails.
In the Kṛta age, the perfection of knowledge comes through meditation; likewise, in the Tretā age, it comes through austerity.
In the Dvāpara age, knowledge is attained through sacrifice; in the Kali age, it is attained by worshipping images.
For whatever the merit or the sin may be, the fruit is indeed of that same nature;
through differences in substance, body, or limb, there is decrease, increase, loss, and so forth.
Adharma is of the nature of injury, whereas dharma is of the nature of happiness.

From unrighteousness one obtains suffering; indeed, from righteousness happiness increases. One should know that suffering arises from evil conduct, while happiness arises from good conduct. Therefore, one should practice the acquisition of dharma for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation.

One should provide a livelihood for a hundred years to a Brahmin together with his family, consisting of four persons; that is known to grant the world of Brahmā. They know that a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa fasts likewise bestow the world of Brahmā.
A Kṣatriya should perform the installation of a thousand families;
he should know that this bestows the world of Indra, while the installation of ten thousand bestows the world of Brahmā.
Whatever deity a man places at the forefront when performing a gift [of installation], [he attains the realm of that deity].
Those who know the Vedas understand that one attains those respective worlds;
likewise, one who is destitute of wealth should always perform purification through austerity.
By means of both sacred fords and austerity, one enjoys imperishable happiness that is to be attained.
Now, with a well-composed mind, I shall explain the acquisition of wealth according to the righteous path:
a Brāhmaṇa should acquire wealth through the acceptance of gifts and through officiating at sacrifices performed with purity, provided it is done without dejection and without excessive hardship.
A Kṣatriya attains success through the strength of his arms; a Vaiśya, through agriculture and the protection of cattle. One attains perfection by giving away wealth acquired through righteous means.
Through the attainment of knowledge, the attainment of liberation comes to all by the grace of the Guru.
From liberation, the perfection of one's true nature arises, and one attains supreme bliss.
O twice-born ones, all of this indeed comes to men through association with the virtuous.
A householder should certainly give away all things, such as wealth and grain.
Whatever collection of objects, fruit, or even grain is available at any time—
all that should indeed be given to the Brāhmaṇas by one who desires his own welfare.
Water and food should always be given for the pacification of the affliction of hunger.

The field, the grain, the cooked food, and the raw food—thus food is of four kinds. For as long as one thrives by eating whatever food [is given], for that long half of the merit earned by the giver belongs to the recipient; of this there is no doubt.

One should effect the purification of sins by giving away what has been seized or likewise through austerity; otherwise, one shall go to the Raurava hell. One should divide one's own wealth into three parts: for the increase of dharma, for religious duties, and for one’s own enjoyment.
One should perform the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites according to the Dharma.
A practitioner should increase his wealth by means of the portion set aside for growth;
he should enjoy his possessions with what is beneficial, moderate, and pure, using the portion intended for enjoyment.
Indeed, one-tenth of the wealth earned through agriculture should be given for the purification of sin;
with the remainder, one should perform dharma and other duties, otherwise one shall go to the Raurava hell. Or else, if one possesses a sinful mind, [the merit] will surely go to destruction.
In the case of profits from trade, a sixth part should indeed be given by the wise;
in the case of pure gifts, a fourth part should be given by the best of the twice-born. When wealth arises unexpectedly, half of it should be given by the best of the twice-born.

All that is received from an unworthy person and all ill-bestowed gifts should be cast into the ocean. A gift should be given after having invited [the recipient] for the sake of the abundance of one's own enjoyment.
Whatever is requested should always be given according to one's own capacity.
For if one does not return a requested object, one will indeed become a debtor in another birth.
Likewise, a wise man should not proclaim the faults of others;
O Brahmin, he should especially refrain from speaking of what has been heard or seen [of them].

A wise man should not speak anything that causes anger in the hearts of all living beings. For the attainment of sovereign power, he should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) during the two twilights;
however, if unable, he may do so at a single time, offering oblations to both the Sun and Agni according to the prescribed rule.
One should prepare rice, grain, clarified butter, fruit, bulbous root, or likewise an oblation,
as well as a *sthālīpāka* (cooked food in a pot), according to the rule and according to the prescribed ritual.
Or, in the absence of an oblation, one may perform at least the principal *homa*.

The wise know that constant application is called *nityasaṃdhāna*; it should be performed incessantly. Alternatively, one who seeks the Self should perform only the recitation (*japa*) or the salutation to the Sun, while one who seeks worldly wealth should do so according to the prescribed rule.
Constantly devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña), as well as to the worship of the gods;
always intent on the worship of the sacred fire and devoted to the worship of the guru;
those who bring satisfaction to the Brāhmaṇas all share in the heavenly realm.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 14.
The Sages said:

"O Lord, tell us in due order about the sacrifice to Agni, the sacrifice to the gods, and likewise the sacrifice to Brahman; as well as the worship of the guru and the satisfaction of the Veda. Sūta said:

Whatever substance one offers into the fire is called the fire-sacrifice (*agniyajña*). For those established in the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya-āśrama*), the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) is indeed their primary duty; likewise, the offering of fuel-sticks into the fire, as well as vows and other specialized sacrifices, constitute their practice.

O twice-born ones, for those in the first stage of life, this applies up until the *aupāsana* fire; likewise for forest-dwellers and ascetics who have internalized the fires within themselves, O twice-born ones,
the offering consists of eating wholesome, moderate, and pure food at its proper time.
Having begun the maintenance of the *aupāsana* fire, it should be well-protected;
it is declared that this [fire] should be kept perpetually either in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or in a vessel (*bhāṇḍa*).
However, due to the power of kings or fate, it may certainly be established within oneself or in the two kindling woods (*araṇi*).
Out of fear of abandoning the sacred fire, it is said that [the evening offering] is called "superimposed" (*samāropita*).
O twice-born ones, the evening oblation to the fire should be known as "wealth-bestowing" (*saṃpatkarī*);
likewise, the morning oblation to the sun should be known as "life-prolonging" (*āyuṣkarī*).

For this is declared to be the fire-sacrifice (agni-yajña), performed by day because of the settling of the sun. That which one offers into the fire, dedicating it to all the gods beginning with Indra— one should know that as the sacrifice to the gods (deva-yajña), including rites such as the sthālīpāka.
Likewise, it should be known that the *caula* and other rites are established in the worldly fire (*laukikāgni*).
A twice-born man should perform the *brahmayajña* once for the satisfaction of the gods.
What is called the *brahmayajña* is the study of the Veda.
This [rite] follows immediately after the daily [obligations], and therefore it is not prescribed separately.
Listen with faith and reverence to the sacrifice to the gods performed without fire.
At the beginning of creation, Mahādeva, the omniscient one and the mine of compassion, [instituted this].
For the sake of benefiting the entire world, the Lord,
the omniscient physician of *saṃsāra* and the medicine for all medicines, fashioned the days (*vāra*). First, the Lord established his own day (*svavāra*), which bestows health.
Then, he made a boon of his own *māyā* that brings about prosperity; thereafter,
once the birth of Kumāra had transcended all difficulties,
the Lord established a day (*vāra*) for the overcoming of indolence and evil.

Likewise, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, the Lord Viṣṇu, the protector, established a watch for the sake of nourishment and protection. Then he established a watch that bestows long life, specifically for the sake of the one who ordains lifespans.
Indeed, for the sake of establishing the lifespan of the world, the Lord Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, the creator of the three worlds, devised the *vāra* (weekday) system;
at the outset, merit and demerit were likewise established for the purpose of the increase of the three worlds.
Then, for those two creators— Indra and Yama—
a [system] was established that bestows enjoyment and removes death for the worlds; likewise,
the sun and other deities were established as the very forms of pleasure and pain, serving as indicators thereof.
Having first conceived the lords of the days as established within the wheel of the luminaries (*jyotiścakra*),
their worship on their respective days bestows their individual fruits:
health, prosperity, and indeed the pacification of diseases.
Nourishment, longevity, as well as enjoyment, and the loss [of these] upon death— these,
they say, are the fruits of the sequence of days, preceded by the propitiation of the deities. Śiva is the bestower of the fruit even for the worship of other deities.
For the pleasure of the gods, worship is prescribed as being fivefold:

the recitation of their respective mantras, burnt offerings (homa), giving gifts, and likewise austerity. These are performed upon the sacrificial ground, in an image, in the fire, and in the person of a Brahmin.

Thus, worship is performed with these sixteen types of offerings. Due to their progressive superiority, each subsequent one is employed in the absence of the preceding. Likewise, for the pacification of diseases of the eyes, the head, or leprosy, [the higher forms are used].
Having worshipped the Sun, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas for a day,
a month, a year, or even for three years;
if the *prārabdha* karma is powerful, then disease, old age, and so forth shall perish.
The wise know that the fruit of reciting [mantras] and so forth for one’s chosen deity depends on the day of the week and other factors.
One should especially offer [worship] on the first day of the week (Sunday),
for it grants preeminent results among the gods and Brāhmaṇas, specifically for the Sun-god.
On Monday, the wise man should worship Lakṣmī and the other goddesses for the sake of prosperity;
likewise, he should feed Brahmins together with their wives with offerings of ghee and cooked rice.
On Tuesday, however, he should worship Kālī and the others for the pacification of diseases.
On the day of the Moon, one should feed the Brahmins with food consisting of a *māṣa* and *mudga* beans and *āḍhaka* rice; likewise, the wise man should worship Viṣṇu with curd-rice.
Through this, there is always prosperity for one's sons, friends, wife, and others.
Desiring long life on Thursday, or for the sake of the prosperity and accomplishment of the gods,
the wise man should worship with a sacred thread (*upavīta*), a garment, milk, and clarified butter (*ājya*).
On Friday, however, one who is composed should worship the gods for the sake of enjoyment.
One should offer food endowed with the six flavors for the satisfaction of the Brahmins;
likewise, for the satisfaction of the women, auspicious items such as clothing should be given.
When Saturn is causing untimely death, the wise man should worship Rudra and the mountains.
One should worship with an oblation of sesame seeds, through gifts, and by feeding others with sesame-rice;
in this manner one should sacrifice to the gods and obtain fruits such as good health.
This applies both to the daily sacrifice to the gods and to special sacrifices.
In bathing, giving gifts, reciting prayers, performing fire-offerings, and in the satiation of Brahmins;
in the conjunctions of lunar days and constellations, and in the worship of various deities;
on the days of the week beginning with Sunday—the Omniscient Lord of the Universe [is present].
In that very form, he bestows the fruits of health and other benefits upon all,
according to place and time, as well as according to the recipient,
the material offered, the degree of faith, and likewise according to worldly custom.

The Lord bestows health and other blessings according to the sequence of their relative merit. A householder should worship the planets, beginning with the Sun, in his own home during the asterisms of his birth and so forth— both at auspicious and inauspicious times— for the sake of attaining prosperity such as health and the like.
Therefore, this place of sacrifice for the gods bestows all desired fruits;
it should always be performed by men according to their capacity, with mantras for the Brāhmaṇas and according to the Tantras for others.
On all seven days of the week, men who desire auspicious results—
whether poor, they should worship the gods through austerity, or wealthy, indeed with wealth—
and furthermore, they perform such dharma with faith.

Furthermore, after having enjoyed various pleasures, he is born upon the earth. One who possesses wealth should always provide shade, water reservoirs, the installation of Brahmanical shrines, and the accumulation of merit, so that his enjoyment may be fully realized.
And through time and the ripening of merit, the perfection of knowledge arises.
O twice-born ones, the man who hears this chapter, or reads it,
or assists in its hearing, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice to the gods.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Vidyeśvara Saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, best among those who know all things, tell us in due order about the regions and so forth.
Sūta said:
"A pure house yields equal fruit for rites such as sacrifices to the gods."
Ten times more than that is a cow-pen; ten times more than that is the bank of a river.

Ten times more than that is the root of a *bilva*, *tulasī*, or *aśvattha* tree. One should know that a temple is ten times more meritorious than that, and the bank of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) is ten times more than that.
Ten times more than that is the merit of a river’s bank, and ten times more than that is the merit of a sacred ford on a river.
Ten times the merit of the banks of the seven Gaṅgās shall be found at the banks of the [following] rivers:
the Gaṅgā, the Godāvarī, the Kāverī, and the Tāmraparṇī.
The Sindhu, the Sarayū, and the Revā are proclaimed as the seven Gaṅgās.
Beyond that, ten [yojanas] from the shore of the ocean, or ten on a mountain peak—
these should be known as superior to all, or wherever the mind finds delight.
In the Kṛta age, sacrifices, gifts, and other such acts should be known to yield their full fruit;

likewise, in the Tretā age, they yield three-quarters, and in the Dvāpara age, it is always remembered that they yield half. In the Kali age, however, one quarter is to be known as the result, and in the period beyond that [the end of the Kali], even less than a quarter.
The wise know that for one of pure soul, a day of purity yields merit equal to [the merit of] a [pure] day;
however, O wise ones, it should be known that at the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), the merit is ten times that,
at the equinox (viṣuva) ten times that, and at the solstice (ayana) it is remembered as ten times that.
Ten [times that] during the transit of the sun into Capricorn, and ten during a lunar eclipse;
thereafter, they know it to be ten times more during a solar eclipse at the most excellent full time.
Due to the conjunction with the poison of the sun, which is the form of the world, it bestows disease.
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying that poison, one should perform ablutions, gifts, and recitations;
because it is the time for the pacification of poison, that time is remembered as merit-bestowing.
They know [this] to be equal to an eclipse of the sun on one's birth-star and at the conclusion of a vow.
The wise know that even a moment spent in the company of the great is equal to ten million solar eclipses.
Those established in austerity, those established in knowledge, as well as yogins and ascetics—
these indeed are the worthy recipients of worship, for they are the cause of the destruction of sin.
Or, by performing the recitation of the Gāyatrī twenty-four hundred thousand times,
a Brāhmaṇa becomes a worthy recipient (*pātra*) who bestows the enjoyment of the complete fruit [of the rite].
In the scriptures, one is designated a *pātra* because they protect [others] from falling.
Because it protects the giver from sin, it is called a *pātra* (a worthy recipient). Indeed, because it protects the singer from falling [into hell], it is called *gāyatrī*.
Just as in this world one who is devoid of wealth does not bestow wealth upon another, so too is that which lacks merit.
In this world, he who is possessed of wealth and bestows it upon another for the sake of his welfare—
being himself pure and of purified soul— is indeed worthy to protect men.
For a Brāhmaṇa who is purified by the recitation of the Gāyatrī is called a truly pure Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, in giving, recitation, oblation, worship, and in every ritual act,
a Brāhmaṇa is worthy to receive a gift and likewise to protect [the donor];
for one who is hungry is a worthy recipient of food, whether that recipient be a woman or a man.
They know that when one has invited an excellent Brāhmaṇa at the proper time with a well-composed mind,
the gift of either a word or a meaning that conveys true knowledge and bestows what is desired,
given to one who has such a wish, yields a complete fruit.
The wise know that what is given immediately after a question yields the fruit of its purpose;
they know that what is given to a servant yields the fruit of his feet.
O best of the twice-born, this applies even to a Brahmin who is merely by birth and lives in a state of wretchedness.
For wealth given for the sake of enjoyment lasts ten years in the world of mortals;
for a Brahmin endowed with Vedic knowledge, it lasts ten years in heaven;
and for one engaged in the recitation of the Gāyatrī, it lasts ten years in the Satyaloka.
They know that what is given to a Brahmin devoted to Viṣṇu bestows Vaikuṇṭha;
they know that what is given to a Brahmin devoted to Śiva bestows Kailāsa.
For all people, giving is intended for the sake of enjoying those respective worlds.
A man who gives food consisting of ten ingredients to a Brahmin on a Sunday attains health for ten years in his next birth. Furthermore,
he receives great respect, invitations, oil massages, and service at his feet.

Clothing, worship with perfumes and so forth, and an abundance of ghee, honey, and excellent rice; side dishes of six flavors, betel leaf, and a concluding gift—this is the ten-fold offering of good food, along with prostration and following after [the deity]. (ŚivP 1.15.27cd–28ab)
A man who gives food consisting of ten ingredients to ten Brahmins on a Sunday enjoys good health for a hundred years;
on Monday and the other days of the week, the fruit is according to the specific quality of that respective day.
The fruit of the gift of food should be understood as occurring in this world and in future births;
even on all seven days of the week, by giving food to ten [persons], one enjoys a hundred years of health and other blessings. (ŚivP 1.15.30cd–31ab)
Thus, by giving [gifts] to a hundred Brahmins on a Sunday,
a man enjoys good health for a thousand years in the world of Śiva;
likewise, by giving to a thousand, he enjoys it for ten thousand years.

Thus it should be understood by the wise regarding the days of the moon and other planets. By giving food on Sunday to those whose minds are purified by the Gāyatrī mantra thousands of times, one indeed attains health and other blessings in the world of truth (Satyaloka).
Likewise, by giving ten thousand [meals], one enjoys [the fruits] in the world of Viṣṇu;
but by giving food in the hundreds of thousands, one enjoys them in the world of Rudra.
Indeed, food should be given to children by men seeking knowledge, regarding them with the thought that they are Brahmins.
Indeed, young men should be worshipped with the thought that they are Viṣṇu by those men seeking sons;
the elderly should be worshipped with the thought that they are Rudra by those men seeking knowledge;
and the best of men, desiring wisdom, should worship children and women with the thought that they are the goddess Sarasvatī.
By the best of men who desire worldly enjoyment, gifts should be given to young women with the thought that they are Lakṣmī;

and by people seeking their own spiritual welfare, gifts should be given to elderly women with the thought that they are Pārvatī. [This applies to wealth] acquired through the practice of gleaning ears of grain, the practice of picking up single grains, or as a teacher’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā).
They say that pure wealth is what bestows the full fruit;
wealth given through the acceptance of gifts from those of pure conduct is called middling wealth;
and wealth acquired through agriculture and trade is called inferior wealth.
They say that for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, wealth acquired through valor and trade is the most excellent; for Śūdras, it is that earned as a laborer.
Likewise, for women who seek dharma, wealth comes from their fathers and their husbands.
One should give cows and the other [twelve] items in the months beginning with Caitra, according to their respective order;
or, having gathered them together at an auspicious time, one should give them for the fulfillment of one's desires.
These are: cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, clarified butter, clothing, grain, and molasses.
Silver, salt, and a gourd, as well as twelve virgins;
by the gift of a cow, and by the beneficial cow-dung provided,
there is the warding off of misfortunes associated with wealth, grain, and other possessions.
But for sins residing in water, oil, and so forth, purification is by means of cow's urine and water;
likewise, for the three types of physical and other sins, it is by means of milk, curd, and clarified butter.
Furthermore, the nourishment of those [sins] should be understood by the wise in the same way.
O twice-born ones, the gift of land is for the sake of stability both in this world and the next;
the gift of sesame seeds is indeed for the sake of strength, and they know it to always bring victory over death. Gold, moreover, increases the digestive fire and likewise bestows virility.

One should know that clarified butter (*ājya*) brings about nourishment, and they understand clothing to bring about longevity. Grain and food are for the sake of prosperity, and molasses (*guḍa*) provides sweet food.
Silver is for the sake of increasing semen, while salt is for the sake of the six flavors.
The wise know that the gift of a *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd brings about the fulfillment of all things and bestows nourishment;
it grants the attainment of all enjoyments both in this world and the next, O twice-born ones.
Indeed, the gift of a maiden is said to grant enjoyment for as long as one lives.
And likewise the fruit of trees such as the jackfruit, mango, and wood-apple;
the fruit of plants such as the plantain and other medicinal herbs, as well as that produced from shrubs;
and the fruit of beans, mung beans, and the like, as well as vegetables and so forth.
Likewise, vegetables such as *marīci* and mustard seeds,
as well as whatever seasonal fruit has been prepared, should indeed be given by the wise man.
Furthermore, the wise man should always provide that which brings satisfaction to the sense organs, beginning with the ears.
She grants satisfaction regarding the ten objects of enjoyment, beginning with sound, as well as the directions and so forth.
Having received the Vedic scriptures and understood them either from the mouth of a guru or by oneself,
the conviction that "there is a fruit for ritual actions" is called *āstikya* (orthodoxy).
Out of fear of the king, one's intellect and faith may be weak;
and in the absence of all [resources], even a poor man should worship through speech or through action.
One should know that vocal worship consists of the recitation of mantras, hymns, and the like.
For they know that physical acts of worship consist primarily of pilgrimages, vows, and the like;
whatever is performed by any means whatsoever, whether little or much,
with the intention of offering it to the deity, conduces to enjoyment.
Both austerity and charity must always be practiced; likewise,
wise men should provide shelter that is adorned with the virtues of one's own class,
which exceedingly satisfies the gods and bestows all enjoyments.
In this world and the next, the wise man shall always obtain the highest birth and full enjoyment;
for by performing [actions] with the intention of dedicating them to the Lord, he shall obtain the fruit of liberation.
That man who always recites this chapter or hears it, [attains these benefits].
"And for him, the intellect regarding the nature of reality and the perfection of knowledge arise.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 16]
The sages said:
"O most excellent one, tell us the procedure for the worship of the image of the Lord of the Earth,
by which procedure of worship every desired object is attained."
Sūta said:
"You have asked most excellently about that which always bestows all goals;
it is the immediate pacification of suffering. Listen, for I shall declare it to you."
O twice-born ones, it removes untimely death and even destroys death at its appointed time;
it immediately bestows wife, sons, wealth, and grain.
From this [source], all things to be consumed such as food, as well as clothing and so forth, are produced.
Therefore, on this earth, the worship of images made of clay and other materials bestows desired fruits;
it is certain that both men and women have the right to perform this.
One should take clay from within the water of a river, a pond, or a well.
Having purified it with fragrant powder and ground it well in a beautiful pavilion,
one should fashion an image with one's own hand, well-prepared with milk,
complete with all its major and minor limbs, and endowed with weapons.

Having placed [the image] in the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should indeed worship it with devotion. A twice-born man should always worship Vighneśa, Āditya, Viṣṇu, Ambā, and Śiva, as well as the Śivaliṅga of Śiva.
One should perform [the worship] with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) for the sake of attaining its fruit.
One should perform the sprinkling with flowers and the consecration (abhiṣeka) accompanied by mantras.
The entire food offering (naivedya) should consist of śāli rice, measured at one kuḍava each.
In the domestic rite, one *kuḍava* is prescribed; for the human rite, a *prastha* is intended.
For the divine rite, three *prasthas* are appropriate, and for the Self-Existent One (Svayaṃbhū), five *prasthas*.
Thus one should know that the fruit is complete; indeed, two or three times more than that yields even greater results.
Through a thousandfold worship, the twice-born attains the world of truth (Satyaloka).
Twelve finger-breadths in length, and twice that or more;
the measure of a single finger-breadth is one, and above that, three sets of five.
A vessel made of ironwood is called *śiva* by the wise.
One-eighth of that is a *prastha*, and that is considered to be four *kuḍavas*.
[There are vessels] of ten *prasthas*, a hundred *prasthas*, and even a thousand *prasthas*.

According to the appropriate measure of water, oil, and other fragrant substances, the worship of the human, ṛṣi, and self-manifested [liṅgas] is called the Great Worship (mahāpūjā). Through the consecration (abhiṣeka), there is purification of the self; through the fragrance, merit is attained.
From the food offering one obtains long life and satisfaction; from incense, wealth is acquired.
From the lamp one attains knowledge, and from betel-leaf one shall obtain enjoyment.
Therefore, one should diligently perform the sixfold rite beginning with the bath.
Both salutation and the recitation of mantras bestow all desired objects;
they should always be performed at the conclusion of worship by men seeking worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having first worshipped mentally, a person should always perform those respective acts.
By worshipping the gods, one shall attain their respective worlds;
and within those intermediate worlds, one obtains whatever enjoyments are desired.
O twice-born ones, listen with faith as I describe those specific details.
By properly worshipping Vighneśa, one shall obtain all desired objects in this world.
On a Friday, on the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the months of Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada,
under the constellation Āśleṣā, or during the month of Dhanus, one should worship Vighneśa according to the prescribed rites.
Whether it be a hundred or a thousand offerings, one should perform them for as many days as that number;
performed with constant faith toward the gods and the sacred fire, this bestows sons and desired objects upon men,
pacifies all sins, and destroys various misdeeds.
They know the worship of the days (vārapūjā) of Śiva and the other deities to be that which bestows purity of the self;
it is the support for all lunar days (tithi), asterisms (nakṣatra), and yogas, and it fulfills all desires.
Likewise, because it is free from increase and decrease, they know it to be of the nature of the perfect Brahman.
The day begins from sunrise for all rites starting with those dedicated to Brahmā;
indeed, worship of the gods at the commencement of the lunar day (tithi) bestows full enjoyment upon men.
However, the first part of the night is praised for offerings to the ancestors (pitṛs).
The latter part of the lunar day is prescribed for the gods during the day;
if that lunar day extends through midday, it should be accepted for rites dedicated to the gods. Likewise, one should accept the auspicious asterisms and other such factors.
Having investigated correctly the lunar days and other factors, one should perform worship, recitation, and so forth.
For the meaning in the Vedas is applied thus: "by this [rite], worship is accomplished.
And through that action, the attainment of the fruit of complete enjoyment arises.
Likewise, mental dispositions and knowledge [constitute worship] through the application of desired enjoyments and objects;

for such is the meaning of the word "pūjā" (worship) as it is renowned in both worldly usage and the Vedas. Regular and occasional rites are [perfected] through time, while in the case of optional rites, the result is immediate when they are properly performed.
By worshipping for a day, a month, a fortnight, and a year respectively,
one attains the fruits of those respective actions and undergoes a corresponding destruction of sins in due order.
On the fourth lunar day of the dark fortnight, one should perform the worship of Mahāgaṇapati.
It destroys the sins of one's side and bestows the fruits of enjoyment for a fortnight;

worship performed on the fourth day of the month of Caitra bestows the fruits of the entire month. It should be known that when performed during the month of Siṃha-Bhādrapada, it bestows the enjoyment of a year.
On a Sunday coinciding with the asterism Śravaṇā, on the seventh lunar day when the moon is in the asterism Hasta,

and on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should perform the worship of Āditya (the Sun). Likewise, on the twelfth day of the months of Jyeṣṭha, Bhādrapada, and Mārgaśīrṣa, when the moon is in the asterism Śravaṇā, [one should do so].

They know that the worship of Viṣṇu on the twelfth day brings about desired prosperity; the worship of Viṣṇu in the month of Śrāvaṇa bestows desired health. Furthermore, the fruit that results from giving twelve objects, such as cows and others, along with their ancillaries—[that fruit is obtained by this].

One obtains that fruit by offering libations to Viṣṇu on the twelfth day (dvādaśī). On the twelfth day, one should worship twelve Brahmins with the twelve names of Viṣṇu and with the sixteen types of ritual offerings; thus one attains His pleasure.
And thus, by means of the twelve names corresponding to each of all the gods,
the twelve-fold Brahma-sacrifice shall become a source of gratification for each respective deity.
On a Monday in the month of Karkaṭaka, on the ninth lunar day under the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa—
One desiring prosperity should worship Ambā, who bestows the fruit of all enjoyments.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja grants all desired fruits,
especially on a Sunday or on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
Worship of Śiva is especially distinguished during the asterisms of Ārdrā and Mahārdrā.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, it bestows all desired fruits;
it grants long life, removes death, and brings about all perfections for men.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, under the constellation Ārdrā, on the fourteenth day,
or under the constellation Ārdrā in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Śiva in His respective form with sixteen types of offerings; then, indeed, one beholds His feet.
The worship of Śiva should be known as that which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
Indeed, the worship of the deities beginning with Varuṇa is especially distinguished during the month of Kārttika.
When the month of Kārttika has arrived, the wise man should worship all the gods.
Through charity, austerity, burnt offerings, recitation, and observance,
as well as through the sixteen modes of worship with images accompanied by Vedic mantras and by the feeding of Brahmins, one becomes a remover of the suffering of those free from desire.
In the month of Kārttika, the sacrifice to the gods bestows all enjoyments;
it brings about the removal of diseases and the destruction of malevolent spirits and planetary influences for men who worship the Sun on Sundays during Kārttika.
From the gift of oil and cotton, there shall be the destruction of leprosy and other such ailments;
from the gift of *harītakī*, black pepper, clothing, milk, and so forth,
as well as through the consecration of a *brahman* (the installation of an image), the destruction of consumption occurs.
From the offering of lamps and mustard seeds, epilepsy shall be destroyed.
For men who perform the worship of Śiva on the Kṛttikā constellation or on Mondays,
it shall be the pacifier of great poverty and the bringer of all prosperity.
By the gift of houses, fields, and so forth, as well as household utensils and the like;
by the worship of Skanda on the days of the Kṛttikās and on Tuesdays;
and indeed by the gift of lamps, bells, and other such items, the perfection of speech (vāk-siddhi) shall soon be attained by men.
For men, the worship of Viṣṇu on the day of the Kṛttikās and on Mondays,
as well as the gift of curd-rice, shall result in a virtuous progeny.
Through the worship of Brahmā with wealth on the day of the Kṛttikās and on Thursdays, [the same result follows].
By the gift of honey, gold, and clarified butter, there shall be an increase in enjoyments for men.
By performing sacrifices with elephants and cows on the days of the Kṛttikās and on Fridays,
and by the gift of perfumes, flowers, and food, there shall be an increase in the objects of enjoyment for men.
A barren woman obtains a virtuous son through the gift of gold, silver, and other such things.
On the days of the Kṛttikās and on Saturdays, one should perform the salutation of the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas),
as well as the worship of the elephants of the directions, the nāgas, and the bridge-protectors (setupas).
[The hymns] of Gajakomeda and Gajavaktra,
of Tryambaka and Rudra, and of Viṣṇu, the remover of sin;
likewise [the hymns] of Brahmā, the giver of knowledge, and of Dhanvantari and the Aśvins.
It removes disease and untimely death, and grants peace from illnesses occurring at that time,
through the gift of salt, iron, oil, black gram (*māṣa*), and so forth;
and through the gift of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), fruits, perfumes, water, and the like.
By means of a *prastha* measure of liquids and solids, and by weighing with *palas*,
one attains heaven during the month of Dhanus; furthermore, worship at dawn of Śiva and all other deities in their proper sequence leads to the attainment of all perfections.
An offering of śāli rice fit for oblation is said to be highly praised;
an offering of various kinds of food is especially distinguished during the month of Dhanus.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, for one who gives food, every desired fruit shall come to pass.
The destruction of evil, the attainment of desired goals, health, and indeed the Dharma;
the complete understanding of the Vedas and their correct practice;
great enjoyments in this world and the next, and finally, eternal Yoga.
One who provides food during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa shall attain perfection in the knowledge of Vedānta.

Indeed, in the early morning of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, for three days or even more, one who desires worldly enjoyment should worship the gods; he shall not be excluded from the benefits of the month-long vow.

The month of Dhanus is prescribed to last until the time of *saṅgava* (the second of the five daily periods). During the month of Dhanus, one who has conquered his senses should remain without food for the duration of a month;
a Brahmin should recite the *Gāyatrī*, the mother of the Vedas, until midday.
Thereafter, he should recite the mantras beginning with the five syllables up to seventy times;
having attained knowledge, the Brahmin shall obtain liberation at the end of his body.
For other men and women, [liberation comes] through bathing three times a day and recitation.

One always attains the pure knowledge of the five-syllabled mantra itself; by constantly reciting one's chosen mantras, one obtains the destruction of great sins. Especially during the month of Dhanus, one should perform the great offering of food (mahānaivedya).
With a load of śāli rice, a prastha of black pepper,
and indeed twelve portions of honey and clarified butter measured by the kuḍava;
with a droṇa of mung beans and twelve kinds of side dishes.
With cakes fried in ghee, sweetmeats (*modaka*), rice-based dishes (*śālikā*) and the like,
with twelve portions of curd and milk,
and likewise with a calculated quantity of coconut fruits and other such items.
When it is provided with twelve betel nuts, thirty-six leaves,
camphor, powdered nutmeg, and the five fragrant substances,
and accompanied by betel leaf, that constitutes the characteristic of the great food offering (mahā-naivedya).
This great food offering (mahānaivedya), having first been offered to the deity,
one should cause it to be distributed among the devotees according to the sequence of their castes.
And by such an offering of cooked rice (odana-naivedya), one shall become a ruler of the realm upon the earth.
By the offering of a great *naivedya*, a man shall attain heaven.
O best of the twice-born, by the offering of a thousand great *naivedyas*,
one shall attain a full lifespan in Satyaloka and in that world.
By offering thirty thousand great food-offerings (mahānaivedya),
one attains the world above that and shall not be subject to rebirth;
thirty-six thousand such food-offerings are said to secure [liberation from] birth.
The offering of *naivedya* at those two times is called the "Great Fullness" (*mahāpūrṇa*).
The *naivedya* of the Great Fullness is desired as the "birth-offering" (*janmanaivedya*).
By the gift of the birth-offering, rebirth no longer exists.

In the month of Ūrja, on an auspicious day, one should perform the offering of food (naivedya) for the sake of [one's] birth. On occasions joined with a solar transit (saṃkrānti), the falling of an asterism, one’s own birth-asterism, the full moon, and so forth, as well as on the anniversary of the year and the day of birth, one should perform the supreme offering of food for the sake of the birth.
During the intervals between months, on the day of one's birth-star (janmarkṣa), on the day of a full conjunction (pūrṇayoga), or even at the time of Saturn’s transit (melana),
one should perform [the rite] ten thousand times.
By offering a birth-oblation (janmanivedya) and surrendering one's birth, one obtains the fruit of dedicating one's very life.
Through the offering of one's birth, Śiva is pleased and indeed grants his own union (sāyujya).
One should offer this very birth as a naivedya to Śiva alone. For Śiva, who manifests in the form of the womb and the liṅga, is the one who defines birth.
Therefore, for the sake of ending rebirth, one should indeed perform worship of Śiva.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of *bindu* and *nāda*.
*Bindu* is Śakti and *nāda* is Śiva; thus, the world has the nature of both Śiva and Śakti.
This Bindu has Nāda as its support; this world has Bindu as its support.
Indeed, Bindu and Nāda are established as the foundation of the world.
When everything is joined with Bindu and Nāda, it becomes the state of being "with parts" (sakala).
Through the process of sakalīkaraṇa (the ritual integration of all parts), one undoubtedly attains birth in the world.
The Liṅga, consisting of Bindu and Nāda, is said to be the cause of the universe.
Bindu is Devī and Śiva is Nāda; this is what is called the Śiva-liṅga.
Therefore, for the sake of ending rebirth, one should worship the Śivaliṅga.
The Goddess is the Mother in the form of the Bindu (the point), and Śiva is the Father in the form of Nāda (the sound).
Indeed, when these two parents are worshipped, there is supreme bliss itself.
One should worship the Śiva-liṅga for the sake of attaining supreme bliss.
She is the Mother of the worlds, and Śiva is the Father of the worlds.
Indeed, by constantly serving one's parents, compassion increases greatly.
For it is through compassion that [the Lord] bestows sovereignty upon the worshiper.
Therefore, O best of sages, for the sake of attaining the bliss contained within,
one should worship the Śiva-liṅga as the very embodiment of one's father and mother.

For Bharga is indeed the form of Puruṣa, while Bhargā is said to be Prakṛti. The embryo whose internal substratum is the unmanifest is called Puruṣa; the embryo whose internal substratum is the manifest is called Prakṛti.
Since the progenitor contains within him the embryo of Puruṣa and so forth,
his first birth is said to be from Puruṣa;
his second birth is said to be when he has attained manifestation from Prakṛti.
The living being, born from birth, undergoes death and rebirth through the Puruṣa.
It is necessarily manifested as something else by Māyā; thus, its birth is described.
Because it decays from the time of its birth, it is traditionally known as the *jīva*.
For the very referent of the term *jīva* is bound by fetters from birth;
indeed, one should worship the *janmaliṅga* for the sake of removing the fetters of birth.
Because it attains increase (*bhaga*), *prakṛti* is called *bhaga*.
Because it is the enjoyment by means of the primary senses through the primary [elements] such as sound and the rest,
the literal meaning of the word *bhaga* is primarily heard as "the enjoyment of this.
However, the primary *bhaga* is *prakṛti*, and the Lord Śiva is called *Bhagavān*.
The Blessed One is the giver of enjoyments; there is no other bestower of enjoyment than He. The Blessed One is the Lord of *bhaga*, and thus He is called *Bharga* by the wise.
The *liṅga* is accompanied by *bhaga*, and *bhaga* is joined with the *liṅga*.

For the sake of enjoyment in this world and the next, and for the sake of eternal enjoyment, one should worship the Blessed Mahādeva, the Śiva-liṅga. The Sun is the progenitor of the worlds; his emblem arises from that act of procreation.
A person should worship the possessor of the *liṅga* (the *liṅgin*), who is the creator of the *liṅga*. That which makes the meaning of the *liṅga* known as a sign is called a *liṅga*;
for this [sign] leads the person, who is the meaning, to Śiva.
The union of the respective symbols of Śiva and Śakti is called the *liṅga*.
Through the worship of one’s own symbol, [the Lord] is pleased, and the function of the symbol is not lost;
indeed, the function of the symbol brings about the cessation of birth and all other such cycles of rebirth.
One should worship the Śiva-liṅga with the sixteen types of offerings, both those produced from external sources and those arising from within, as well as with ordinary people. Thus,
on a Sunday, this worship indeed brings about the cessation of rebirth.
On Sunday, one should worship the great primordial Liṅga with the *praṇava* alone.
On Sunday, an ablution with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is especially distinguished.
Cow dung, cow urine, milk, curd, and clarified butter constitute the *pañcagavya*.
One should likewise offer milk and other substances, as well as honey and sugarcane juice;

the food offering (naivedya) consisting of cow’s milk and rice should be presented with the *praṇava* alone. The *praṇava* is the sound-liṅga (*dhvaniliṅga*), while the self-existent one is the resonance-liṅga (*nādaliṅga*).
The *bindu* is the *liṅga*, while the letter *ma* is established as the *yantra*.
The letter *u* is the mobile *liṅga*, and the letter *a* is the form of the Guru.
By the constant worship of these six *liṅgas*, one becomes liberated while living; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, worship of Śiva with devotion brings liberation from rebirth for men.
By wearing rudrākṣa beads, one attains one-quarter [of the fruit]; by wearing sacred ash (vibhūti), one-quarter;
by the recitation of mantras, three-quarters; and through worship, one becomes possessed of complete devotion.
By worshipping both the Śivaliṅga and the devotee, a man shall attain liberation.
O twice-born ones, for one who reads this chapter or listens to it with a concentrated mind,
his devotion to Śiva will increase and become very firm.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
The sages said:
O great sage, tell us in due order the greatness of the *praṇava* and the six *liṅgas*,
as well as the worship of the devotee of Śiva, O Lord.
Sūta said:
This question has been rightly asked by you, whose wealth is asceticism;
Mahādeva alone knows the answer to it, and no one else.
Nevertheless, I shall indeed speak of it solely through the grace of Śiva.
May Śiva grant us and you abundant protection from this great ocean of saṃsāra, which is born of primordial nature (prakṛti). The wise know the Praṇava to be indeed a new, inner boat.
Those who know your *praṇava* understand it to be free from the proliferation of conceptual elaboration (*prapañca*) and devoid of existence and non-existence;
because it leads you pre-eminently (*prakarṣeṇa*) to liberation, they know it as the *praṇava*. It belongs to those yogins who recite it themselves and to the worshiper of its own mantra.
Having brought about the destruction of all karma, he possesses a new, primordial knowledge;
they describe him alone as being free from *māyā*, as the ever-new one.
They describe that Great Soul as preeminent, ever-new, and pure in his essential nature.
The wise know that as the *praṇava* because it indeed brings forth what is new.
The *praṇava* is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as subtle (*sūkṣma*) and gross (*sthūla*).
One should know the subtle to be the single syllable (*ekākṣara*), while they know the gross to be the five-syllabled (*pañcākṣara*).
The subtle [mantra] consists of five unmanifest syllables, while the other is clearly manifest.

For one who is liberated while living, the subtle mantra is indeed the essence of all, for it is his very core. It is the contemplation of the meaning of the mantra until the dissolution of one's own body.
When it has dissolved into one's own body, one attains Śiva in his fullness; this is certain. However, one who merely recites the mantra attains yoga; this is certain.
One who recites it thirty-six million times shall attain the certainty of yoga.
The subtle [sound] is to be known as twofold, distinguished by its short and long durations.
Following that are the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*;
for these are joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, and are endowed with the divisions of sound, time, and kalās.
Indeed, for yogins, the long *praṇava* resides within the heart;
however, the short *praṇava* is said to consist of the three principles ending with the syllable *ma*.
Śiva, Śakti, and their union—these three constitute the nature of the syllable *ma*.
Thus, this short mantra is to be recited by those who desire the destruction of all sins. Furthermore,
it is said that ten directions— earth, wind, gold, the ocean, and the sky, as well as the ten beginning with sound—
have subsequently proceeded from the lineage of the quarters.
For those engaged in worldly activity, it is indeed short; for those who have withdrawn from activity, however, it is long.

At the beginning of the *vyāhṛtis* and at the beginning of mantras, it may optionally be joined with the syllable *kāmam*. It should be employed at the beginning of the Vedas, as well as during salutations and the two daily junctions (*saṃdhyā*).
Having recited nine crores, a person becomes purified;
furthermore, by another nine crores, one attains victory over the earth;
and again, by another nine crores, one indeed attains victory over the waters.
Furthermore, by reciting it nine crores of times, one shall attain victory over fire;
again, by nine crores, one shall obtain victory over wind;
indeed, by reciting it nine crores of times, one attains victory over space.
By reciting the mantra nine crores of times for each of the [elements] beginning with smell in their respective order,
and again by reciting it nine crores of times for the ego (ahaṃkāra),
a person shall become eternally pure through the recitation of the mantra one thousand times.
Thereafter, O twice-born ones, there is indeed the recitation (japa) for the sake of one's own perfection.
When this has been recited one hundred and eight crores of times with the *praṇava*,
one who is awakened shall attain pure yoga.

One who is united with the yoga of purity is undoubtedly liberated while living (jīvanmukta). Constantly reciting and constantly meditating upon Śiva in the form of the Praṇava, that great yogi established in samādhi is indeed Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the sages, meters, deities, and so forth upon the body, one should then recite [the mantra].

The *praṇava* joined with the *mātṛkā* shall be the sage (*ṛṣi*) of this "body" [mantra]. By performing all this—the ten sages, the six paths (*adhvan*), and so forth—one obtains the fruit of the *nyāsa*.
For those who are active and mixed [in their practice], the gross praṇava is prescribed. Śiva-yogins are of three kinds, engaged in ritual action, austerity, and recitation;
they are distinguished by wealth and other possessions, as well as by the hands and other limbs, and by acts such as prostration.
One who is engaged in ritual action and worship is called a *kriyā-yogin*.
One who is devoted to worship, eats moderately, possesses mastery over the external senses,
and is free from malice toward others, is called a *tapo-yogin*.

One who is endowed with these qualities, who is ever free from anger and has renounced all desires and the like, who is always devoted to *japa* and is tranquil— him they know as a *japa-yogin*. [He should worship] the *śiva-yogins* with the sixteen types of ritual services (*upacāra*).
Through the sequence beginning with *sālokya* and so forth, a purified man shall attain liberation.
Now I shall explain the yoga of recitation (*japa*); listen to it, O twice-born ones!
Recitation is declared for the practitioner of austerity; it cleanses away even sacrifice.

O twice-born ones, preceded by "Śiva-nāma-namaḥ" in the dative case, there is the fivefold principle; for the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva is indeed the form of the gross *praṇava*. By the mere recitation of these five syllables, a person shall attain all perfections.

One should always recite the five-syllabled mantra joined with the *praṇava* (OM). Having received the instruction from the guru, O twice-born ones, one should begin on the first day of the bright fortnight and continue until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight while dwelling happily on auspicious ground.
The months of Māgha and Bhādrapada are distinguished as the most excellent among all times. Having restricted one's food, controlled one's speech, and restrained the senses,
one should constantly perform service toward oneself, the king, and the elders.

By merely reciting it a thousand times, one becomes pure; otherwise, one remains a debtor. One should recite the five-syllabled mantra five hundred thousand times while remembering Śiva—Śiva seated in the lotus posture, bestowing grace, and adorned with the Gaṅgā and the crescent moon.
He was resplendent with the Śakti seated upon his left thigh, surrounded by great hosts of attendants;
he meditated upon Sadāśiva, the Lord who holds a deer and an axe, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness,
and who is ever the bestower of grace.
Having first worshipped [the deity] mentally within his own heart or in the solar orb,
one who performs pure deeds should recite the five-syllabled mantra while facing the east. Having completed his daily rites on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight at dawn, he should proceed.
In a delightful and pure place, with a restrained and purified mind,
he should mutter twelve thousand recitations of the five-syllable mantra.
He should then choose excellent Śaiva Brahmins together with their wives as officiants.
She should choose one excellent preceptor who is a disciple of the venerable Lord and whose form is that of Ambā;
as well as five other excellent twice-born devotees of Śiva: Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Sadyojāta.
Having procured the materials for worship, one should begin the worship of Śiva.
Having performed the worship of Śiva according to the prescribed rule, one should commence the fire sacrifice (homa).
Having completed the rites up to the "mouth" [of the ritual] according to one's own manual, one should commence the fire sacrifice.
The wise man himself should offer ten, or one hundred,
or even one thousand oblations with *kāpila* ghee;
or he may have it performed by devotees of Śiva, numbering one hundred and eight.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, a pair of cows should likewise be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru.
Having meditated upon those [deities] beginning with Īśāna as being identical in form to the Guru accompanied by Ambā,
one should perform a ritual bath for one’s own head with the water used for washing their feet.
One obtains the fruit of an immediate bath in thirty-six crores of sacred fords. One should offer ten-fold food (daśāṅga-anna) to them with devotion;
and with a supreme mind, one should [worship] the wife of the Guru according to the sequence beginning with Īśāna.
Having honored [the guest] with the finest food according to the extent of one's wealth,
and having first offered Rudrākṣa beads and garments along with vaṭakas and apūpas,
one should then perform the bali offering and partake of a substantial meal.
Then, having prayed to the Lord of Gods, one should complete the recitation;
by performing the *puraścaraṇa* in this manner, a man becomes a master of the mantra (*mantrī*).
Furthermore, through five hundred thousand recitations, there shall be the destruction of all sins.
Beginning from Atala and proceeding in order up to Satyaloka,
one shall attain sovereignty over each respective world through five hundred thousand recitations.
If such a practitioner of recitation should die in the interim, he will be born on earth after the exhaustion of his [celestial] enjoyments.
Furthermore, by five hundred thousand [recitations], one shall attain proximity to Brahman;
furthermore, by another five hundred thousand, one shall attain the sovereignty of having the same form as [Brahman].
By a total of ten million [recitations], one shall become directly equal to Brahman.

Having thus attained union with the effected Brahman (kāryabrahman), he indeed enjoys whatever pleasures he desires until the dissolution of that Brahman. When another kalpa has commenced, he is born again as a son of Brahmā.
Furthermore, illuminated by ascetic fervor, he will gradually become liberated.
From the primary elements, beginning with earth, the worlds were created in succession—
the fourteen worlds from Pātāla up to Satyaloka, including the realms of Brahmā.

Above Satyaloka, extending up to Kṣama, are the fourteen worlds of Viṣṇu. In the world of Kṣama, Viṣṇu resides in the excellent city of Vaikuṇṭha; there, having performed protection through his great consort Lakṣmī, he presides over all activities.
Above that, twenty-eight worlds ending with Aśuci are situated.
In the world of Śuci, on Kailāsa, Rudra indeed dwells as the heart of all beings.
Above that, fifty-six worlds ending with Ahiṃsā are situated.
Having established himself in the world of non-violence (ahiṃsā) in the city of Kailāsaka, which is composed of knowledge,
the Lord of Action (Kāryeśvara), having caused all things to become unmanifest, presides over them.
At the end of that is the Wheel of Time (kālacakra), and beyond that is he who has transcended time (kālātīta).
There, presided over by Śiva, is the one called Kāleśvara;
adopting the nature of a buffalo, he joins all beings with Time (Kāla).
He is untruth, impurity, violence, and indeed mercilessness.
He has untruth and the other [vices] as his four feet; he possesses all parts and assumes forms at will.
He is the Fortune of Atheism, always associated with evil company and sounds outside the Veda.
He is joined with anger, black in color, and wears the guise of a great buffalo.
Maheśvara is said to exist only so long as [the state of] concealment (tirodhāna) persists;
indeed, below that is the experience of karma, while above that is the experience of knowledge.
Below that is karma, which arises from Māyā; above that is knowledge, which arises beyond Māyā.
The enjoyment of fortune through ritual action is called *vyatimāyā*; the enjoyment of fortune through knowledge is also called *vyatimāyā*.
They know that which is beyond that to be eternal enjoyment, while that which is below it is perishable.
Below that level there is concealment; above that, there is no concealment. Below that level there is indeed bondage by fetters; above that, there is no bondage.
Below that level, those who follow actions performed for desire undergo transmigration.
The enjoyment of the fruit of desireless action is proclaimed as being above that;
those devoted to the worship of the *bindu* revolve below it.
Indeed, those who worship the *liṅga* without desire proceed upwards from there.
Those who worship other gods while turning away from Śiva fall below;
those who are solely devoted to Śiva proceed upward beyond that.
Below that lies the limit of individual souls (jīva-koṭi), and above that lies the supreme limit (para-koṭi).
Those who are subject to saṃsāra remain below that [level], while those who are liberated indeed go above it. Those who worship material substances (prakṛti-dravya) revolve below that;
for those who worship the substance of the Supreme Person (puruṣa-dravya) go above it.
That which is below it is the *śakti-liṅga*, while that which is above it is the *śiva-liṅga*.
That which is below it is the veiled *liṅga*, whereas that which is above it is indeed unveiled.
That which is below it is the conceptualized *liṅga*, while that which is above it is truly non-conceptualized.
Below that is the external liṅga, and above that is the internal one.
Indeed, below that are the hundred and twelve worlds of Śakti;
below that is the form of Bindu, and above that is the form of Nāda.
Below that is the world of karma, but above that is the world of knowledge.
Above that indeed is salutation (*namaskāra*), which destroys the ego-sense of "I.
For it is said: "It does not obstruct the concealment of birth for living beings."
For it is the very meaning of the word "knowledge" (jñāna) that it wards off concealment; indeed,
those who worship the material (ādhibhautika) aspect revolve below it,
while those who worship the spiritual (ādhyātmika) aspect truly proceed beyond it.

Within that great Liṅga which is the Self of the worlds, extending as far as the boundary of the Vedas, even the eightfold bondage beginning with Prakṛti is established as the object of knowledge. Thus, everything pertaining to both the worldly and the Vedic should be understood in this manner.
Those who are endowed with virtues such as truthfulness and are devoted to the worship of Śiva cross over Kālacakra, which is mounted upon the buffalo of unrighteousness (adharma).
Above that is the Bull, Dharma, who bears the form of celibacy (brahmacarya).
But the bull, endowed with the feet beginning with truth (satya), stands at the forefront of the world of Śiva;
it has patience for its horns, tranquility for its ears, is adorned by the sound of the Vedas,
possesses faith as its eyes, and has a mind heavy with wisdom for its breath.
The Bull of Action (Kriyāvṛṣabha) and the others are always to be known as existing within the Causes (Kāraṇas).
That Bull of Action, which is Dharma, presides over that which transcends time (Kālātīta).
A single day of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa is said to be equal to their respective lifespans.
Beyond that, there is neither day nor night, nor birth, death, and so forth.
Furthermore, those [beings] ending with the Satya-loka of the cause are likewise created from the causal Brahman;
indeed, they are eternally fashioned beyond that from the elements beginning with smell.
The fourteen worlds are situated above Sūkṣmagandhasvarūpa;
again, the fourteen worlds are situated above Kāraṇaviṣṇu;
and the twenty-eight worlds are considered to be above Kāraṇarudra.
Furthermore, there are fifty-six worlds above that of the Lord of Causes (Kāraṇeśa).
Beyond that is the world known as Brahmacharya, which is esteemed by Śiva.
It is located right there in Jñānakailāsa, which is endowed with five enclosures (āvaraṇas).

Endowed with the five circles (pañcamandala) and possessed of the five portions of Brahmā (pañcabrahmakalā), and joined with the primordial power (ādiśakti), that indeed is the primordial liṅga (ādiliṅga). This is declared to be the abode of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
United with the supreme power (paraśakti), the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) is right there;
he is proficient in the fivefold acts— creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace— and his form consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
He whose nature is meditation and who is ever intent upon bestowing grace,
seated in the posture of *samādhi*, shines as one who finds delight in his own self (*svātmārāma*).
The ritual of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā-karma*) for him is performed through the sequence of meditation and other such practices.
Through the performance of daily rites and sacrifices, one’s mind should be directed toward the actions of Śiva.
By means of these and other Śiva-related rituals, one should accomplish the knowledge of Śiva.
All those who have attained that vision are indeed liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Liberation is indeed the state of delighting in one's own self by means of the true nature of the Self.
One who is well-established in the practices of ritual action, austerity, recitation, knowledge, meditation, and dharma,
and who has obtained the vision of Śiva, indeed attains that very state of delighting in one's own self.
Just as the sun will dispel impurity with its own rays,
so shall Śambhu, who is skilled in compassion, dispel ignorance. But when ignorance has ceased, the knowledge of Śiva proceeds.

Through the knowledge of Śiva, one shall attain the state of delighting in the Self, which is one's own true nature. Upon the perfect realization of this self-delight, a person becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done; furthermore, by means of ten million recitations, he shall attain the station of Brahman.
Furthermore, by a hundred lakhs [of recitations], one shall attain the station of Viṣṇu;
furthermore, by a hundred lakhs, one shall attain the station of Rudra;
and furthermore, by a hundred lakhs, one shall attain the station of sovereignty.
Furthermore, by means of such recitation alone, being well-composed,
one shall indeed attain the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra), which consists of the worlds beginning with the realm of Śiva.
The Wheel of Time consists of five wheels, each succeeding one [attained] in successive order.

The wise know that the Brahma-wheel consists of the delusion of creation (*sṛṣṭi-moha*), while the Vaiṣṇava-wheel consists of the delusion of enjoyment (*bhoga-moha*). They know the Raudra-wheel to consist of the delusions of anger (*kopa-moha*), and the Īśvara-wheel to consist of wandering (*bhramaṇa*).
The Śiva-wheel consists of the delusion of knowledge (*jñāna-moha*); thus the wise know the five wheels.
Furthermore, by ten crores [of recitations], one attains the station of the causal Brahman;
and again, by another ten crores, one shall attain the sovereignty of that station.
In this manner, having attained the stations of Viṣṇu and the others of great majesty in due order—
Having gradually attained the sovereignty of those [deities] of the Great-Souled One,
and having recited the mantra one hundred and five crores of times without sloth,
he attains the world of Śiva, which lies outside the fifth enclosure.
There, the royal assembly hall is the supreme abode of Nandin;
there, the Bull, whose form is asceticism, is likewise seen.
That is the station of Sadyojāta, the fifth and highest enclosure.
Furthermore, the abode of Vāmadeva is the fourth enclosure;
next is the residence of Aghora, the supreme third enclosure;
and the auspicious second enclosure belongs to Sāmba Puruṣa himself.
Then follows the first enclosure of Īśāna, the supreme;
next is the station of Dhyānadharmā, the fifth pavilion;
and there is the abode of Balinātha, which bestows the full nectar of immortality.
Afterwards, the fourth pavilion is the form of Candraśekhara;
the third supreme pavilion is the station of Somaskanda;
and the second pavilion, the devotees call the dance pavilion (Nṛtyamaṇḍapa).
First is the root-place of Māyā; that very location is beautiful.
Beyond that is the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), the supreme and auspicious station of the Liṅga.
After the station of Nandin, they do not know the full majesty of Śiva.
Nandīśvara, standing outside, worships the five-syllabled [mantra].
Thus, it was obtained by me again from Nandīśa through the lineage of gurus.
Beyond that, it is to be realized within oneself; O Śiva, it has not been experienced by anyone else.
"By the grace of Śiva alone, the majesty of the world of Śiva can be directly known by all;
it cannot be known otherwise," so say the believers.
