In this manner, those Brahmins who have conquered their senses shall be liberated.

I shall now describe the sequence for others; listen with respect as I speak. For Brāhmaṇas, the mantra ending in "namaḥ" is to be recited according to the teacher’s instruction. According to the rule, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra five hundred thousand times for the sake of longevity.
To remove the state of womanhood, however, one should again recite five hundred thousand times;
having become a man through the mantra, the wise one shall be liberated in due course. A Kṣatriya will likewise remove his status as a Kṣatriya by means of five hundred thousand recitations.
Furthermore, a Kṣatriya shall become a Brāhmaṇa by means of five hundred thousand [recitations];
through the attainment of mantras and recitation, that man shall gradually become liberated. A Vaiśya, moreover, shall remove his Vaiśya-status by means of five hundred thousand [recitations].
Furthermore, by five hundred thousand [recitations], he is called a *mantra-kṣatriya*;
furthermore, by five hundred thousand, he will cast off his status as a *kṣatriya*;
furthermore, by five hundred thousand, he is called a *mantra-brāhmaṇa*.
And a Śūdra, by reciting [the mantra] twenty-five hundred thousand times preceded by "Namaḥ" and "Oṃ," attains the status of a mantric Brahmin and thereafter becomes a pure twice-born.
Whether it be a woman, a man, a Brahmin, or anyone else.
One who is afflicted by disease should always recite [the mantra] ending in *namaḥ* or preceded by *namaḥ*.
Then, the preceptor should likewise demonstrate the procedure for women in due order.
Indeed, at the conclusion of five hundred thousand recitations, the practitioner should do so for the sake of pleasing Śiva.
Having performed the great consecration offering (*mahābhiṣeka-naivedya*), one should honor the devotees;
through the worship of a devotee of Śiva, Śiva becomes most pleased.
There is no difference between Śiva and the devotee of Śiva, for he is indeed Śiva himself.
Indeed, by the retention of the mantra whose nature is Śiva, one becomes Śiva himself.
For in the body of a devotee of Śiva, Śiva becomes the supreme reality.
Devotees of Śiva know all ritual actions to be the entirety of Vedic rites.

To whatever extent the Śiva-mantra has been recited by someone in due order, to that same extent the presence of Śiva truly resides in that body; of this there is no doubt. Likewise, for a woman who is a devotee of Śiva, her form becomes the liṅga of the Goddess.
Indeed, as long as one recites the mantra of the Goddess, her presence remains.
The wise man, himself assuming the form of the Word (Śabda), should worship Śiva;
having himself become Śiva, he should worship the Supreme Śakti.
One should worship the Śakti, the Bera, and the Liṅga through the illusion of painting;
having regarded the Śiva-liṅga as Śiva himself and one’s own self as the form of Śakti,
and having regarded the Śakti-liṅga as the Goddess and oneself as the form of Śiva.
The Śivaliṅga consists of the form of Nāda and the form of Bindu, along with Śakti;
as the subordinate and primary elements, they are mutually attached as the Liṅga.
One should worship Śiva together with Śakti through the fundamental contemplation that Śiva is inseparable from Śakti.
One should worship those devoted to Śiva— who are the very form of the Śiva-mantra and the very form of Śiva—
with the sixteen types of offerings, and thus obtain one's desired goal;
for by means of such service and other acts toward a devotee of Śiva who bears the *liṅga*, [one attains the fruit].

The wise man should cause joy to arise, and Śiva will become exceedingly pleased. He should always worship the devotees of Śiva, together with their wives, five, twelve, or even a hundred at a time, providing them with food and other offerings.
He who is non-deceptive regarding wealth, body, mantra, and meditative visualization, being of the very nature of Śiva and Śakti, is not born again on this earth.
The portion from the navel downwards belongs to Brahmā; the portion up to the throat belongs to Viṣṇu.

The body of a devotee of Śiva is declared to be the "face-liṅga. Whether the deceased have been subjected to cremation and other rites, or whether they have not been cremated, one should indeed worship Śiva alone as the primordial ancestor (ādi-pitṛ) on their behalf.
Having performed worship of the Primordial Mother, one should also honor the devotees of Śiva.

Upon death, having reached the world of the ancestors, one shall become liberated through the gradual process. One who is endowed with austerity is superior to ten who are merely engaged in ritual action.

One engaged in recitation (*japa*) is superior to hundreds who are engaged in austerity (*tapas*). One who possesses the knowledge of Śiva is superior to thousands who are engaged in recitation. Among hundreds of thousands of those possessing the knowledge of Śiva, one engaged in meditation (*dhyāna*) is superior.
One established in meditative absorption (samādhi) excels over ten million who are merely engaged in dhyāna.
Due to this progressive excellence, each subsequent stage of worship possesses a progressively superior fruit,
the nature of which is difficult even for the wise to comprehend.

Therefore, what man can truly know the greatness of a devotee of Śiva? The worship of Śiva and Śakti is the worship of the devotee of Śiva; the man who performs this with devotion becomes Śiva himself and prospers in auspiciousness.

The Brahmin who recites this chapter, which is meaningful and esteemed by the Vedas, shall become a knower of Śiva’s wisdom and rejoices together with Śiva. O lords of sages, one who knows the distinctions should cause the devotees of Śiva to hear it.
"O wise ones, through the grace of Śiva, there shall be the attainment of Śiva's favor.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 18.
The sages said:
"O best of those who know all things, please explain the true nature of bondage and liberation.
Sūta said:
I shall speak of bondage, liberation, and the means [thereto]; listen with respect.
Bound by the eightfold bond beginning with *prakṛti*, he is called the individual soul (*jīva*).
Released from the eightfold bond beginning with *prakṛti*, he is called liberated.
The mastery over primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the rest is called liberation by its very nature. A bound soul, when released, is then called a liberated soul.
Prior to primordial nature are intellect (*buddhi*) and ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which consist of the qualities (*guṇas*).
These five subtle elements (tanmātras) together with the eight beginning with primordial nature (prakṛti) are known as the group of eight starting with prakṛti.
The body born from these eight beginning with prakṛti is said to be produced by karma;
furthermore, the body is born from karma, and birth and karma occur again and again.
The body is to be known as threefold: gross, subtle, and causal.
The gross is said to provide the capacity for activity; the subtle provides the enjoyment of the senses;
and the causal exists for the sake of the soul's experience, in accordance with the karma of the individual soul.

One experiences the fruit of pleasure and pain through meritorious and sinful actions. Therefore, bound by the rope of karma, the individual soul (jīva) revolves incessantly like a wheel, driven by the actions of the three bodies.
One should praise the Maker of the Wheel for the sake of ceasing the wheel’s rotation.
Śiva is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the great wheel;
indeed, Maheśa is the Maker of the Wheel because he stands beyond primordial nature.
Just as a living child drinks or vomits water,
so does Śiva preside over Prakṛti and the rest, having brought them under his control.
Because everything has been brought under his control, he is remembered as Śiva.

For Śiva alone is omniscient, perfectly complete, and free from desire. The omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, and eternally undiminished power of the Great Lord (Maheśvara) constitute that infinite power which the Veda perceives as mental sovereignty.
Therefore, by the grace of Śiva, one may come under the influence of Prakṛti and the other [principles].
For the sake of obtaining the grace of Śiva, one should worship Śiva alone.
But how can there be any worship for him who is desireless and complete?
Action performed for the sake of Śiva shall produce grace. One should worship Śiva in a *liṅga*, an image, or among the devotees;
one should worship Him with body, mind, speech, and even with wealth.
Indeed, through worship, Maheśa— Śiva, who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti)—
truly bestows his grace, especially upon the worshipper.
By the grace of Śiva, one's karma and other factors gradually come under one's own control.

When everything, from the commencement of action to its very nature, comes under one's control, then one is said to be liberated; as one who delights in his own self, he shines forth. When the body of karma has become subject [to him] through the grace of the Supreme Lord, [he is liberated].

Then, dwelling in the world of Śiva is called *sālokya* (residing in the same world). When one has come under his control through that alone, one attains *sāmīpya* (proximity) to Śambhu. But then, through [the mastery of] weapons and so forth, as well as ritual actions and so forth, one attains *sāyujya* (union) with Śiva.
And through the attainment of great grace, the intellect shall also come under control.
For the intellect is the effect of primordial nature (prakṛti); its creation is thus described.
Furthermore, by means of great grace, primordial nature will come under control.
Then, the sovereignty of Śiva will be attained without effort;
having acquired the sovereignty of Śiva, such as omniscience and the rest, he shines within his own self. Those devoted to the Vedas and Āgamas call this *sāyujya*.
In this manner, liberation shall come through worship of the *liṅga* and so forth by one's own effort.
Therefore, for the sake of Śiva’s grace, one should worship Śiva with ritual actions and other means.
One should always perform Śiva-rituals, Śiva-austerities, and the recitation of Śiva-mantras.
One should practice the knowledge of Śiva and meditation on Śiva more and more;
indeed, one should spend the time from sleep until death in the contemplation of Śiva.
One should worship Śiva with flowers such as the *sadyojāta* and others, and [Śiva] will come.
The sages said:
"Tell us in its entirety the procedure for the worship of Śiva at the beginning with the *liṅga*.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, listen as I describe the sequence of the *liṅgas* exactly as it is.
That very first *liṅga* is the *praṇava*, which fulfills all desires;
for its form is the subtle *praṇava*, and its nature is indeed subtle and fruitless [in terms of worldly results].
The gross liṅga is indeed with parts (sakala), and it is called the five-syllabled mantra.
The worship of these two is declared to be austerity; both directly bestow liberation.
There are also many other liṅgas consisting of the Puruṣa and Prakṛti.

Śiva alone knows how to describe those in detail, and no one else; I shall declare to you the signs known as the modifications of the earth. First is the self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅga, and second is the bindu-liṅga.
The stationary and the moving, and the Guru-liṅga as the fifth;
Śiva, pleased by the asceticism of the divine sages, indeed remained present there for their sake.
Within the earth, Śarva exists as the seed in the form of sound (nāda).
Like the sprout of a stationary plant, he emerged clearly from the earth;
because he was born of himself, they know him as Svayambhū (the Self-Existent).
Through the worship of that liṅga, knowledge increases spontaneously.
Whether on gold, silver, or the like, or even upon a mound of earth,
one should draw a *liṅga* with one’s own hand, accompanied by the pure *praṇava* mantra.
Having drawn the *yantra-liṅga*, one should perform the rites of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and invocation (*āvāhana*).
Whatever linga there may be, whether stationary or mobile, consists of the Bindu and Nāda;
for this is undoubtedly seen by Śiva as consisting of pure contemplation (bhāvanāmaya).
Wherever Śambhu is trusted, there He bestows the fruit upon that person.
When this is written by one’s own hand upon a yantra, whether natural or artificial,
one should invoke and worship Śambhu with the sixteen types of ritual offerings (upacāras). By doing so, one personally attains sovereignty, and through practice, wisdom shall arise.
Indeed, by the gods and the sages as well, for the sake of their own spiritual perfection,
that supreme *liṅga* was established within a pure maṇḍala with mantras and their own hands,
and installed with pure contemplation.
They say that the *pauruṣa-liṅga* is what is called "established" (*pratiṣṭhita*).
By the constant worship of that *liṅga*, one shall attain human sovereignty.
[It is worshipped] by great Brahmins as well as by kings of great wealth.
A linga fashioned by an artisan and installed with mantras is indeed natural (prākṛta),
and it bestows worldly power and enjoyment. That which is powerful and eternal is called the "human" (pauruṣa) [linga].
That which is weak and impermanent is indeed called *prākṛta* (material).
The *liṅga* [is located] at the navel, the tongue, the tip of the nose, and the crest, in that order;
the final *ādhyātmika-liṅga* (internal liṅga) is situated in the three worlds beginning with the hips.
Mountains are said to be *pauruṣa* (human-made), while the surface of the earth is known as *prākṛta* (natural).
Trees and the like are to be understood as *pauruṣa*, whereas shrubs and the like are known as *prākṛta*.
The sixty-day ripening grain (*ṣāṣṭika*) is to be known as *prākṛta*, while rice and wheat are *pauruṣa*.
One should know that *aiśvarya* (sovereignty) is the human power that bestows the eight supernatural attainments (*siddhis*), beginning with *aṇimā*.
The orthodox (*āstikas*) say that the *prākṛta* (natural) [power] has as its objects beautiful women, wealth, and the like.
First, among the mobile *liṅgas*, the *rasaliṅga* is proclaimed.
The *rasaliṅga* grants all desired objects to Brāhmaṇas;
the auspicious *bāṇaliṅga* bestows great sovereignty upon Kṣatriyas;
and the *svarṇaliṅga* indeed grants the status of a great lord of wealth to Vaiśyas.
A stone *liṅga* is auspicious and brings great purification for Śūdras;
a crystal or *bāṇa-liṅga* grants all desires to everyone.
In the absence of one's own [liṅga], the worship of another’s is not prohibited.
For women, O King, the linga is made of stone, especially for those who have husbands; for widows who follow the path of active worldly life (pravṛtta), one made of crystal is prescribed;
for widows who have turned away from worldly life (nivṛtta), a linga of mercury is highly recommended.
Whether in childhood, youth, or even old age, O observers of good vows,
for women a linga made of pure crystal bestows all enjoyments.
For those engaged in worldly life, the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā) on earth grants all desired objects.
Having proceeded with the vessel itself, one should perform all the worship.
At the conclusion of the consecration, one should offer an oblation (*naivedya*) of śāli rice.
At the end of the worship, one should install the *liṅga* in separate caskets within the house.
Those who have desisted from ritual worship with hands should offer their own food [to the deity].
For those who have attained the state of cessation (nivṛtta), the supreme, subtle liṅga alone is distinguished as superior.
One should perform the worship of sacred ash (vibhūti) and offer sacred ash [as the oblation].

Having performed worship, one should always carry that liṅga upon one's head. Ashes are said to be of three kinds: those from the world, those from the Vedas, and those from the fire of Śiva. One should employ the ash produced from the worldly fire for the purpose of purifying substances.
For objects made of clay, wood, or metal, as well as for grains such as sesame seeds and other substances,
and likewise for garments and the like—
even for those that have become stale— purification by means of ash is desired.
For those things defiled by dogs and the like, purification by means of ash is prescribed. One should apply ash with water or without water as is appropriate;
likewise, one should wear at the conclusion of those rites the ash produced from the fire of the Vedas.

The karma produced by mantras and ritual actions assumes the form of ash within the fire; through the wearing of that ash, the karma becomes transferred into one's own self. One should burn bilva wood with the Aghora mantra.
It is proclaimed as the "Auspicious Fire" (Śivāgni); by that [fire] is burnt what is born of the Auspicious Fire.
First, one should take the dung of a tawny cow, or indeed only that which is purely bovine;
or else the wood of the *śamī*, *aśvattha*, *palāśa*, *vaṭa*, *āragvadha*, and *bilva* trees.
One should burn that purified [body] with the fire of Śiva; that indeed is the ash born from the fire of Śiva.
Or, while reciting the Śiva-mantra, one should burn a piece of wood in a fire of *darbha* grass.
Having thoroughly purified it with a cloth, one should place it in a new jar.
That [ash] is to be accepted for the sake of illumination, and it is also honored; for Śiva,
in the beginning,
established the very meaning of the word "bhasman" (ash) in such a way that a king takes tribute from his own domain.
Just as non-human beings, having consumed crops and the like, extract their essence;
and just as the digestive fire within the body, having consumed various and abundant foods,
nourishes its own body with the most refined essence from that essence.

Likewise, Śiva, the Supreme Lord, though the creator of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), having burnt away the essence of that world which was to be presided over by him, took hold of it; and having burnt the phenomenal world,
Śiva deposited its ashes within his own self.
Under the pretext of smearing himself with ashes (uddhūlana), he seized the essence of the universe;
he established his own jewel within his very body.
His hair was formed from the essence of space, and his face from the essence of wind.
The heart [should be marked] with the essence of fire, the waist with the essence of water, and the knees with the essence of earth;
likewise, all other limbs [should be marked].
The triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra) is indeed the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
Likewise, Maheśvara exists at the edge of the forehead in the form of an *atilaka*.
Through his own increase (*bhavṛddhi*), he himself considers all this;
by him alone has the entire essence of the world-process (*prapañca*) been brought under control.

Therefore, because there is no one who can subjugate him, he is remembered as Śiva. Just as among all wild beasts there is the "beast-slayer" (mṛgahiṃsaka), the lion, so too, because there is no "beast" (mṛga) capable of harming him, he is called Siṃha.
The letter *i* is known as the Puruṣa, who is eternal peace, bliss, and joy;
the letter *va* is Śakti, the immortal. Their union is called Śiva.
Therefore, having thus made one's own self Śiva, one should worship Śiva.

Therefore, one should first apply the smearing of ashes and then wear the supreme triple mark (tripuṇḍra). Indeed, at the time of worship, it should be with water for the sake of purification, or without water. Whether by day or by night, whether a woman or a man—ŚivaP 1.18.78ab–79ab.

For the sake of worship, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* with water and ashes. He who performs worship after applying the *tripuṇḍra* with water and ashes certainly attains the full fruit of the worship of Śiva, including all its constituent parts.
By wearing [the ashes] with the Bhasma-Śiva mantra, one indeed becomes a transcendent ascetic (atyāśramī).
Because he is solely devoted to Śiva, he is proclaimed a "Śiva-ascetic" (śivāśramī). For one who is steadfastly dedicated to the vow of Śiva, there is neither impurity nor birth-defilement (sūtaka).

One should wear a tilaka of ash on the forehead, applied with clay, either by one's own hand or by the hand of a guru; this is the mark of a devotee of Śiva. The etymological analysis of the word *guru* is said to be "one who restrains (*rundhati*) the qualities (*guṇa*)."
He restrains and dispels the qualities such as rajas along with their modifications;
having transcended the qualities, Paraśiva, assuming the form of the Guru,
casts aside the triad of qualities and first awakens [the disciple] to Śiva.
To those disciples who place their full trust, he is called "Guru.
Therefore, the wise man should understand that the body of the Guru is indeed the Guru-liṅga;
the worship of the Guru-liṅga consists in the service of the Guru.
He makes his learning heard through service by body, mind, and speech.
Whatever has been previously spoken by the Guru— whether it be possible or indeed impossible—
he certainly performs it, being one whose soul is purified, even at the cost of his life or his wealth.

Therefore, one who is fit for the Vaiśasa initiation is called a disciple. Having offered everything, including his body and other possessions, to the Guru, the good disciple should first offer the first-fruits of his cooking and then eat with the Guru’s permission.
The disciple is called "son" because of his constant union with the state of being a disciple.
Having been poured as the semen of the mantra from the linga of the tongue into the womb of the ears,
the son born of the mantra should worship his father, the Guru.

The biological father indeed causes his son to sink into the cycle of worldly existence; however, the spiritual teacher, who is the father who awakens one, delivers him from that very cycle. Having understood the difference between these two, one should worship both the biological father and the spiritual teacher.
One should also serve the guru with personal attendance and with wealth acquired by oneself;
for the limbs of the guru, beginning from the feet and ending with the hair, are the very forms of the Liṅga,
[to be honored] through sandals and other such items, and by attending to his feet and so forth.
One should worship with ritual baths, consecrations, food offerings, and meals.
Indeed, the worship of the Guru is itself the worship of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Whatever remains from the Guru’s portion shall bring about the purification of one's own self.
O twice-born ones, the remnants of the guru, consisting of water, food, and so forth, left over from Śiva,
should be accepted and consumed by disciples who are devotees of Śiva.
Without the permission of the guru, all such things would be like those belonging to a thief.
One should diligently seek out a teacher who knows the distinctions [of the scriptures], for even a teacher must be one who understands these particulars.
For it is the one who knows the distinctions who can grant liberation, since the goal to be accomplished is the release from ignorance.
Furthermore, at the outset, the pacification of obstacles must be performed so that the ritual action may reach its completion.
"A rite performed without obstacles and with all its constituent parts becomes truly fruitful.
Therefore, at the beginning of every ritual action, a wise person should worship Vighneśa.
For the sake of removing all impediments, a wise person should worship all the gods."

Fever and other diseases, as well as ailments caused by knots [in the body], are considered to be afflictions of an internal nature (*ādhyātmika*). Likewise, there are those arising from *piśācas*, jackals, and the like, as well as those originating from anthills and similar formations;
and even when lizards and other such creatures suddenly fall [upon one].
Even when seeing a house-tortoise, a snake, a woman, or a wicked person,
and even regarding the birth of trees, women, cows, and so forth,
future suffering arrives; therefore, that is material desire.
Impurity, the fall of Saturn, and likewise the great pestilence;
fever, the plague, cholera, cow-plague, and smallpox;
[the afflictions caused by] the transit of planets at one's birth star, planetary conjunctions, and when one's own zodiacal sign is affected.

The sight of bad dreams and so forth, as well as those [omens] pertaining to the external world and the divine; the touch of a corpse, a *caṇḍāla*, or one who has fallen [from grace], occurring when one has gone inside the house—
when such things arise, they are indicators of future suffering.
The wise man should perform a peace-offering (*śāntiyajña*) for the pacification of those defects,
either in a temple, a cow-pen, at a sacred shrine (*caitya*), or in the courtyard of his house,
upon an altar (*dhiṣṇya*) one span high, measuring two cubits, and well-decorated.
Having set aside a measure of rice and grain sufficient for a single meal, and having moved around it,
one should draw a lotus in the center and likewise draw [the other symbols] in the cardinal directions.
Then, a water-pot wrapped with thread and fumigated with fresh guggulu resin [should be placed there].
One should place a great pitcher in the center and likewise arrange them in the cardinal directions;
similarly, one should place pitchers with stalks, mango leaves, *kūrca* grass, and so forth, in the eight [directions].
One should fill them with water purified by mantras and endowed with the five substances.
Likewise, one should sequentially cast in the nine gems, beginning with sapphire;
then the wise man should select a preceptor who is knowledgeable in ritual action and accompanied by his wife,
and he should place therein golden images of Viṣṇu and of Indra and the other deities.
One should invoke and worship Viṣṇu in the central pitcher together with his head;
then one should worship Indra and the others in order, starting from the east, according to their respective mantras,
using their individual names in the dative case followed by "namaḥ" in the proper sequence.
The preceptor alone should perform all the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
Together with the officiating priests (ṛtvij), the preceptor should recite the mantra one hundred times for each of those measures.
At the conclusion of the recitation, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the western part of the water-pot (kumbha).
The wise should perform [the rite] ten million times, one hundred thousand times, a thousand times, or one hundred and eight times;
or for a single day, or nine days, or even just a maṇḍala,
according to what is appropriate and in accordance with the time and place.
For the purpose of pacification, one should perform the *śamī* oblation; for the sake of livelihood, [one should use] the *palāśa* tree.
One should offer oblations with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), rice, and clarified butter as the sacrificial materials, using either the name [of the deity] or the mantra.
Whatever material was used at the commencement, that same material should be employed until the conclusion of the rite.
At the conclusion of the *puṇyāha-vācana*, one should sprinkle [the area] with water on that day;

afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas according to the number of oblations (*āhuti*). The preceptor (*ācārya*) and the learned officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should subsist on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
Having worshipped the planets beginning with Āditya, at the very conclusion of all the fire-offerings (homa),
one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) consisting of the nine gems in their proper order.
Thereafter, one should perform the tenfold gift (daśadāna), and after that, the abundant gift (bhūridāna).
The wealth of children, of those who have been initiated, of householders,
and of forest-dwellers; as well as that of maidens, of those with husbands, and thereafter of widows—
all these, along with all the ritual implements, one should offer to the preceptor.
Yama is remembered as the lord of portents, epidemics, and suffering;
therefore, for the sake of pleasing Yama, one should cause a gift of time (kāladāna) to be bestowed.
One may do so with a hundred niṣkas, or again, with ten niṣkas.
One should fashion an image of Kāla in human form, holding a noose and a goad;
one should then perform the gift of that golden image along with a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā).
Thereafter, one should perform a gift of sesame seeds for the sake of attaining a full lifespan.
One should perform the offering of ghee and the inspection [of the deity] for the cessation of disease.
One should feed a thousand Brahmins, or even a hundred if one is poor;
if there is a lack of wealth, the poor man should act according to his capacity.

One should perform the great worship of Bhairava for the pacification of spirits and other malevolent forces. At the conclusion, one should perform the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka) and offer food (naivedya) to Śiva.
Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins in the form of a grand feast.
By performing the sacrifice in this manner, one shall attain the pacification of all defects.
One should perform this *śānti-yajña* every year in the month of Phālguna;
however, in the event of an inauspicious sight or similar misfortune, one should perform it immediately, even within a single month.
Upon encountering great sins and the like, one should perform the worship of Bhairava;
upon the onset of a major disease, one should again perform a formal vow (*saṃkalpa*);
and when impoverished in all respects, one should then perform the offering of a lamp.
If one is unable even for that, having bathed, one should certainly perform some act of giving;
the wise man should offer salutations to the Sun-god with the mantra one hundred and eight times, or he may cause it to be performed one thousand,
ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or ten million times.
All the deities shall be satisfied by the sacrifice consisting of prostration.
When the intellect is offered into Your own nature, it finds no pleasure in anything other than You, who are never empty.
And that sense of "I" which belongs to us is abandoned once You have been seen.
"I am bowed down before you with my own body; O Lord, you are the great sky.
You are not empty, for you are my very own nature; I am now your servant. One should perform the self-sacrifice of salutation in a manner that is appropriate."
Then, having offered the food offering (naivedya) to Śiva, one should take the betel leaf.
One should personally perform one hundred and eight circumambulations of Śiva;
otherwise, one may have another perform a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or even ten million.
By circumambulating Śiva, every sin is destroyed in an instant.
Disease is the root of suffering, for sin is indeed the root of disease. It is taught that the removal of sins occurs through dharma alone.
Dharma performed for the sake of Śiva is capable of dispelling sin.
Among the dharmas of Śiva, circumambulation is declared to be the direct witness.
Indeed, the *praṇava* in the form of recitation is the circumambulation through action.
Birth and death are declared to be the dual wheel of Māyā.
Indeed, this wheel of Māyā belonging to Śiva is called the *balipīṭha*.
Starting from the *balipīṭha*, one should proceed indeed in a clockwise direction.
Having gone from one step to another, one should enter the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha).
Then, one should perform a prostration; this is declared to be the circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa).
Departing [from the altar] constitutes the attainment of rebirth, while the prostration is the surrender of the self.
Birth and death are a pair bestowed by the *māyā* of Śiva;
one to whom this pair is granted by the *māyā* of Śiva shall not again become a master of his own self. As long as the embodied being is dependent on action, he is called bound.
The wise declare that liberation consists in the mastery over the three bodies.
For Śiva, the supreme cause, is the director of the wheel of Māyā;
Śiva wipes away the duality bestowed by the Māyā of Śiva.
One should offer whatever pair of opposites has been fashioned by Śiva right there;
the wise should know that circumambulation and salutation are exceedingly dear to Śiva.
Circumambulations and prostrations are for Śiva, the Supreme Self.
The performance of worship with the sixteen services bestows the fruit [of liberation].
Indeed, there is no sin on the surface of the earth that cannot be destroyed by circumambulation;
therefore, one should destroy all evil solely through circumambulation.

Devoted to the worship of Śiva, observing silence, and endowed with virtues such as truthfulness, he should practice each one of these: ritual action, austerity, recitation, knowledge, and meditation. Through this, he attains sovereignty, a divine body, knowledge, and the removal of ignorance and doubt.
The proximity of Śiva is the fruit of these [acts], beginning with ritual action (kriyā). Through the instrument [of knowledge], one attains the fruit by the removal of darkness;
and those [impurities] produced by the intellect of the ignorant are wiped away from birth.

A devotee of Śiva should perform rituals and other duties according to the place, the time, the body, and the wealth, as is appropriate. A wise person should dwell in a sacred site of Śiva with well-acquired wealth earned through righteous means.
They know that water and food which are free from injury to living beings and devoid of excessive hardship,
when consecrated with the five-syllabled mantra, lead to happiness. Alternatively, they say that for a poor person, food obtained through begging may bestow knowledge.
The alms-food of a devotee of Śiva increases devotion to Śiva;
they call the alms-food of a Śiva-yogin the "sacrificial session of Śambhu.
By whatever means and wherever on earth it may be, [one should accept it].
Always eating pure food and observing silence, one should not reveal the secret [teaching].
Indeed, one should proclaim only the majesty of Śiva to his devotees.
No one other than Śiva knows the secret of the Śiva-mantra.
A devotee of Śiva should always reside taking refuge in the Śiva-liṅga;
by taking refuge in the liṅga of Sthāṇu, O brahmins, he himself becomes Sthāṇu.
Through the worship of the mobile liṅga (cara-liṅga), he will certainly be liberated in due course.
Everything regarding the supreme means and the goal has been told in brief,
as it was previously taught in detail and as I myself heard it in the past. May there be welfare for you all, and may that devotion to Śiva remain firm.

O wise ones, the man who always reads this chapter or hears it shall obtain the knowledge of Śiva through the grace of Śiva. Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Śiva-liṅga," in the Sādhyasādhanakhaṇḍa of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 19. The Sages said: "O Sūta, O Sūta, may you live long! You are blessed and possessed of devotion to Śiva. (ŚivaP 1.19.1ab)
The greatness of the *liṅga*, which bestows its fruits, has been correctly described by you. Now,
O Vyāsa, tell me once more about the greatness of the earthen *Māheśa-liṅga*,
which has been declared to be the most excellent of all.
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, with true devotion and without exception;
the greatness of the earthen liṅga of Śiva is being proclaimed by me.
Among these aforementioned types of lingas, the earthen linga is the most excellent.
O Brahmins, by worshipping it, many have attained perfection—
namely Hari, Brahmā, the ṛṣis, and likewise the Prajāpatis.
Having worshipped the earthen liṅga, all the twice-born attained their desired goals.
Gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas—
as well as many others— having worshipped it, attained supreme perfection.
In the Kṛta age, the liṅga is made of jewels; in the Tretā, it is produced from gold;
in the Dvāpara, mercury is best; but in the Kali age, the earthen one is supreme.
Among all the eight forms [of Śiva], O noble ones, the earthen form is indeed the most excellent.
Therefore, for Brāhmaṇas who have not been worshipped by others, asceticism yields great fruit.
Just as Maheśvara is the eldest and most excellent among all the gods,
so too is the earthen linga declared to be the most excellent among all lingas.
Just as among all rivers the celestial Gaṅgā is the eldest and most excellent,
so among all liṅgas the earthen one is said to be the best.
Just as among all mantras the Praṇava is indeed remembered as the greatest.
Thus, this earthen [liṅga] is indeed the most excellent, worthy of being propitiated and worshipped;
just as among all castes the Brāhmaṇa is said to be the best,
so among all liṅgas the earthen one is said to be the best.
Just as Kāśī is remembered as the most excellent among all cities,
so the earthen linga (pārthiva-liṅga) is said to be the best among all lingas;
and just as the Śivarātri vow is supreme among all vows.
Just as among all goddesses, the power of Śiva (Śaivī-śakti) is remembered as supreme, so too among all lingas, the earthen one (pārthiva) is declared the best.
Just as among all goddesses, the power of Śiva is remembered as supreme,
so too among all lingas, the earthen one is declared the best.
If one worships another deity while possessing a *liṅga* made of earth that belongs by nature to Śiva, that worship becomes futile;
likewise, bathing, giving gifts, and so forth become in vain.
The propitiation of the earthen *liṅga* is meritorious, auspicious, and increases one’s lifespan.
This rite, which bestows contentment, nourishment, and prosperity, should be performed by the most excellent practitioners of spiritual means. Endowed with devotion and faith,
one should worship the earthen linga— which grants the fulfillment of all desires and goals— using whatever offerings are available.
He who, having fashioned an earthen liṅga on an auspicious pedestal, worships it,
becomes wealthy and glorious in this very world and is born as Rudra in the end.
He who, having fashioned an earthen liṅga from bilva wood, worships it at the three junctions of the day...
Listen to the fruit of his merit, which extends up to ten times elevenfold:
by this very body, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
It destroys the sins of all mortals through both sight and touch.
He who is liberated while living is omniscient Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt.
Merely by the sight of him, both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise.
He who constantly worships Śiva, having fashioned an earthen liṅga, [attains these].
Until the end of his life, he goes to the abode of Śiva;
for immeasurable years, he dwells in the world of Śiva with Mṛḍa.
Having returned again with his desires fulfilled, he shall become a lord of kings in Bhārata.
Free from desire, one should constantly worship the excellent earthen liṅga;
then, remaining forever in the world of Śiva, one shall attain union with him.
If a brahmin does not worship the earthen Śiva-liṅga, [he incurs sin].
One might otherwise go to a terrible hell, most dreadful, where one is impaled on a stake;
therefore, one should cause a Liṅga to be fashioned according to some ritual procedure,
and one should examine it according to the rule of the five threads by means of the earthen [Liṅga].

That [liṅga] should be made unbroken; one should not fashion it as broken. However, one who makes it in two pieces will certainly not obtain the fruit of worship. Likewise, a liṅga made of gems, gold, mercury, or crystal— Śiva Purāṇa 1.19.28ab–29ab.
One should cause a solid linga made of ruby (puṣparāga) to be fashioned;
indeed, a solid linga is known as mobile (cara), while one that is split is known as immobile (acara).
This distinction between being whole and split is recorded for both the mobile and the immobile.
The deity Maheśvara is the Liṅga of the Great Vidyā along with the altar;
therefore, in a stationary Liṅga, the best [portion] and so forth are remembered as being divided.
Indeed, a stationary Liṅga should be made in two parts according to the prescribed rule.

Those who know the Śaiva Siddhānta declare that the mobile [liṅga] is indivisible; however, those deluded by ignorance fashion the mobile liṅga as having two parts. The sages who know the Siddhānta and are experts in the scriptures do not do so.
Those deluded men who fashion a stationary liṅga that is broken or one that is mobile [when it should be stationary] do not partake in the fruit of worship.
Therefore, according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, [one should worship] the unbroken liṅga known as "mobile."
A stationary *liṅga* should be made with two sections with supreme joy;
however, for a mobile one, worship performed on a single unbroken [section] bestows the full fruit.
But for a mobile one, worship performed on two sections is traditionally held to bring about great loss.
"In an unbroken and stationary [liṅga], worship does not bestow the fruits of one's desires;
rather, it is said by those who know the scriptures that it constantly brings about transgression.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Worshipping the Earthen Śiva-liṅga," in the Sādhyasādhana-khaṇḍa of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 20. Sūta said:
Now, the worship of the earthen image by those devoted to the Vedas is described.
By this Vedic path, she bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having bathed according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtras and having performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) according to rule,
one should first perform the Brahma-sacrifice (brahmayajña) and then carry out the libation (tarpaṇa).
Having first performed the daily rites in their entirety according to his desire,
a person should then wear sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads while recollecting Śiva,
in accordance with the procedure prescribed in the Vedas, for the sake of attaining the complete and perfect fruit.
One should worship this supreme earthen liṅga with supreme devotion on a riverbank,
by a pond, on a mountain, or even in a forest;
the worship of the earthen [liṅga] is prescribed in a temple of Śiva or in a pure place.

O twice-born ones, having diligently gathered earth produced from a pure location, one should fashion a Śiva-liṅga with great care. For a Brāhmaṇa, it is remembered as white; for a Kṣatriya, red; and for a Vaiśya, yellow in color.
One should diligently collect clay from the footprints of a Vaiśya woman, or from wherever such clay may be found, for the purpose of fashioning the liṅga; then,
one should place that auspicious clay in an exceedingly pure location.
Having purified it with water and gradually kneading it into a ball,
one should fashion an auspicious earthen liṅga according to the Vedic path.
Then, for the sake of attaining the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should worship it with devotion.

I shall describe that method; listen to it according to the prescribed procedure. One should perform worship with the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya" and sprinkle the ritual materials. With the mantra "Bhūr asi," one should effect the consecration of the site.
One should perform the consecration of the water with the mantra *āpo asmān*.
The binding of the crystal [seal] is prescribed with the mantra *namas te rudra*.
One should effect the purification of the site (*kṣetra*) with the mantra *śambhavāya*.
One who is devoted should perform the sprinkling of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) preceded by the word "namaḥ," using the mantra "Nīlagrīva" preceded by "namaḥ";
thus he should carry out the excellent installation of the liṅga of Śaṅkara.
Then, out of devotion, one who follows the Vedic path should offer a beautiful seat with the mantra "etatte rudrāya.
One should perform the invocation with the mantra "mā no mahāntam."
One should perform the act of seating with the mantra "yāte rudreṇa.
With the mantra "yāmiṣum," one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Śiva.
And with the mantra "adhyavocat," one should lovingly perform the consecration (*adhivāsa*).
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities with the mantra "This is Jīva" (*asau jīva iti*);
one should perform the ritual of withdrawal (*apasarpaṇa*) with the mantra "He who creeps away" (*asau yaḥ apasarpati*).
One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) with the mantra "Salutation to the blue-necked one" (*namo astu nīlagrīvāya*).

One should offer the *arghya* with the *Rudragāyatrī* and the water for sipping (*ācamana*) with the *Tryambaka* mantra. One should perform the bath with milk using the mantra "payaḥ pṛthivyām," and one should cause the bath with curd to be performed with the mantra "dadhi krāvṇo akāriṣam."

The bathing with ghee is performed with the mantra "khalu ghṛtam, ghṛtaṃ yāvā" (ŚivP 1.20.21ab), and the bathing with honey is prescribed using the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā," "madhu naktam," and "madhumānnaḥ" (ŚivP 1.20.21cd); this is known as the *pañcāmṛta* (five nectars) bath. (ŚivP 1.20.22ab)
Alternatively, one should perform the bath with the *pādya* mantra and with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
With the mantra "mānastoke," recited with love, one should perform the binding of the waist-cloth.
Or, with the mantra "namo dhṛṣṇave," one should cause him to put on the upper garment.
With the four Vedic verses beginning with "yā te heti," a devotee should perform the offering of clothing to Śiva according to the prescribed rite;
likewise, the wise one should offer perfume with the verse "namaḥ śvabhyaḥ" out of love.
One should offer unbroken grains (akṣata) with the mantra "namas takṣabhyaḥ," or one may offer flowers with the mantra "namaḥ pāryāya," or offer bilva leaves with the mantra "namaḥ parṇyāya."
One should offer incense according to the prescribed rite with the mantra "namaḥ kapardine";
one should offer a lamp as stated with the Ṛgvedic verse "nama āśave";
and one should offer the most excellent food offering (naivedya) with the mantra "namo jyeṣṭhāya."
Manu has prescribed the sipping of water (ācamana) again with the mantra "Tryambakam.
One should perform the offering of the fruit with the verse "Imā rudrāya," and one should offer everything to Śambhu with the verse "Namo vrajyāya."

Then, with the two mantras "mano mahāntam" and "mā nastoke," one should worship the Rudras with eleven unbroken grains of rice (*akṣata*). With the three verses beginning with "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ," one should present the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
A wise person should perform the consecration with the mantra *devasya tvā*;
or, one should perform the ritual of waving lights (*nīrājana*) for Śambhu with the lamp-mantra.
One should devoutly offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the three verses beginning with *imā rudrāya*.
The wise man should perform circumambulation with the mantra "mānomahāntam";
the intelligent one should prostrate himself with all eight limbs using the mantra "mānastoke";
and he should display the *śivamudrā* with the mantra "eṣa te".

With the verse beginning "yato yataḥ," one should show the mudrā called Abhayā; with the "tryambaka" mantra, the Mahāmudrā; and with the mantra "namo senābhyaḥ," one should display the Dhenumudrā using this ṛc: "namo gebhyaḥ."
Then, having displayed the five mudrās, one should perform the recitation of the Śiva-mantra;
the expert in the Vedas should recite with the Śatarudriya mantra.
Thereafter, the expert in the Vedas should perform the recitation of the five-limbed (pañcāṅga) prayer.
One should perform the dismissal of Śambhu with the mantra beginning "devāgātu".
Thus has been described in detail the Vedic procedure for the worship of Śiva;
now hear in brief the supreme Vedic rite.
One should perform the fetching of the clay with the verse beginning "asadyojātam";
one should perform the casting of water with the mantra "vāmadevāya";
and one should perform the fashioning of the liṅga with the mantra "aghora".
One should perform the invocation according to the rules with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra;
one should place [the deity] upon the altar with the *īśāna* mantra.
The wise practitioner should perform all other rites in brief.
Or likewise, with the five-syllabled mantra given by the Guru,
the wise man should duly perform the worship with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) according to the rule:
"We meditate upon Mahādeva, the source of existence and the destroyer of worldly existence."

With this mantra, "To Ugra, to the destroyer of the fierce, to Śarva, whose crest is the moon," the wise person should worship Śaṅkara. Abandoning delusion with true devotion, Śiva bestows fruit through devotion alone.
"Having thus honored that which was proclaimed as the Vedic sequence of worship,
O twice-born one, another procedure is now correctly described as being common [to all]:
the worship of the earthen liṅga is fully declared by means of the names of Śiva."
Listen to that, O best of sages, which grants all desires:
Hara, Maheśvara, Śambhu, Śūlapāṇi, Pinākadhṛk,
Śiva, Paśupati, and Mahādeva— these are his names in sequence.
The bringing of clay, its kneading, the installation, and the invocation; likewise,
the bathing, the worship, and the dismissal with the words "forgive me"—
all these should be performed in sequence using the names beginning with the syllable *Aṃ* and ending in the dative case, followed by *namaḥ*.
All ritual actions should be performed with supreme devotion and joy.
Having properly performed the rite of *nyāsa* on the six limbs and the two hands,
one should then practice meditation with the six-syllable mantra.
One should meditate upon Him who is seated in the center of the Kailāsa throne, being worshipped by devotees such as Nanda and others;
who is the forest fire that consumes the suffering of His devotees, who is immeasurable, and who is embraced by Umā, the ornament of the universe.

One should constantly meditate upon Maheśa, who resembles a mountain of silver, who has the beautiful moon as his crest-jewel, whose limbs shine with jeweled ornaments, and who is gracious, holding an axe, a deer, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in His hands.
"Seated upon a lotus, surrounded on all sides by hosts of immortals, wearing a tiger skin, the first of the universe, the seed of the universe, the remover of all fears, five-faced and three-eyed"—
having thus meditated upon and worshipped the supreme earthen *liṅga*,
one should recite the five-syllabled mantra bestowed by the guru according to the prescribed rule.
The wise one, bowing down, should praise the Lord of Gods with hymns;
O best of Brahmins, he should recite the *Vaiśvarudriya* with various names.
Then, having joyfully taken rice-grains and flowers in his joined palms—
One should pray to Śaṅkara with devotion and with these mantras, full of sincere faith:
"O Gracious One (Mṛḍa), I am yours; my life-breath consists of your qualities; my mind is fixed on you.
Knowing me to be thus, O Lord of Beings, O Treasure of Compassion, be gracious to me."

O Śaṅkara, whatever recitation, worship, or other rites have been performed by me through ignorance or even out of lack of knowledge, may that become fruitful through your grace. I am indeed a great sinner, yet you are the Great Purifier.
"Knowing this, O Lord of Gaurī, do as you desire.
By the Vedas, the Purāṇas, the Siddhāntas, and even by various ṛṣis, we have not known you, O Mahādeva; how much less can I know you, O Great Śiva?"
"In whatever way possible, O Maheśvara, I am yours in every respect;
you must indeed protect me—be gracious, O Supreme Lord.
Having spoken thus, he offered unbroken grains and flowers upon Śiva.

O Sage, one should prostrate with devotion before Śambhu according to the rule of the eight-limbed salutation (sāṣṭāṅga). Then, the wise person should perform circumambulation according to the prescribed rite.
Furthermore, filled with faith, one should praise the Lord of Gods with hymns of praise.

Then, making a sound with the throat, one of pure and humble intellect should prostrate; having made a formal request with respect, one should then perform the dismissal. Thus have the tigers among sages been instructed regarding the ritual procedure for the worship of the earthen image.
Bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and increasing devotion to Śiva—
whosoever reads or even hears this chapter with a pure mind shall have their soul purified of all sins and attain all desires.

This supreme narrative bestows longevity, fitness, fame, and even heaven; it grants the happiness of sons, grandsons, and so forth. Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Worshipping the Earthen Śiva Liṅga," in the Sādhyasādhanakhaṇḍa of the Pravidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 21.
The Sages said: O Sūta, O highly fortunate Sūta, salutations to you, the disciple of Vyāsa! ŚivaP 1.21.1ab.

"O Father, you have correctly described the procedure for the worship of the earthen linga of the Lord. Now, out of compassion for us who are distressed, O beloved one, please tell us the number of earthen lingas of Śiva according to their ritual prescriptions, based on the distinctions between their respective desires."
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, to the ritual procedure for the worship of the earthly [image],
by the mere performance of which a man becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
If one worships another deity without having made an earthen *liṅga*, that worship is in vain;
likewise, fasting, giving gifts, and so forth are in vain.
The number of earthen *liṅgas* is now declared according to one's desire.
According to the determination of the best of sages, this [consecration] yields its fruit immediately upon completion.
Therein, the initial invocation, the installation, and the worship are each distinct;
likewise, everything regarding the form of the *liṅga* should be understood as being individually separate.

A man seeking knowledge should worship a thousand earthen liṅgas of Śiva with devotion; indeed, they certainly bestow that fruit. A man seeking wealth should worship half of that number of earthen liṅgas.

One seeking sons [obtained] fifteen hundred; one seeking garments, five hundred; one seeking liberation, ten million-fold; and one desiring land, one thousand. One seeking compassion obtained three thousand, and one seeking sacred fords, two thousand.
One who desires friends should recite three thousand times; one seeking subjugation, eight hundred;
one seeking death, seven hundred; one seeking delusion, eight hundred;
and one intent on eradication, one thousand, according to the prescribed rule.
One seeking to paralyze [an enemy] should recite it one thousand times; one seeking to cause hatred, half of that (five hundred);
and one desiring release from fetters, one thousand and five hundred—the best [number], as should be known by the wise, when there is fear of a great king.

In times of danger from thieves and the like, it should be known that two hundred [mudrās] are for kings; in fear of ḍākinīs and others, five hundred are prescribed as the *japa*-mudrā. For poverty, five thousand are required, while ten thousand grant all desires.
Now I shall declare the rules for the temporary [linga]; listen, O best of sages!
One linga is said to remove sins; two lingas grant the accomplishment of goals;
three lingas are proclaimed as the supreme cause for the fulfillment of all desires.
In this manner, the procedure for the previously mentioned groups shall proceed in successive order.
Now, I shall state another opinion regarding the number [of rites] according to the different sages:
having prepared ten thousand earthen *liṅgas*, the wise man—*Śiva Purāṇa* 1.21.16ab–17ab.

O Great King, one will surely become fearless; indeed, [this rite] removes fear. For the sake of liberation from prison and similar confinement, a wise person should cause ten thousand [recitations] to be performed. Likewise, in the face of fear from ḍākinīs and other malevolent beings, one should cause seven thousand to be performed.
One who has no son should cause fifty-five thousand [liṅgas] to be fashioned;
by ten thousand liṅgas, one obtains a lineage of daughters;
and by ten thousand liṅgas, one attains sovereignty like that of Viṣṇu and others.
By means of ten million lingas alone, one shall attain incomparable prosperity.
That man on earth who makes ten million lingas becomes Śiva himself;
there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
The worship of earthen liṅgas bestows the fruit of ten million sacrifices;
it eternally grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation to men who desire them.
For him whose time passes constantly without the worship of the liṅga...
A great loss shall befall that wicked and evil-minded person.
On one side are all gifts and various vows;
on the other side, it is traditionally held, are the sacred fords, religious observances, sacrifices, and the worship of the Liṅga.
The worship of the *kalau-liṅga* is seen as the most excellent in this world;
such is the firm conclusion of the scriptures that there is nothing else like it.
The *liṅga* bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and wards off manifold calamities.
By worshipping it constantly, a person shall attain union with Śiva.
This Liṅga, which consists of the name of Śiva, is to be worshipped perpetually by the great sages;
since it is present within all Liṅgas, it should therefore be worshipped according to the prescribed rites.

The *liṅga* is said to be of three kinds—superior, middling, and inferior—in terms of its measurement, O tigers among sages; listen as I describe it. [The superior one] is four finger-breadths in height, beautiful, and provided with a pedestal (*vedikā*).
The supreme *liṅga* has been declared by the sages who are experts in the scriptures;
half of that is said to be the middling, and half of that is remembered as the inferior.
Thus, three kinds have been described, each succeeding one being superior to the preceding.
One who is constantly endowed with devotion and faith should worship the many-liṅga-yoni;
he shall obtain the desires cherished by his mind.
There is no merit greater than the propitiation of the liṅga within the four Vedas.
This indeed is the definitive conclusion of all the scriptures:
having completely abandoned this entire web of ritual actions without exception,
the wise man should worship the single *liṅga* with supreme devotion.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, is pervaded by the worship of the Liṅga.
For those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, there is no other means of crossing over;
for those blinded by the darkness of ignorance and whose minds are attached to sense objects, [the Liṅga is the sole refuge].
In this world, there is no means of crossing over [saṃsāra] other than the worship of the Liṅga.
The gods, beginning with Hari and Brahmā; the sages, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
the gandharvas, cāraṇas, and siddhas; as well as the daityas and dānavas—[all these depend upon it].
The Nāgas, beginning with Śeṣa, as well as the Garuḍas and other birds,
along with the Prajāpatis, other Manus, Kinnaras, and human beings,
having worshipped the Liṅga— which grants the fulfillment of all aims— with great devotion.
Having obtained all those various desired objects of their heart's desire,
whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or those born of inverse unions (pratiloma),
they should constantly worship the Liṅga with devotion using the respective mantra for each.

O sages, what is the use of speaking at length? Furthermore, O twice-born ones, all—including women—possess the right to worship the *śivaliṅga*. However, for the twice-born, worship according to the Vedic path is superior.
"The worship of other living beings is not approved by the Veda;
the worship of Vedic Brahmins must be performed by the twice-born according to the Vedic path and not by any other way— thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śiva."
Due to the curse of Dadhīca, Gautama, and others, whose minds were not consumed by it,
faith in Vedic rites does not arise at all in those twice-born ones; for whoever,
If a mortal should perform anything else, he shall not obtain the fruit of his resolve.
Having thus performed the worship of Śambhu according to the injunctions up to the offering of food (naivedya),
one should worship the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti) who comprise the three worlds right there.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the sun, the moon, and the sacrificer—these are proclaimed as the eight forms (mūrtis).
Śarva, Bhava, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, and Īśvara; [Paśupati and Mahādeva].
Mahādeva Paśupati should worship these [deities] with their respective forms; thereafter,
one should worship the retinue of Śambhu with great devotion,
using sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and leaf-offerings, in the sequence beginning with Īśāna.
Īśāna, Nandin, Caṇḍa, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin,
Vṛṣa, Skanda, Kapardīśa, Soma, and Śukra in that order;
and Vīrabhadra in front, as well as Kīrtimukha at the back.
Then, one should worship the eleven Rudras according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, having recited the five-syllable mantra and the Śatarudriya,
and having offered various kinds of hymns of praise as well as the recitation of the *Pañcāṅga*.

Then, having performed circumambulation and bowed to the Liṅga, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*). Thus has the worship of Śiva been described in its entirety with due reverence. One should always perform the rites for the deity at night facing the north.

One who is pure should always perform the worship of Śiva facing north. One should not face east toward Śambhu, nor north toward those associated with the Śakti, nor west, as that would be his back; therefore, one should take refuge in the proper direction.
Without the triple mark of ashes, without a rosary of rudrākṣa beads,
and without a bilva leaf, a wise person should never worship Śaṅkara. O best of sages, when the worship of Śiva has commenced, [this applies] even if the ashes have not been obtained.
"Therefore, the *tripuṇḍra* should be made on the forehead even with clay.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of the Earth-Element," in the section on Means and Ends within the first book, the *Vidyeshvara-saṃhitā*, of the glorious *Shiva Mahapurana*.
Chapter 22.
The sages said:
"We have previously heard the statement that the food offering (naivedya) of Śiva is not to be accepted.
O virtuous sage, tell us the resolution of that matter, as well as the greatness of the bilva fruit."
Sūta said: Listen now, all you sages, with full attention; I shall tell you everything out of affection. Blessed are you, who are devoted to the vows of Śiva.
A devotee of Śiva who is pure, clean, firm in his vows,
and resolute should consume the food offered to Śiva (naivedya) and abandon the notion that it is unfit to be accepted.
Even upon merely seeing the naivedya of Śiva, all sins depart far away.
When one partakes of the food offering (naivedya) of Śiva, millions of merits accrue.
There is no need for a thousand sacrifices, nor even for ten million sacrifices;
by consuming the naivedya of Śiva, one attains union with Śiva (śivasāyujya).
That house in which the distribution of Śiva’s *naivedya* (food offering) takes place becomes entirely pure and a cause for the purification of others.
Having received the arrived *naivedya* of Śiva, one should joyfully carry it upon one's head.
One should eat with effort, preceded by the remembrance of Śiva;
furthermore, it is said that the *naivedya* (offered food) of Śiva may be accepted even when it arrives at another time.
For indeed, in a human being, a connection with sin certainly arises through delay.

He in whom no desire arises to partake of the *naivedya* (food offering) of Śiva is the most sinful and base of men; he certainly goes to hell. [This applies even if it is offered] in a vessel made of moonstone, gold, silver, or other such materials.
It is declared that this [food] is to be eaten by a devotee who possesses the Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā).
A devotee endowed with Śiva-initiation may eat the auspicious food offering (naivedya) of all liṅgas, which is known as "great grace" (mahāprasāda).

O twice-born ones, listen with affection to the definitive conclusion regarding the consumption of the *naivedya* (food offerings) of Śiva for those initiated into other [systems] who are devoted in soul to the worship of Śiva— specifically concerning the Liṅga produced from the Śālagrāma stone as well as the mercury Liṅga (*rasaliṅga*). ŚivP 1.22.12–13ab.
In stone, silver, gold, or those established by the Suras and Siddhas;
in Kāśmīra, in crystal, or in gems— in all these Jyotirliṅgas,
the consumption of the food offering (naivedya) of Śambhu is declared to be equal to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Even a slayer of a Brahmin becomes pure if he wears the remains of an offering (nirmālya) [to Śiva];
by consuming it immediately, all his sin is destroyed.
That which is under the authority of Caṇḍa must not be consumed by men.
In those places where Caṇḍa has authority, that which is to be eaten must be offered with devotion.
In the case of a Bāṇaliṅga, a metal (lauhaliṅga), a Siddhaliṅga, a self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅga,
and in all images, Caṇḍa shall have no authority.
Whoever drinks three times the water used for bathing the Liṅga according to the prescribed rite,
his threefold sin is quickly destroyed in this world.
The food offering (naivedya) to Śiva— including leaves, flowers, fruits, and water— is not to be taken [as ordinary food].
Through contact with a Śālagrāma stone, everything becomes purified.
O lords of sages, whatever substance is upon a leaf is not to be accepted;
yet that which is outside the touch of the Liṅga should be known as perfectly pure.
Thus, O best of sages, the determination regarding the food offering has been declared.
Now listen with attention and reverence to the majesty of the *bilva* tree;
this *bilva* is the very form of Mahādeva, praised even by the gods.
How can the greatness of this [tree] be known in any way? Whatever holy pilgrimage sites (tīrtha) are renowned throughout the worlds,
all those tīrthas indeed reside at the root of the bilva tree.
The meritorious soul who worships Mahādeva, the imperishable one in the form of a *liṅga*, at the root of a *bilva* tree, will certainly attain Śiva. Furthermore,
he who sprinkles water upon his own head at the root of a *bilva* tree— [Śiva Purāṇa 1.22.24–25ab]

He would be as one who has bathed at all sacred fords; he alone is a purifier upon this earth. Seeing that most excellent water-basin at the root of this *bilva* tree, filled with water, Mahādeva becomes exceedingly pleased.
The man who worships the root of the *bilva* tree with perfumes, flowers,
and other offerings attains the world of Śiva, and his lineage increases in happiness.
He who respectfully arranges a garland of lamps at the root of the *bilva* tree—

One endowed with the knowledge of true reality becomes absorbed within Maheśa. Having taken a branch of the *bilva* tree with its fresh sprouts in his hand, he should worship the *bilva*; thus, he is liberated from all sins.
Whoever, out of devotion, feeds one who is devoted to Śiva at the root of a bilva tree,
his merit becomes multiplied ten million times.
At the root of a bilva tree, milk-rice mixed with ghee should be offered.

He who gives [this] to a devotee of Śiva shall never be born poor. O twice-born ones, the worship of the Śivaliṅga is said to be complete with its limbs and sub-limbs; it is twofold according to the distinction between those engaged in worldly action (*pravṛtta*) and those withdrawn from it (*nivṛtta*).

For those engaged in the practice, one should perform the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhapūjā) and all other forms of worship. At the conclusion of the consecration (abhiṣeka), one should offer an oblation of cooked rice (naivedya).
At the end of the worship, one should place the liṅga in a pure casket within a separate room.
To those who have desisted from ritual worship with hands, one should offer one's own food.
For those who have desisted [from all external rites], even the most subtle *liṅga* alone is distinguished as superior.
One should perform the worship of sacred ash (*vibhūti*) and offer that very ash.
"Having performed worship, one should always carry the Liṅga upon one's head.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Naivedya Offered to Śiva," in the Sādhyasādhanakhaṇḍa of the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 23.

He in whose body these three always abide—

The sages said:

Sūta said:

listen with devotion and respect to that majesty.
