Except for Maheśvara, everything in the universe—whether existent or non-existent—is subordinate to him.
I shall speak, according to my devotion and in brief, of the greatness of his name;
listen with affection, O Brahmins, for it is the supreme destroyer of all sins.

O Śaunaka, the mountains of great sins are reduced to ashes without effort by the forest fire named Śiva; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. Even the various sufferings rooted in sin [are likewise destroyed].

The name of Śiva alone destroys [all sins], and nothing else can destroy them in any way. That man on earth who is constantly devoted to the chanting of Śiva’s name is considered to be one who possesses the Vedas, one whose soul is meritorious, one who is blessed, and one who is wise.
O Sage, for those who have faith in the chanting of the name of Śiva, various dharmas become manifest with immediate fruit; all sins whatsoever perish by means of the name of Śiva.
O Sage, even those most heinous sins committed by men— O Sage, the immeasurable heaps of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin—
are swiftly destroyed in their entirety when the name of Śiva is uttered by men.
Having obtained the boat that is the name of Śiva,
those who cross the ocean of saṃsāra undoubtedly destroy the sins that are the root of saṃsāra,
O great sage— of those very sins that constitute the foundation of worldly existence.
Destruction is certain to occur by means of the axe that is the name of Śiva.
The nectar of Śiva’s name is to be drunk by those tormented by the forest fire of sin;
for those scorched by the forest fire of sin, there is no peace without it.

Those great-souled ones in whom devotion to the name of Śiva has arisen are drenched by a continuous downpour of nectar raining from that very name; they never grieve, even in the midst of the forest fire of saṃsāra.
For those of such a kind, liberation occurs in every way after a thousand [lives].
O Lord of Sages, for one by whom penance has been performed over many births,
devotion to the name of Śiva arises, which removes all sins.

For one whose unbroken devotion to the name of Śambhu is unique and shared by no other, liberation is thus easily attained; for no one else, this is my conviction. Even after committing many sins, one who is devoted to the chanting of the name of Śiva [is liberated].
One becomes liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt. Just as trees in a forest are reduced to ashes when consumed by fire, so too are those many sins burnt away by the name of Śiva.
O Śaunaka, one whose limbs are constantly purified by ashes and who is devoted to the chanting of Śiva’s names certainly crosses over even this most terrible cycle of existence (saṃsāra),
even if he has seized the property of a Brahmin or killed many Brahmins.

A person who is devoted to the chanting of Śiva’s name is not defiled by sins. Having examined all the Vedas, the ancients have determined that the chanting of Śiva’s name is the supreme means for crossing over the cycle of worldly existence.
O best of sages, what is the use of much speaking? I shall tell you in a single verse about the greatness of Śiva’s name, which removes all sins;
for the purifying power of Śambhu’s name is indeed capable of destroying all evils.
A man is never able to commit even a minor sin;
yet, by the power of Śiva’s name, he attained the supreme goal.
O Sage, in former times, King Indradyumna was a great sinner.

Likewise, O sage, a certain Brahmin woman who was a great sinner attained the supreme goal through the power of Śiva’s name. Thus, O best of the twice-born, the supreme majesty of the Name has been told to you.
"Listen to the majesty of the sacred ash (bhasma), which purifies all that purifies.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Śiva Forest," in the section on the Means and the Goal within the Vidyeśvara Saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 24.
Sūta said:
"Bhasma is declared to be of two kinds, both of which bestow supreme auspiciousness.
I shall describe its varieties; listen with focused attention."
There is one [kind of] ash to be known as "Great Ash" (mahābhasma) and a second called "Small" (svalpa). That which is called "Great Ash" is the supreme ash of various kinds.
That ash is said to be threefold: Vedic (śrauta), Smṛti-based (smārta), and worldly (laukika).
Ash alone is proclaimed in many ways by those of limited understanding.
For the twice-born, it is proclaimed as both Vedic (śrauta) and Smṛti-based (āsmārta);
for all others, there is another kind of ash, which is worldly (laukika).
The wearing [of ashes] by the twice-born has been declared by the foremost of sages to be accompanied by mantras;
for others, it should be understood as wearing alone, devoid of mantras.
The ash produced from burnt cow dung is called *āgneya* (fiery).
Even then, O great sage, it is said that the substance for the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be ash arising from the Agnihotra sacrifice, to be collected by wise men; or else,
ash arising from other sacrifices may also be used for the wearing of the triple mark.
With the seven mantras beginning with "Agni," as found in the Jābāla Upaniṣad, one should perform the smearing with ash mixed with water;
this should be done for all castes and stages of life, mantra by mantra.

The application of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) have been proclaimed by the Jābālas with great reverence; indeed, one who desires liberation must not abandon even the horizontal triple mark through negligence— such is the sacred tradition.
Śiva and Viṣṇu likewise wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on their animal forms;
so too do Umā and Lakṣmī, as well as other goddesses, constantly [wear it].
It is worn by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even those of mixed castes.
Those who, though bearing ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) applied with Apabhraṃśa words,
do not perform the smearing of ashes and the triple mark with faith—
for them there is no proper conduct consistent with their caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama).

Those who do not practice the smearing of ashes (*uddhūlana*) and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with faith—for them there is no liberation from saṃsāra even in ten million births. Those who do not practice the smearing of ashes and the triple mark with faith... [Śiva Purāṇa 1.24.14–15ab]

For them, there is no knowledge of Śiva even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. Those who do not practice the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with faith are joined with great sins; such is the determination of the scriptures.
For those who do not practice the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with faith,
all their religious observances indeed lead to contrary results;
this is especially true for creatures burdened by great sins who are hostile toward Śiva.
O Sage, a very firm aversion to the *tripuṇḍra* and the smearing [of ashes] arises [in him].
A man who, having performed the fire-rite for Śiva, applies the *triyāyuṣa* himself as a knower of the Self,
is liberated from all sins by being touched with the sacred ash (*bhasman*).

He who applies the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with white ashes at the three junctions of the day is liberated from all sins and rejoices together with Śiva. One should apply the triple mark on the forehead with white ashes.
Indeed, one who has reached the worlds that have existed since beginningless time would become as if dead if he were to die without having performed the bath with ashes.
One should not recite the six-syllable mantra without having performed the bath with ashes;
rather, having fashioned the *tripuṇḍra* according to the prescribed rule with ashes, one should then recite it.
Whether he be the highest or even the lowest, whether he be possessed of all sins,
or even possessed of the sins of the dawn, or a fool, or even an outcast—
whichever land he constantly inhabits while joined with the command of Bhūti, [there he shall be honored].
The presence of all sacred fords and all sacrifices is always established [in him].
A living being endowed with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is worthy of worship by all gods and demons;
even one burdened by sin becomes pure in soul, how much more so one who is possessed of faith?

In whatever land a knower of Śiva, endowed with the teaching of sacred ash, has gone even by chance, there all holy fords (tīrthas) assemble even today. What more need be said here? The wise should always maintain the practice of wearing sacred ash.
The worship of the *liṅga* should always be performed, as well as the recitation of the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*).
Even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the sages, and the gods,
it is impossible to fully describe the greatness of wearing the sacred ashes (*bhasmadhāraṇa*).
Thus,
even one who has abandoned the conduct and rituals of his caste and stage of life is liberated from sin by wearing the *tripuṇḍra* once;
and those men who perform their duties while disregarding one who wears the sacred ash— [they too are liberated].

For them, there is no liberation from *saṃsāra* even after millions of births. That Brahmin has not studied anything from his teacher, nor has he performed any [religious duty], by whom the *tripuṇḍra* mark with ashes has been placed upon his head.
O Brahmin, the wise man should infer that those people who, upon seeing one who wears the ashes, strike him, will take birth as outcasts (caṇḍālas).
One should wear the ashes consecrated with the mantra *Mānastoke*.
A Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya who are devoted to the aforementioned limbs [of the mantra] should perform it with the *Tryambaka* mantra;
a Vaiśya with the same, and a Śūdra with the five-syllabled (*pañcākṣara*) mantra.
For other widowed women, the rule is declared to be like that of the Śūdra.
The rite for the householder is prescribed with the *mantras* beginning with the five Brahmās;
the rite for the student (*brahmacārin*) is with the *Tryambaka* mantra;
and the rite for the forest-dweller is recorded as being with the *Aghora* mantra.
A renunciant (yati), however, should perform the triple-mark (tripuṇḍra) and other rites with the *praṇava* alone.
Because of his supreme contemplation that "I am Śiva," he is eternally beyond the [distinctions of] castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśramī*).
And a Śiva-yogi should always wear [the marks] with the *īśāna* [mantra] as well.

The supreme wearing of ashes must not be abandoned by members of any caste, nor indeed by others who live according to their own means; such is the teaching of Śiva. As many particles of ash as are established upon one's own body through the bath of ashes, [so many worlds does one conquer].
The wearer here bears as many Śiva-liṅgas as there are [of those mentioned]:
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even those of mixed castes;
likewise women, widows, children, and even heretics who have attained [this state].
Whether he be a celibate student, a householder, a forest-dweller, a renunciant, or one who observes no vows,
as well as women marked with the ash-tripundra— there is no doubt that they are liberated through knowledge,
whether by the power of their own realization or even from another; it is just like the burning away of wood by fire.
The ash worn with knowledge or even without it purifies every man.

One should not eat water or even a small amount of food without wearing the ash and the rosary; for if a householder, a king, an ascetic, or one of the castes eats without them, he becomes an outcaste. Such a sinner goes to hell, but that may be remedied by the recitation of the Gāyatrī for those of the [other] castes, while for an ascetic, it is removed by the recitation of the primary Praṇava.
Those who revile the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) revile Śiva himself;
those who wear it with devotion wear him himself.
Fie upon the forehead devoid of ashes! Fie upon the village that is not the abode of Śiva!
"Fie on the worship of one who is not the Lord! Fie on a birth that takes refuge in inauspicious knowledge!
Those who revile Hara—the Great Lord, the support of the three worlds—who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), incur sin by even looking upon them.
They are born as outcasts, swine, demons, donkeys, dogs, jackals, and worms; being supreme sinners, they are destined solely for hell."

Having seen this, let them not merely behold the moon and sun by night or day in their dreams; rather, they shall be liberated by the recitation of the *Śatarudrīya* hymn from the *Śruti*, provided they do not disregard it. By conversing with those who are established in the wearing of ashes and other [emblems], one becomes delivered from hell. But those dull-witted ones who censure such a person—O Sage, neither he who follows the Tantras nor he who bears the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is authorized [to do so].
One who bears the mark of the heated discus is excluded here from the sacrifice to Śiva.
Regarding this, many people have been impelled by the Bṛhajjābāla [Upaniṣad];
these should be investigated with effort, and thereafter one should become devoted to the sacred ash (bhasma).

Indeed, even if mixed with sandalwood or sandal-paste, one should wear only the sacred ash as the *tripuṇḍra*; for if people possess discernment, they should always wear some vibhūti upon their foreheads. Women should wear the *tripuṇḍra* as far as the hairline, and likewise the twice-born and widows should wear the ash.

In the same way, those who abide in the [four] stages of life should maintain the pure manifestation [of ash], which bestows the fruit of liberation and destroys all sins. He who applies the *tripuṇḍra* with ash according to the prescribed rule is liberated from the multitude of great sins (*mahāpātaka*) as well as the minor sins (*upapātaka*).
Whether they be celibate students, householders, forest-dwellers, or ascetics;
whether they be Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, or even others who are fallen and base—
by applying the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), they become pure.
Having properly cast off the heap of sins through the ritual of the sacred ash (bhasma),
the wearer of ash is especially liberated from the great crimes such as the killing of women or cows;
he is also freed from the slaying of a hero or the killing of a horse— of this there is no doubt.
The seizing of another's property, the violation of another's wife,
censuring others, the taking of another's field, and the inflicting of pain upon others;
the theft of crops, gardens, and so forth, as well as acts such as setting fire to houses— these [are likewise forbidden].
The acceptance of cattle, gold, buffaloes, and so forth, as well as sesame, woolen blankets, garments,
food, grain, water, and the like from low-born persons;
and [sexual union] with ten types of women— prostitutes, Matangīs, Śūdra women, and actresses.
Sexual intercourse with girls who have reached puberty, with widows, and with menstruating women;
the sale of meat, hides, liquids, and salt;
backbiting, false speech, and the giving of false testimony by those who desire to deceive witnesses.

Innumerable sins and various kinds of evils such as these are destroyed instantly by the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra*. Even the theft of Śiva’s property and the reviling of Śiva anywhere [are likewise destroyed].
The censure of those devoted to Śiva is not purified even by penances.
He who has a rudrākṣa on his limbs and the triple-tilaka mark on his forehead is to be honored—
even if he be a caṇḍāla— as the most excellent among all castes.
He who bears the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) on his forehead has effectively bathed in all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and rivers such as the Gaṅgā that exist in this world.
The seven million great mantras, headed by the five-syllabled mantra, [reside in him].
Likewise, O Sage, there are other mantras by the millions that are the causes of liberation through Śiva;
and there are other mantras of the gods that bestow all happiness—
all of these come under the control of whoever wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
He who applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) shall uplift a thousand ancestors already born and a thousand yet to be born within his own lineage and kinsmen;
having enjoyed all pleasures here on earth, he shall live a long life free from disease.
And at the end of his life, he attains death with ease;
having obtained a divine body endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers,
he ascends a celestial chariot served by the divine gods.

Having enjoyed vast pleasures in the worlds of all the Vidyādharas and the Gandharvas of great luster, as well as in the realms of Indra and the other world-protectors, and in the positions of the lords of creatures, in due order; ŚiP 1.24.69–70ab.
Having reached the station of Brahmā, one obtains a hundred maidens there;
having enjoyed manifold pleasures for the duration of Brahmā’s lifespan,
one shall obtain enjoyment in the world of Viṣṇu until the passing of a hundred Brahmās.

Then, having reached the world of Śiva and obtained his desired, imperishable wish, he attains union with Śiva; no doubt arises in this matter. Having repeatedly contemplated the essence of all the Upaniṣads...

For this alone has been determined as the supreme good: the *tripuṇḍra*. Any Brahmin who indeed censures the sacred ash (*vibhūti*) is of a different birth; he shall dwell in a terrible hell for as long as the four-faced Brahmā exists.
In the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), sacrifice (*yajña*), recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), the *vaiśvadeva* offering, and the worship of the gods,
a person who has applied the triple-ash mark (*tripuṇḍra*) becomes pure in soul and conquers death. A bath in water serves to remove physical impurities, whereas a bath in ashes is always purifying.

The bath with mantras removes sin; the bath of knowledge leads to the supreme state. Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords—a man who performs the ash-bath obtains that very fruit.

The bath of ashes is the supreme sacred site; it is equivalent to bathing in the Gaṅgā day after day. Śiva is manifestly present in the form of ashes, and ashes purify the three worlds. There is no penance greater than that, no meditation greater than that, no gift greater than that, and no recitation of mantras greater than that.
Whatever is performed by a Brahmin without the *tripuṇḍra*,
as well as by forest-dwellers, virgins, and men who have not received initiation; likewise,
[the rite] prior to midday is accompanied by water, while after that time it is devoid of water.

Thus, he who constantly applies the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with a disciplined mind should be known as a devotee of Śiva; he attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Even a single rudrākṣa worn upon one's body bestows great merit.
His birth would be in vain if he were devoid of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Thus, the greatness of the tripuṇḍra has been briefly recounted by me;
this secret of all living beings must be guarded by you.
O best of sages, three lines indeed appear in all the aforementioned locations,
starting from the forehead and so forth, as prescribed by the wise, O sage;
beginning from the middle of the eyebrows, they extend as far as the ends of the eyebrows.
One should maintain the *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead of that same measure;
the line made with the thumb upon the middle of the middle and ring fingers, applied in reverse order,
is designated as the *tripuṇḍra*.
Taking ash carefully with the three middle fingers,
one should devoutly wear the supreme *tripuṇḍra*, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Within each of the three lines, there are nine deities.
Listen attentively as I shall describe [these] in all their limbs:
the letter *A* is the Gārhapatya fire, the Earth, Dharma, and the quality of *rajas*;
it is also the *Ṛgveda*, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and the morning libation (*prātaḥ-savana*).
And Mahādeva is to be known as the deity of the first line,
O tigers among sages, by those devoted to the initiation of Śiva.
The syllable *u*, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, the principle of space (*nabhas-tattva*), and likewise the Yajurveda [are associated with it].
The midday libation (madhyandina-savana) consists of desire (icchā) and power (śakti) as its inner self;
it is the deity of the second line of Maheśvara,
O tiger among sages, which should be known by those devoted to the initiation of Śiva.
The letter *ma* and the Āhavanīya fire, as well as the Supreme Self and the sky of darkness (*tamas*);
the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), the Sāmaveda, and likewise the third libation (*savana*);
and Śiva himself is the deity of the third line.
O tiger among sages, those who are devoted to the initiation of Śiva should be known [as such]. Having thus constantly paid homage with true devotion to the deities of the site,
one who is purified should wear the *tripuṇḍra* and shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Lord of Sages, having been thus addressed, [the Lord spoke of] the deities residing in all the limbs.
Now listen with devotion to their respective locations within the thirty-two sites (*dvātriṃśat-sthānaka*) and also within the sixteen sites (*ṣoḍaśa-sthānaka*).
One should not apply [the ashes] in eight places, nor even in five; rather,
[they should be applied] on the head, the forehead, the two ears, and likewise the two eyes, the nose, the mouth, and the throat, and thereafter on both hands.
In the two elbows, the wrists, the heart, the two sides,
the navel, the two testicles, the two thighs,
the two ankles, and the two knees, as well as the two shanks and the two feet— these are the thirty-two supreme locations.

[He worshipped] Agni, Water, Earth, Wind, Space, the Directions, and the Guardians of the Directions, together with the Vasus: Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa; these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
The wise should wear the *tripuṇḍra* by means of these names alone;
or, being composed, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* in sixteen locations:
on the head, the forehead, the neck, the two shoulders, and the arms.
At the elbows, the wrists, the heart, the navel, the flanks,
and likewise at the back— for the sake of the *Pratiṣṭhā* [kalā]— one should worship there the two Aśvins as the presiding deities,
as well as Śiva-Śakti, Rudra, Īśa, and Nārada.
These sixteen deities, including the nine powers beginning with Vāmā, are proclaimed;
likewise, the two Aśvins are celebrated as Nāsatya and Dasra.
Furthermore, they are located on the head, in the hair, in the two eyes, and in the mouth.
On the two arms, the heart, both thighs, the two knees,
the two feet, and on the back— these sixteen [are assigned].
Are they Śiva, Candra, Rudra, Ka, Vighneśa, or Viṣṇu?
Śrī herself is in the heart, and Śambhu is at the navel; Prajāpati is there as well.
The Nāgas and Nāga maidens, as well as the daughters of the Ṛṣis, are on both sides.
The oceans are at his feet, and the sacred fords (tīrthas) extend across his broad back.
Thus, sixteen locations are now described:
the secret place, the forehead, the two unsurpassed ears,
the pair of shoulders, the heart, and the navel— these constitute the eightfold group.
"Brahmā, the seven sages, and the deities are thus proclaimed," so it has been declared by those who know the sacred ash, O lords of sages.
Alternatively, [the marks are applied] to the head, the two arms, the heart, and the navel.
Those who know the science of the sacred ash have declared these five places for its application.
One should perform them as far as possible, taking into account the requirements of place, time, and other factors.
If one is unable even to smear the body with ash, one should at least apply the *tripuṇḍra* and other such marks.
Meditating upon Śiva— the three-eyed, the substratum of the three qualities (guṇas), and the progenitor of the three Vedas—
one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark on the forehead while reciting "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," and on the two sides [of the forehead] while saying "Iśānābhyāṃ namaḥ."
Having said "Salutation to the two seeds" (*bījābhyām namaḥ*), one should place [the hand] on the two forearms.
One should perform [the offering] below for the two ancestors (*pitṛbhyām*) and likewise above for Umā and Īśa.
Then, one should do so on the back for Bhīma and likewise at the back of the head.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wearing of Ashes," in the Vidyeśvara Saṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Sūta said:
O Śainakarpa, O highly wise one, O great lord whose form is Śiva!
Listen to the majesty of the rudrākṣa; I shall describe it to you in brief.
The rudrākṣa should be known as the most beloved of Śiva and the supreme purifier.
It is remembered as the remover of all sins through seeing, touching, and chanting [it].
O Sage, in former times, the greatness of the rudrākṣa was recounted by Śiva,
the Supreme Self, before the Goddess for the sake of benefiting the world.
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess Maheśāni, to the greatness of the rudrākṣa, O Auspicious One.
Out of love for you and with the desire for the welfare of my devotees, I shall speak of it.
Formerly, O Maheśānī, for thousands of divine years,
while he was performing penance, his mind became agitated; yet, having restrained it, he was [graced] by me,
the independent Supreme Lord who acts for the benefit of the world.
O Supreme Goddess, my eyes were opened by me in sport;
from my two beautiful eyes, drops of water fell.
There, those teardrops became trees known as rudrākṣas.
Having attained a stationary state for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees,
he gave them to the four castes who were devoted to Viṣṇu;
and from the earth, he produced rudrākṣas, which are dear to Śiva.
In Mathurā, Ayodhyā, Laṅkā, and likewise on Mount Malaya;
on the Sahya mountain, in Kāśī, and similarly in ten other places—
[these are] for the purpose of shattering the flood of unbearable sins, as impelled by the Vedas.

By my command, the Rudrākṣas on this earth have arisen as Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; they are auspicious beads belonging to those respective castes. The wise should know their colors to be white, red, yellow, and black, respectively.
The Rudrākṣa should be worn by men according to their own caste, following the sequence of castes; indeed,
that fruit [of each caste] should be worn by those desiring the fruits of enjoyment and liberation,
especially by devotees of Śiva, for the constant pleasure of Śiva and Śivā.
That which is the size of an *dhātrī* fruit is declared to be the best;
however, that which is the size of a *badarī* fruit is proclaimed as middling;
and the lowest would be the size of a *caṇa* grain—this is the procedure taught by the ancients.
Listen with great affection, O Pārvatī, out of a desire for the welfare of devotees.
O Maheśvarī, even that which is as small as a jujube fruit (badarī-phala) indeed yields fruit in this world,
increasing happiness and good fortune.
That which is equal in size to an *dhātrī* fruit destroys all misfortunes (*ariṣṭa*). That which is similar to a *guñjā* berry is the means for accomplishing all goals.
To the extent that it is smaller, it bestows even greater fruit.
The wise have declared that the fruit of each single [Rudrākṣa] is increased by one-tenth;
the wearing of Rudrākṣas is proclaimed as the means for the destruction of sin.
Therefore, it should certainly be worn, for it is the certain means for accomplishing all goals.
O Supreme Goddess, no other rosary is seen in the world that bestows such auspicious fruit as the rudrākṣa. Those beads that are uniform,
smooth, firm, thick, and endowed with thorns are auspicious.

O Goddess, rudrākṣas always grant desires and bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. One should avoid six types of rudrākṣas: those infested with worms, those that are split or cracked, those devoid of thorns, those marked by wounds, and those that are not round.

If a Rudrākṣa has its opening formed by itself, it is considered superior; however, that which is produced through human effort is middling. The wearing of Rudrākṣas, when obtained, brings about the destruction of great sins.

A man who wears [the ashes] in the number of one hundred Rudras becomes one who possesses the form of Rudra himself. The fruit that is obtained here by wearing them eleven hundred times cannot be described even in hundreds of years.
A man of excellent devotion should properly fashion a crown from five hundred Rudrākṣas, using fifty of them for each of the ten thousand [beads]; furthermore,
he may likewise do so with three hundred and sixty beads arranged in three repetitions.
One intent on devotion should fashion a sacred thread (*upavīta*) from *rudrākṣa* beads;
O Maheśvarī, it is taught that there should be three *rudrākṣas* on the crest-lock,
and likewise six each on the left and right ears.

One hundred and one [rods] should be worn on the neck, and eleven on each of the arms; likewise, they should be placed at the elbows and the wrists. Men devoted to the worship of Śiva should wear three sacred threads (upavīta).
One should wear the remaining five Rudrākṣas on the waist. O Supreme Goddess, he by whom Rudrākṣas are worn in this number must be saluted and praised by all like Maheśvara himself.
When one has established people in such a state of meditation through [proper] postures,
and upon seeing them utters "Śiva," they are liberated from sins;
this is the rule proclaimed for a hundred or even a thousand [people].
In the absence of that [the previous method], another auspicious way is proclaimed by me:
one should wear a single rudrākṣa on the topknot, thirty on the head,
fifty on the neck, and sixteen on each of the two arms.
On the wrist, twelve [beads] on each arm, and five hundred on the shoulders;
with one hundred and eight [beads], one should fashion a garland or a sacred thread (upavīta).
Thus, he who is firm in his vow should wear a thousand rudrākṣas.
All the gods bow down to him, for he is just like Rudra himself.
He wears a single rudrākṣa on his crest-lock, forty on his head,
thirty-two around the region of his neck, and one hundred and eight upon his chest.
Six on each ear, sixteen on each of the two arms,
and twice that number [thirty-two] on the two hands according to the Avimāna— O Lord of Sages, he who maintains this numerical devotion is also a supreme devotee of Śiva.

Indeed, he is to be worshipped like Śiva and should be constantly saluted by all. The *Īśāna* mantra should be placed on the head, and the *Tatpuruṣa* mantra on the ears; the *Aghora* mantra should be worn on the throat, and likewise on the heart.
The wise one should wear [the rosary] on his hands with the Aghora-bīja mantra;
on his belly, he should wear one strung with fifteen beads with the Vāmadeva mantra;
and he should wear three or five or seven rosaries as limbs (aṅgas) with the five Brahmans.
Alternatively, one should wear all these [herbs] with the root-mantra (*amūla-mantra*). Thereafter,
one should avoid liquor, meat, garlic, onions, and *śigru*,
as well as the *śleṣmātaka* fruit and the dung of a village pig, in eating.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the white rudrākṣa is prescribed for those of brahminical body;

the bright red for kṣatriyas; the yellow, which is greatly rejoiced in, for vaiśyas; and likewise, the black, which may be cut, broken, split, or cracked, is to be worn daily by śūdras—this is the path declared in the Vedas.
One should regularly wear these—the student, the female ascetic, the householder, and the renunciant—and this supreme secret should not be disclosed to anyone other than a twice-born.
This wearing of the rudrākṣa beads is attainable through meritorious deeds; having abandoned it, people go to all the hells.
First, those that are naturally smaller than an āmalaka fruit, then those that are diseased, those bitten by thorns, those infested with worms, and likewise those lacking the holes for the thread.
Those desiring auspiciousness must certainly wear rudrākṣas, even as much as a single chickpea; for the rudrākṣa is the auspicious emblem of Rudra, O Umā, subtle and always praiseworthy.

By the command of Śiva, rudrākṣas are to be worn at all times by those of all stages of life (āśramas) and castes (varṇas), including women and śūdras; indeed, they are to be worn by ascetics with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).
Bearing [the ashes] made at night during the day, and bearing those made during the day at night—
at dawn, midday, and evening— one is liberated from all sins.
Those in this world who wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and those who wear matted hair (jaṭādhārin), [are likewise purified].
Those who wear rudrākṣas indeed go to the world of Śiva.
He who bears a single rudrākṣa on his head and likewise a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) in the middle of his forehead,
and those who mutter the five-syllabled mantra— they are indeed virtuous men worthy of being honored by you.
"Bring to the abode of Yama anyone on whose limb there is no rudrākṣa, who has no tripuṇḍra on the surface of his forehead,
and who has no five-syllabled mantra in his mouth—
whether they have known its power or not— those who wear the ashes and the rudrākṣas. (Śiva Purāṇa 1.25.51–52ab)
"These venerable ones must always be honored by us; they must never be led away.
Thus did Kāla command his own servants. Accepting this with "So be it," they all remained silent, greatly astonished.

Therefore, O Great Goddess Pārvatī, the Rudrākṣa is the destroyer of even the heaviest sins; it is dear to me, and one who wears it becomes pure even if they have committed great transgressions. He who wears the Rudrākṣa on his hands, his arms, or likewise upon his head—
Invulnerable to all beings, he shall wander upon the earth in the form of Rudra;
he shall always be worthy of salutation by all gods and asuras alike. Indeed, when seen, he shall destroy the sins of those who behold him, just like Śiva himself.
Even one who is not liberated through meditation and knowledge, if he wears a rudrākṣa,
being freed from all sins, attains the supreme goal.
Reciting a mantra with a rudrākṣa, the merit becomes ten million times greater.
A person obtains ten billion-fold merit from merely holding [this mantra].
For as long as that [mantra] remains within the body of a living being,
O Goddess, for that long even a slight death does not afflict him.
Having seen one who is endowed with the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*), whose limbs are adorned with *rudrākṣa* beads,
and who is muttering the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, one obtains the fruit of Rudra;
such a person is dear to the five deities and likewise dear to all the gods.
O beloved, one should recite all mantras with devotion using a rosary of rudrākṣa beads.
Devotees of Viṣṇu and other gods should also wear them, without a doubt;
however, a devotee of Rudra, in particular, should always wear rudrākṣas.

Various types of rudrākṣas have been described; I shall now tell you their distinctions, O Pārvatī, listen with true devotion, for they bestow the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation. A single-faced rudrākṣa is Śiva himself, directly bestowing the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
By the mere sight of him, the sin of killing a Brahmin is dispelled.
Wherever he is worshipped, there Lakṣmī is never far away.
All calamities perish, and indeed all desires are fulfilled.
The Lord of the God of Gods, who has two faces, bestows the fruits of all desires;
specifically, one who possesses rudrākṣas destroys the sin of cow-slaughter swiftly.
That rudrākṣa which has three faces is the direct giver of spiritual accomplishments at all times.
By its power, all the three Vedas shall become firmly established;
Brahmā himself, possessing four faces, removes even the sin of killing a human being.
Through sight and touch, it immediately bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
The five-faced one is Rudra himself, the Lord known by the name Kālāgni;
he is the bestower of liberation from everything and the granter of the fruits of all desires.
[He destroys] the sin of approaching those who should not be approached and the consumption of what should not be eaten.
In this way, the five-faced one removes all sins. By wearing the six-faced Kārttikeya on the right arm, one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
O Maheśānī, the one named Anaṅga has seven faces;
by wearing it, O Goddess of Devas, even a pauper becomes a lord.
And the eight-faced Rudrākṣa is Vasumūrti Bhairava.
By the retention of that [mantra], one attains a full lifespan; upon death, one becomes the wielder of the trident (Śiva).
Bhairava is the nine-faced one, and Kapila is remembered as the sage.
Durgā is the presiding deity of the wind, the Great Goddess in her nine forms.
One who is devoted to me should wear that Rudrākṣa on the left hand;
he will surely become the Lord of All, equal to me, without a doubt.
O Maheśānī, the ten-faced one is indeed the god Janārdana himself.
O Goddess of the gods, by wearing it, one shall obtain all desires.
O Supreme Goddess, that rudrākṣa which has eleven faces, by wearing it along with Rudra,
one shall be victorious everywhere.
One should wear a twelve-faced rudrākṣa on the region of the hair;
for all those twelve Ādityas are likewise stationed there.
A human being who wears a thirteen-faced rudrākṣa becomes the Viśvedevas.
One obtains all desires and attains good fortune and auspiciousness.
Indeed, the fourteen-faced rudrākṣa is Supreme Śiva himself;
whoever wears it upon their head with devotion, all their sins are destroyed.
Thus, O daughter of the Lord of the Mountains, the varieties of rudrākṣas have been declared according to their differences in orientation.
Now, out of affection, hear from me in due order their respective mantras:
1. *aṃ hrīṃ namaḥ* 2. *aṃ namaḥ* 3. *aṃ klīṃ namaḥ* 4. *aṃ hrīṃ namaḥ* 5. *aṃ hrīṃ namaḥ* 6. *aṃ hrīṃ huṃ namaḥ*
6. Aṃ huṃ namaḥ; 7. Aṃ huṃ namaḥ; 8. Aṃ hrīṃ huṃ namaḥ; 9. Aṃ hrīṃ namaḥ namaḥ; 10. Aṃ hrīṃ huṃ namaḥ; 11. Aṃ kroṃ kṣauṃ rauṃ namaḥ; 12. Aṃ hrīṃ namaḥ; 13. Aṃ namaḥ; 14.
Endowed with devotion and faith, this is for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (Śivapurāṇa 1.25.82ab)

One should wear rudrākṣas while reciting mantras, avoiding all indolence. But that man on earth who wears a rudrākṣa without a mantra goes to a terrible hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
Upon seeing one wearing a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas,
as well as the ḍākinīs, śākinīs, and others who cause harm, along with whatever artificial spells, malevolent rites, and the like there may be— [are all rendered powerless].
Seeing him from afar with a suspicious appearance,
yet wearing a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, Śiva, Viṣṇu,
the Goddess, Gaṇapati, Sūrya, and all other gods become pleased, O Pārvatī.
"O Maheśvarī, having thus understood the greatness of the rudrākṣa,
they should be properly worn with mantras and with devotion for the increase of dharma.
Thus was it spoken by Śiva, the Supreme Self, in the presence of Girijā."
The greatness of sacred ash and rudrākṣa bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Those who wear sacred ash and rudrākṣa should be known as exceedingly dear to Śiva;
for by the power of wearing them, one attains both enjoyment and liberation—of this there is no doubt.
He who wears ashes and rudrākṣas is called a devotee of Śiva;
he who is intent on the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra is perfect in the presence of the True One.
[But] without the triple mark of ashes and without a rosary of rudrākṣas...
Even when worshipped, Mahādeva does not grant the desired fruit [without these].
O Lord of Sages, all that was asked has been fully explained:
the greatness of the sacred ash (bhasma) and the rudrākṣa beads, which bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
Whoever should constantly hear this supreme and auspicious majesty of Rudrākṣa and sacred ash with devotion shall obtain all desires;
having enjoyed every happiness in this world, joined by sons, grandsons, and other kin.
In the hereafter, one shall obtain perfect liberation and become exceedingly dear to Śiva.
O lords of sages, this *Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā* has been narrated to you;
by the command of Śiva, it eternally bestows all perfections and grants liberation.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Rudrākṣa," in the Sādhyasādhana-khaṇḍa of the first section, the Vidyeśvara-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
